game-boy__legend-of-zelda-link-s-awakeni.detail: It began as an unofficial „after hours" project by part of the A Link to the Past team and was originally meant to be a port of that game; in the end it grew into a title of its own. It is the first portable Zelda and the first not to take place in Hyrule — the island of Koholint is the dream of a sea creature called the Wind Fish, and the whole world vanishes when you wake him, which gives the game an unexpectedly melancholic tone. It features cameos from the Mario series (Chain Chomps, Goombas), because the team allowed itself to play around. The DX version from 1998 added color and a color dungeon playable only on the Game Boy Color. The 2019 Switch remake confirmed its status as a classic.
game-boy__legend-of-zelda-link-s-awakeni.article:
You wake up in a stranger's bed, the sea murmurs outside the windows, and the first thing you see is a girl leaning over you. No kingdom of Hyrule, no Princess Zelda — Link's Awakening begins with a shipwreck on the island of Koholint, and from the very first minute it makes clear that this is going to be a different Zelda than the one you know.

It came about almost by accident. As an unofficial "after hours" project by part of the team that had just finished A Link to the Past, it was originally meant to be nothing more than a port of that game to the handheld Game Boy. But the developers' enthusiasm turned it into a fully standalone title — the first-ever portable Zelda and the first entry in the series not set in Hyrule. That alone was enough to make it a small revolution.

Mechanically it rests on proven pillars: exploring an intricate world, gradually unlocking new abilities through items, and cleverly built dungeons full of puzzles and keys. On the Game Boy's tiny monochrome screen, the developers managed to cram in a surprisingly rich world with its own logic and rhythm. The game also became famous for how gladly it breaks the fourth wall and enjoys itself — you'll meet Chain Chomps and Goombas from the Mario series here, because the team simply allowed itself to play.

Beneath the playful surface, however, hides a surprisingly melancholic story. The entire island of Koholint is nothing but a dream of a creature called the Wind Fish, and the moment you wake him, everything — including the characters you grew fond of — disappears. This bittersweet premise gives the game an emotional depth no one would expect from a portable action-adventure from 1993, and it still makes it one of the most acclaimed episodes of the series.

In 1998 came the expanded version Link's Awakening DX, which added color and a single color dungeon playable exclusively on the Game Boy Color. And if you had any doubts about its status as a classic, the fully remade version for the Nintendo Switch from 2019, with its charmingly toy-like visuals, confirmed that the dream of Koholint island hasn't aged a day even after decades.

**Why play it:** It is the most personal and dreamlike Zelda, one that managed to conjure up an unforgettable world on the Game Boy's tiny screen.

game-boy__pokemon-red-blue-yellow.teaser: The game that defined the whole „gotta catch 'em all" genre. A cultural phenomenon, not just a game.
game-boy__pokemon-red-blue-yellow.detail: Satoshi Tajiri developed the game over six years, inspired by his childhood hobby — collecting insects. Game Freak was on the brink of collapse, and the game was saved by Shigeru Miyamoto and the idea of releasing two versions that had to be connected via a link cable so the player could catch all 151 Pokémon — a brilliant business and community move. The famous „MissingNo." glitch and Mew, hidden in the game by a developer without management's knowledge, are among the best-known gaming legends. The series is today the most profitable media franchise in the world (ahead of Star Wars and Marvel), and it all started here.
game-boy__pokemon-red-blue-yellow.article:
One hundred fifty-one — that number is known today by anyone who ever held a Game Boy. Pokémon Red and Blue weren't just a game; they were the door to a phenomenon that within a few years swept the entire world, and it began quietly right here, on a gray handheld console.

The idea ripened in Satoshi Tajiri's head for a full six years. He was inspired by his own childhood hobby — catching insects — and a desire to give city kids the feeling of hunting and collecting creatures. Studio Game Freak was meanwhile teetering on the edge of collapse during development, and the game was effectively saved by two things: the support of Shigeru Miyamoto and the brilliant idea of releasing two slightly different versions. To collect all 151 Pokémon, the player had to connect via a link cable with a friend and trade — a business and community move the likes of which no one had seen until then.

The game itself is a surprisingly deep JRPG. You catch creatures in Poké Balls, train them, evolve them, and build a team that has to hold its own in turn-based battles built on a system of strong and weak types. Beneath the accessible surface hides a layer of tactics that players still dissect today. And then there's the legendary layer of secrets: the "MissingNo." glitch, which could scramble your saved game, or the Pokémon Mew, which one of the developers supposedly hid in the code without management's knowledge. These stories have become an immortal part of gaming mythology.

The Yellow version then tied in with the ongoing animated series — your loyal companion became Pikachu, who followed you at every step and changed the mood as well as the difficulty. It was a clever response to how quickly Pokémon had become an unstoppable media machine.

And just how big did it end up being? Pokémon is today the most profitable media franchise in the world — it has surpassed both Star Wars and Marvel. Movies, a card game, anime, toys, dozens of other video games. All of it grew from this single cartridge, where you first chose between Bulbasaur, Charmander, and Squirtle.

**Why play it:** This is where it all began — the roots of the planet's biggest entertainment franchise, and it's still a catchy, addictive, and surprisingly timeless RPG.

game-boy__super-mario-land-2-6-golden-co.teaser: Wario appears here for the first time. Bigger, more colorful, and more playable than the first game.
game-boy__super-mario-land-2-6-golden-co.detail: It was developed by Gunpei Yokoi's team (not the main Mario team, EAD), which is why it has a slightly different „feel." This is the first appearance of **Wario** — he was created as a villain parodying Mario, and his name is a pun: the Japanese „warui" (bad) + Mario. The game has a nonlinear map where you choose the order of worlds, and a bigger, more detailed Mario sprite than the first game. Wario was so popular that he immediately got his own series.
game-boy__super-mario-land-2-6-golden-co.article:
Mario stands before his own castle — and isn't allowed inside. Someone has occupied it, turned the whole island against him, and acts as though he's belonged there all along. That someone is Wario, and Super Mario Land 2 is the game that brought him into the world.

It was developed by Gunpei Yokoi's team at Nintendo R&D1, not the main Mario team EAD, and you can tell. The game has its own, slightly different "feel" — more laid-back, more playful, at times bizarre. Its greatest contribution, though, is the villain: Wario was created as a parody of Mario, his name a pun joining the Japanese "warui" (bad) with Mario, and his greedy, mischievous nature was instantly captivating.

Compared to the austere first game, the sequel took a huge leap forward. Mario's sprite is markedly bigger and more detailed, the world more colorful, and above all — the map is nonlinear. You choose for yourself which of the six worlds to head into and in what order to collect the six golden coins that unlock the path to the final showdown. From a space zone through a giant house to Mario's own castle, the game offers an unexpected variety of settings and ideas.

The gameplay, meanwhile, is exactly that Mario reliability you can count on — precise jumps, secret exits, power-ups including the beloved bunny ears that let Mario glide through the air. On a handheld console it was smooth, readable, and fun, far more so than in the first Super Mario Land.

In the end, Wario steamrolled even the very game he debuted in. He won over players and Nintendo alike so thoroughly that he immediately got his own series — and a parodic villain became one of the most distinctive faces of the brand.

**Why play it:** Bigger, more colorful, and more playable than the first game — and on top of that it's the birth certificate of one of the best side characters Nintendo ever devised.

game-boy__wario-land-super-mario-land-3.teaser: The slower, exploration-focused counterpart to Mario. Collecting treasure and hunting for secret exits is addictive.
game-boy__wario-land-super-mario-land-3.detail: Here Wario was promoted from villain to a playable antihero and defined his own gameplay philosophy: instead of Mario's speed, it's about slow, thorough exploration, smashing walls with his shoulder, and collecting treasure that determines which ending you'll see. The more money you collect, the better the ending. This „loot-driven" mechanic set Wario Land apart from all other platformers and ran through the entire series.
game-boy__wario-land-super-mario-land-3.article:
What happens when you turn a villain into a hero? It's not just the name on the box that changes — the whole philosophy of the game changes. Wario Land took the freshly born villain and built a platformer around him that is the exact opposite of everything you know from Mario.

Mario is about speed, elegance, and smooth forward motion. Wario is about the exact opposite: slow, thorough exploration of every corner. Instead of jumping on enemies' heads, you ram them with your shoulder, smash walls, turn levels inside out, and hunt for secret exits. He's cumbersome but strong, and the whole game is tailored precisely to his stout, coarse personality.

But the heart of it all is loot. Along the way you collect coins and, above all, treasure, and it's the accumulated wealth that determines which ending you'll see — the more money you amass, the better the ending the game grants you. This "loot-driven" mechanic turned Wario's greed into an outright gameplay system and gave the game an entirely different rhythm than classic platformers. Suddenly you're not rushing to the finish but searching every cellar and smashing every suspicious brick.

Wario was thus promoted from a mere antagonist in the previous game to a full-fledged playable antihero with his own identity. He's no cute rescuer of princesses — he's a covetous, selfish looter, and the game has great fun with it. This individuality set it apart from the flood of other platformers of the era and became the cornerstone on which the entire Wario Land series would then stand.

On a handheld console it was a surprisingly extensive and elaborate experience that rewarded curiosity and persistence. Once you get used to Wario's pace, you'll find that searching the levels and chasing hidden coins is unexpectedly addictive.

**Why play it:** It's a clever, loot-driven counterpart to Mario platformers — slower, craftier, and all the more addictive thanks to the chase for treasure and secret exits.

game-boy__tetris.teaser: The pack-in title that sold the Game Boy. Possibly the most perfect puzzle of all time.
game-boy__tetris.detail: The original Tetris was created by Soviet scientist Alexey Pajitnov in 1984 on an Elektronika 60 computer; the rights were for years the subject of international legal chaos across the Cold War. Nintendo fought for the portable rights and bundled the game with the Game Boy — that decided the handheld battle, because adults were buying the console because of Tetris. Over 35 million copies of the GB version were sold. The music „Korobeiniki" (a Russian folk song) became iconic. A perfect example of „easy to learn, impossible to master."
game-boy__tetris.article:
The first block falls, you rotate it, slide it into the gap — and five hours later the falling squares are projected onto the inside of your closed eyelids. Tetris isn't just a game. It's a touchstone of what a perfectly simple idea can do to the human brain.

It was born in 1984 in the head of Soviet scientist Alexey Pajitnov, who programmed it on an Elektronika 60 computer. What followed were years of international legal chaos — the rights to the game were, during the Cold War, bought, sold, and litigated across borders in one of the most tangled disputes in gaming history. Nintendo ultimately fought for the portable rights, and that was the move that decided the entire handheld battle.

Tetris was bundled directly with the Game Boy as a pack-in title. And it was Tetris that sold the console — not to children, but to adults. Passengers on the subway, managers on planes, people who would otherwise never have bought a handheld suddenly found they couldn't stop. Easy to grasp within ten seconds, impossible to master perfectly — that is the definition of the ideal puzzle game.

The music contributed to the magic too. The main melody "Korobeiniki," an arranged Russian folk song, became one of the most iconic gaming tunes ever and to this day is inseparably tied to the falling blocks. The Game Boy's beeping sound gave it just the right hypnotic touch.

The numbers speak clearly: over 35 million copies of this version were sold, placing it among the best-selling video games in history. Tetris became a cultural symbol that transcended the boundaries of media, generations, and ideologies — few games have united such different people over such a simple task.

**Why play it:** Possibly the most perfect puzzle of all time — and the game that literally sold the Game Boy. One round is enough to understand why.

game-boy__kirby-s-dream-land-2.teaser: A cute but surprisingly rich platformer with animal companions and ability combinations.
game-boy__kirby-s-dream-land-2.detail: The second installment brought a key novelty: three animal companions (Rick the hamster, Kine the fish, and Coo the owl) who change how Kirby's copied abilities work — ability + animal combinations yield dozens of variants. It was directed by Masahiro Sakurai (later the creator of Super Smash Bros.). The game hides a true ending available only after collecting all the Rainbow Drops, which gives you a reason for careful exploration.
game-boy__kirby-s-dream-land-2.article:
A pink ball that swallows an enemy and steals its ability — players already knew that from Kirby. What they didn't expect, though, was a gang of animal friends who can turn that single ability into dozens of brand-new ones. Kirby's Dream Land 2 took the proven idea and cleverly multiplied it.

The key novelty is three animal companions: Rick the hamster, Kine the fish, and Coo the owl. Each of them changes how Kirby's copied abilities work. The same fire ability behaves completely differently when you ride Rick, swim with Kine, or float with Coo — and from the ability-plus-animal combinations arises a whole array of variants that invite experimentation. What was a simple "swallow and imitate" mechanic became a surprisingly rich toy.

It was directed by Masahiro Sakurai, the same creator who would later spawn the phenomenon Super Smash Bros. His signature shows in the thoughtful yet accessible design — the game can be cute and welcoming at first glance, but beneath the surface it hides depth for those who want more.

And it's precisely for them that the true ending exists. It's available only to whoever collects all the so-called Rainbow Drops, hidden in hard-to-reach places across the worlds. Suddenly you have a solid reason to search every level thoroughly, not just run to the exit. This layer of collecting gives the otherwise undemanding game unexpected replayability.

On the monochrome Game Boy, Dream Land 2 also excels in craftsmanship — readable graphics, pleasant pacing, and that unmistakable Kirby serenity that makes playing a balm for the nerves. It's a platformer that doesn't want to punish but to reward curiosity and play.

**Why play it:** A cute platformer with unexpected depth, where the combinations of abilities and animal companions and the hunt for the true ending give you a reason to come back again and again.

game-boy__donkey-kong.teaser: A brilliant hybrid of platformer and puzzle game; 100+ levels, far beyond the original arcade.
game-boy__donkey-kong.detail: Under the guise of an arcade remake hides what is essentially a new game: after four classic levels, 97 more open up, where the goal is to get the key to the door using acrobatics — Mario can do a backflip, a handstand, a triple jump, and lift objects over his head, a repertoire he had nowhere else. It was the first game to support the Super Game Boy (borders and colors on the SNES). By design it foreshadowed the Mario vs. Donkey Kong series.
game-boy__donkey-kong.article:
To hide, under the label „remake of an old arcade game," one of the most inventive games on the Game Boy — that was a move worthy of a master. Donkey Kong from 1994, known among fans as **Donkey Kong '94**, starts out exactly as you'd expect: four classic levels in which Mario climbs after the kidnapped Pauline and dodges the barrels DK hurls from above. And then, at the moment you feel it's all over, the game only truly opens up — and dumps another ninety-seven levels of an entirely new type on you.

This is no longer a race upward. It's a puzzle platformer in which the goal of each floor is to find and grab the key and carry it to the door. That means manipulating the environment, moving objects, timing moving platforms, and pulling levers — and above all learning to control Mario in ways he never could before or since. He can do a backflip, a handstand, a triple jump, he can lift an enemy or object over his head and throw it, climb a ladder, and do a backflip off a handstand. This acrobatic repertoire makes the character an unexpectedly flexible tool and turns every level into a little puzzle about movement.

It was built by Nintendo R&D1 — the incubator that also produced Metroid and the Game Boy itself — and the game proudly embraced new hardware peripherals: it was one of the first titles to support the **Super Game Boy**, thanks to which players could play it on a TV via the SNES, with color and decorative borders around the image. That turned a rather modest-looking handheld game into a bit of an event.

What still fascinates about Donkey Kong '94 today is its pacing and structure. A hundred-plus levels gradually add new elements — elevators, conveyors, switches, colored doors — and the game doles them out with such patience that you never feel overwhelmed. Now and then you also encounter a boss fight, with Donkey Kong in the lead role of course, so the classic motif never fully disappears. It's a display of design confidence: taking a forty-year-old arcade concept and building something much bigger on top of it, without betraying its spirit.

The influence of this game, meanwhile, is tangible. Its design DNA — a Mario who solves puzzles rather than jumps on enemies, and Donkey Kong as the opponent in puzzle scenes — later crystallized into the entire **Mario vs. Donkey Kong** series, which builds on this foundation to this day. Few „hidden" titles in Mario's catalog had such a long reach.

**Why play it:** It's one of the cleverest hybrids of platformer and puzzle game on the Game Boy, and Mario in it can do things he never showed anywhere else — a hundred levels that age more slowly than most modern games.

game-boy__metroid-ii-return-of-samus.teaser: A dark, claustrophobic hunting expedition. It was ahead of its time in atmosphere.
game-boy__metroid-ii-return-of-samus.detail: The only Metroid on the original (monochrome) Game Boy and long the most overlooked entry. The task is explicit — exterminate the entire Metroid species on their home planet — and a counter of remaining units replaces the map as your guide. This is the first appearance of the baby Metroid and the Queen Metroid, key to the plot of Super Metroid. Fans created the acclaimed remake AM2R (2016), and Nintendo then made its own Samus Returns (2017).
game-boy__metroid-ii-return-of-samus.article:
A gray monochrome display you almost have to bite into to make out what's crouching in front of you — and yet Metroid II breathes more atmosphere than many of today's games in full color. This is the only Metroid ever released on the original black-and-white Game Boy, and for many years also the most overlooked entry in the series. Unjustly.

The task this time is brutally clear and, frankly, chilling: Samus Aran receives orders to descend to the Metroids' home planet and exterminate the entire species. No visual guide in the form of a classic map — instead the game is driven by a counter. On screen you see how many Metroids remain to be eliminated, and only when their number drops does the acid level recede and open your path deeper into the planet. It's an elegant solution to the hardware's limits: forward progress directly reflects your completion of the mission, so you never feel lost even though the surrounding world is a labyrinth of corridors and shafts.

The work of Nintendo R&D1 rests above all on atmosphere. Claustrophobic tunnels, loneliness, the ticking counter, and the gradual transformations of the Metroids — from larva to alpha, gamma, zeta, omega — create the feeling of a scientific hunting expedition into a hostile nest. Here the game is ahead in something: the oppressive, almost horror-like tone that Super Metroid would refine to perfection a few years later is born right here, in four shades of gray.

Metroid II is moreover not just an interlude. For the series' mythology it is absolutely crucial. Here you first encounter the **baby Metroid**, whose relationship with Samus becomes the emotional core of Super Metroid, and here you first face the **Queen Metroid**. The entire story arc on which one of the most revered games of the nineties stands has its roots in this underrated handheld expedition.

What best testifies to its significance, in the end, is how much love others devoted to it. The fan remake **AM2R (Another Metroid 2 Remake)** from 2016 was received enthusiastically as one of the best fan projects ever, and Nintendo shortly thereafter released its own official remake **Metroid: Samus Returns** (2017) on the 3DS. A game that few took seriously for years thus doubly earned its return to the spotlight.

**Why play it:** In atmosphere and dread it was ahead of its time and laid the story foundations of Super Metroid — anyone who wants to understand where Samus comes from must descend here.

game-boy__mega-man-v.teaser: The peak of the GB Mega Mans with its own bosses (not NES recycling). Excellent level design.
game-boy__mega-man-v.detail: The fifth and last of the GB Mega Mans and the only one with entirely original bosses (the Stardroids named after planets), instead of recycling the eight from the NES games. Mega Man here gains a robot dog helper, Tango, and the powerful Mega Arm weapon (a launching fist). Considered the best of the handheld five; it came out late and in small numbers, so it's expensive for collectors.
game-boy__mega-man-v.article:
The fifth and final stop of the blue bomber on the Game Boy — and at the same time the one fans swear by. Mega Man V from 1994 did something the previous handheld entries hadn't dared: it stopped recycling and struck out entirely on its own.

The Game Boy Mega Mans up to then worked cleverly but cautiously — they always mixed bosses and ideas from two different NES entries and assembled a handheld game from them. The fifth threw that habit off the table. It brings a completely **original gallery of bosses** — the so-called Stardroids named after planets of the solar system (Mercury, Venus, Mars, and others) — so for the first time you play against enemies you'll meet nowhere else. This gives the whole game its own identity, its own level design, and the feeling that it's not an echo but a full-fledged entry.

The tools in hand are new too. Mega Man here gets a robot companion — a dog named **Tango** who can curl into a ball and attack enemies — and above all the **Mega Arm** weapon, a launching fist that replaces the classic buster and can be charged and upgraded with acquired abilities. This gives the gameplay a fresh rhythm, and the game feels as though it finally allowed itself to experiment with what Mega Man can do.

The level design is often praised as the best of the entire handheld five — carefully built stretches, readable and fair challenges, and the traditional Mega Man structure where a defeated boss hands over a weapon usable against the next one. Capcom (with development in cooperation with Minakuchi Engineering) demonstrated here that even on a small screen the series can maintain its famous balance between difficulty and fairness.

There is, however, one catch that turned the game into a collector's idol: it came out **late and in small numbers**, at a stage when interest in the monochrome Game Boy was already waning. Original cartridges are therefore rare today, and on the collectors' market their price regularly climbs high. For a long time it was one of those titles fans spoke of with reverence but few held in hand — until a later digital release made it accessible to a wider audience.

**Why play it:** The peak of the Game Boy Mega Mans with its own bosses and clever novelties — not only the best of the handheld five, but also a rightly prized rarity.

game-boy__final-fantasy-adventure.teaser: The roots of the Mana series; an action RPG that had no rival on the handheld.
game-boy__final-fantasy-adventure.detail: Despite the name Final Fantasy, it is the first game of the **Mana** series (Seiken Densetsu in Japan) and a spin-off, not a main FF. It combines real-time action combat à la Zelda with an RPG system of experience and equipment — a rarity on the Game Boy at the time. The music is by Kenji Ito. It received a remake (Adventures of Mana, 2016). It laid the foundations for Secret of Mana.
game-boy__final-fantasy-adventure.article:
A game whose name is something of a lie — and yet one of the most important mix-ups in the history of Japanese RPGs. Final Fantasy Adventure from 1991 is, despite its name, not a Final Fantasy at all. It is the first installment of the series that would later become known as **Mana** (Seiken Densetsu in Japan), and the Final Fantasy brand ended up on the box overseas mainly to help sell an unknown newcomer.

What Square offered was almost unheard-of on the portable hardware of the time: an action RPG taking place in real time. Instead of the turn-based battles console RPGs were used to, here you swing your sword directly, dodge, time your attacks — the combat resembles Zelda more than classic Final Fantasy. But on top of that a full-blooded RPG system is added: experience, levels, equipment, magic, and an inventory. This combination of instant action and character building made Final Fantasy Adventure an absolute rarity without rival on the Game Boy.

The composer **Kenji Ito** contributed to the music, and his melodies gave the game a surprisingly rich and moving tone you wouldn't expect from the Game Boy's four-channel chip. Together with a more serious, at times downright melancholic story about a knight, a girl, and the Mana tree, it made the title an experience you remember longer than many a more expansive console game.

The significance of this game lies above all in what it started. The mechanics and world Square first tried out here became the foundation for **Secret of Mana** on the SNES — one of the most beloved action RPGs ever — and the entire subsequent Mana series. Final Fantasy Adventure is thus not a dead end nor a mere spin-off, but the root of a branching and revered family tree.

That it's a classic worth rediscovering was confirmed by the remake **Adventures of Mana** (2016), which brought the original game into a more modern form for mobiles and the PlayStation Vita and reminded everyone how timeless its foundation was. Even after years, Final Fantasy Adventure remains a demonstration of how a big story can be told on a tiny screen.

**Why play it:** The roots of the Mana series and an action RPG that had no rival on the Game Boy — historically pivotal and still playable ancestor of Secret of Mana.

game-boy__gargoyle-s-quest.teaser: A Ghosts 'n Goblins spin-off with RPG elements; cult and unexpectedly deep.
game-boy__gargoyle-s-quest.detail: A Ghosts 'n Goblins spin-off where you play as an enemy from that series — the winged demon Firebrand. It combines side-scrolling platformer action stretches with a top-down overworld and RPG progression (you extend flight duration, health, strength). An unusually deep structure for the Game Boy. It got an NES prequel (Gargoyle's Quest II) and an SNES entry (Demon's Crest).
game-boy__gargoyle-s-quest.article:
What if that annoying winged demon who made your life miserable in Ghosts 'n Goblins became the main hero? It's on exactly this cheeky question that Gargoyle's Quest from 1990 rests — a spin-off in which you don't play as the knight Arthur but as one of his enemies. You take on a winged demon named **Firebrand**, and suddenly you're looking at the whole world from the other side.

Capcom didn't stop at a simple role reversal, though. Gargoyle's Quest is a surprisingly deep game that blends several genres at once. Most of the time you move through side-scrolling platformer stretches where Firebrand uses his most characteristic ability — he can hover in the air for a limited time and cling to walls, which gives movement an entirely different logic than ordinary jumping. Between the action passages, however, you find yourself on a **top-down overworld** reminiscent of an RPG, where you meet characters, enter towns, and advance the story.

And it's precisely the RPG layer that lifts the game above an ordinary spin-off. Firebrand grows over the course of the adventure: the duration of his flight lengthens, his health increases, his attacks grow stronger. This progression gives the gameplay structure and a reason to explore — on the Game Boy in 1990 it was an unusually ambitious fusion of action and character building that made the title a cult affair among connoisseurs.

The game's tone is dark and distinctive, far from the cheerful colors of other handheld titles, and Firebrand as an antihero lends the whole expedition a character of its own. It's no wonder that this character and his world earned sequels across platforms — Capcom followed up the success with the NES prequel **Gargoyle's Quest II** and later the culminating SNES entry **Demon's Crest**, which took the concept to a visually rich form.

Gargoyle's Quest thus remains one of those titles that define why it's worth digging through the Game Boy catalog even beyond the biggest names. It's a small but confident work that proves even a side character can yield a surprisingly rich adventure.

**Why play it:** A cult Ghosts 'n Goblins spin-off that combines platforming, RPG progression, and a dark atmosphere — and kicked off a prized trilogy capped by Demon's Crest.

game-boy__castlevania-adventure.teaser: A demanding classic; more a historical milestone than a smooth ride.
game-boy__castlevania-adventure.detail: The very first portable Castlevania and a Game Boy launch title. You play as Christopher Belmont, an ancestor of Simon. It's slow and stiff (no multi-directional attack, the whip upgrades but you lose it when hit), today more of historical interest. It got an improved remake (The Adventure ReBirth, 2009). The direct successor, Belmont's Revenge, is significantly better.
game-boy__castlevania-adventure.article:
There are games you love for how smoothly they run, and then there are games you revere for where they stood at the beginning of the journey. Castlevania: The Adventure belongs unambiguously to the second category. When it arrived in 1989 as one of the first titles for the freshly released Game Boy, it was the very first portable Castlevania in history — and with it Konami sent a clear message: even this iconic series belongs in your pocket.

You play as **Christopher Belmont**, ancestor of the legendary Simon, and set out on the classic route across Dracula's castle with a whip in hand. The series' basic DNA is unquestionably present here — the gothic atmosphere, the stairs, the chasms, the skeletons, and the final clash with the lord of darkness. But the monochrome Game Boy and the console's early era took their toll. Christopher moves **slowly**, lacks a multi-directional attack, and the upgraded whip you laboriously earn is lost again after a single hit. That makes playing an exercise in patience, where every jump across a chasm feels like a life-or-death bet. All the more, though, the period atmosphere shines: Castlevania's music always belonged to the best Konami could do, and even in its stripped-down Game Boy form the melodies retain that unmistakable gothic urgency that pulls you onward even in moments when the controls betray you.

It's precisely this stiffness that's the reason The Adventure is viewed today more as a **historically interesting milestone** than a smooth experience. The difficulty here often stems from technical limitations and controls, not clever design — a difference a seasoned player senses immediately. The game doesn't punish you because it wants to, but because it simply couldn't do otherwise. Whoever makes it through the entire castle all the way to Dracula comes away more with the feeling of a conquered summit than the joy of smooth action.

Konami was aware of this relic's value and in 2009 released the significantly improved remake **The Adventure ReBirth** as part of WiiWare, which wrapped the original skeleton in a modern pixel-art presentation and fairer design. If you're drawn to the story of Christopher Belmont in its best form, reach instead for the direct sequel **Castlevania II: Belmont's Revenge** — it's a game several classes better, one that showed what a GB Castlevania could really do.

The Adventure thus remains above all a chapter in the textbooks. It's a title you admire more for the courage to bring gothic horror onto a gray-green display in 1989 than one you'd return to regularly. For a fan of the series it's a mandatory stop; for the ordinary player, more of a museum exhibit.

**Why play it:** If you're interested in the roots of the portable Castlevania and want to experience firsthand where the series began on the handheld — otherwise jump straight to the better successor, Belmont's Revenge.

game-boy__kid-dracula.teaser: A lighthearted, funny Castlevania spin-off. A hidden Konami treasure.
game-boy__kid-dracula.detail: A self-parodying detour from the Castlevania universe: you play as a cute little Dracula who tosses spells and projectiles instead of cracking a whip. Originally released on the Famicom (1990, Japan only), the GB version is a remake with new elements. Its lighthearted tone and colorful design make it the complete opposite of the serious Castlevania. Western players remained unaware of it for a long time.
game-boy__kid-dracula.article:
What happens when a series famous for gothic horror and whipping the undead decides to poke fun at itself? You get Kid Dracula — a mischievous, colorful and surprisingly adorable spin-off from the Castlevania universe that is its perfect opposite. Instead of a grim Belmont, you play as a tiny, irresistibly cute Dracula who deals with enemies not by whipping them, but by hurling spells and magic projectiles.

With this title, Konami showed it could be playful too. The premise is pure self-parody: all those spine-chilling motifs the series was built on are deliberately turned inside out into a cartoonish adventure. The gameplay is brisker and breezier than in the parent series — it focuses on firing projectiles, collecting abilities and traversing cleverly designed levels laced with tongue-in-cheek detail at every turn. It is a platformer that mainly wants to entertain you, not break you.

Kid Dracula's roots reach deeper than you might expect. It originally launched on the **Famicom in 1990 exclusively in Japan**, so for the Western world it long remained an unknown treasure. The 1993 Game Boy version is essentially a remake that brings its own new elements and adapts the game to the handheld format. For players outside Japan it was for years the only way to experience this little joke at all — and even then, hardly anyone knew about it.

That is exactly why Kid Dracula earned its reputation as a **hidden Konami gem**. It is a title easily overlooked in the shadow of the serious Castlevania entries, yet it rewards anyone who gives its lighthearted tone and colorful design a chance. It works wonderfully as a palate cleanser — short, funny and packed with a distinctive humor you would never expect from a brand associated with vampires and tombs.

Today, as collectors and retro fans once again dig through the forgotten corners of gaming history, Kid Dracula is finally getting the attention it deserves. It is a charming reminder that even the most serious series sometimes need to stick out their tongue and laugh at themselves.

**Why play it:** An adorable, funny self-parody of Castlevania and a genuine hidden Konami treasure for anyone who wants something unexpectedly cheerful from the vampire brand.

game-boy__bionic-commando.teaser: No jumping, just grappling — addictively different controls.
game-boy__bionic-commando.detail: Built on a single bold design choice: the hero **cannot jump**. All vertical movement is handled by firing and swinging on a mechanical arm (grapple), creating a unique rhythm no other action game ever had. The version is based on the NES classic. The mechanic was so distinctive that Capcom returned to it in a modern 3D reboot (2009).
game-boy__bionic-commando.article:
What if an action game designer took away your jump button? It sounds like sabotage — and yet from exactly this bold, seemingly suicidal idea came one of the most distinctive experiences on the Game Boy. Capcom's Bionic Commando stakes its entire existence on a single rule: **the hero cannot jump.**

All vertical movement is therefore handled solely by the mechanical arm — you fire the grapple, latch onto a ceiling or ledge, and swing yourself up. It sounds limiting, but the result is an utterly **unique rhythm of movement** that no other action game of the era offered. Instead of mindlessly mashing jump, you have to plan every swing, read the level layout and perceive space in a completely different way. What looks like a handicap quickly turns into an addictive, almost dance-like flow of movement that cannot be mistaken for anything else.

The Game Boy version is based on the **NES classic** and carries its concept onto the small screen with surprising fidelity. The action alternates shooting, collecting equipment and progressing through varied levels, but it always comes back to that one defining mechanic — the arm. That is precisely why the game still holds cult status: it is not just another run-and-gun, but a design gem that proves how radically a single limitation can change the entire feel of playing.

The grappling mechanic ultimately proved so strong and distinctive that Capcom proudly returned to it many years later. The modern **3D reboot from 2009** built its entire identity on swinging with the bionic arm — proof that an idea born in the eight-bit era carried a timeless power within it. Few game mechanics survive two decades so untouched.

Bionic Commando on the Game Boy is thus not just a clever port, but a small lesson in game design. It reminds us that sometimes a single bold decision — like taking away the player's most basic ability — is all it takes to create an experience you never forget.

**Why play it:** An action game without jumping, where swinging on the grapple creates a rhythm you will not experience anywhere else — a bold design that has held up even after decades.

game-boy__operation-c.teaser: Contra on a handheld that works better than it should.
game-boy__operation-c.detail: The third Contra and the first portable one (released in Europe as „Probotector“ with robots instead of humans due to violence censorship). It alternates side-scrolling and top-down levels like Super C, keeps the series' iconic weapons (spread, laser) and its brutal pace on the small screen. Short but intense.
game-boy__operation-c.article:
When you say Contra, most players picture a TV, two controllers and a screen overflowing with lead. Could this brutal, adrenaline-fueled series really be squeezed onto an unlit gray-green display? Operation C proves that it can — and that it works better than any reasonable expectation would allow.

This is the **third Contra in order and the very first portable one** in the series' history. Konami did not take the path of least resistance. The game faithfully carries over everything that made Contra Contra: the frantic pace, one-hit death and, of course, the **iconic arsenal of weapons** led by the legendary spread shot and laser. Just like Super C, Operation C alternates **side-scrolling and top-down levels**, so it never slides into monotony even on the small screen — it constantly changes both the perspective and the way you have to fight your way through hordes of enemies.

The title's European history is intriguing too. Due to the era's sensitivity toward depictions of violence, the game was released on the old continent under the name **„Probotector“**, where robots replaced the human soldiers — the same fate that befell other entries in the series in Europe. Under the hood, though, it was the same uncompromising action, just with different cosmetics for the heroes.

What sets Operation C apart from the home console entries is its tightness. It is **short but all the more intense** — a concentrated dose of Contra madness you can beat in one sitting, yet one that still forces you to break a serious sweat. No dead spots, no padding; just pure, dense action from the first level to the last. On a handheld, where you often only dip in for a moment, it is actually the ideal format.

In the end, Operation C belongs among those handheld conversions that deserve respect. Instead of a gutted substitute, it offers a full-fledged piece of the series that understands why people love Contra, and it manages to preserve that essence even at a much smaller scale. For fans of the run-and-gun genre, it is small proof that screen size does not determine intensity.

**Why play it:** A full-fledged, uncompromising Contra in your pocket — a short but brutally intense dose of run-and-gun action that unexpectedly excels on the small screen.

game-boy__trip-world.teaser: A Sunsoft curiosity with gorgeous animation; rare and beloved.
game-boy__trip-world.detail: A cult rarity famed for its gorgeous, fluid animation (Sunsoft were masters) and an unusually peaceful tone — the hero Yacopu can transform into different forms and some enemies do not harm him at all. It released only in Japan and Europe, never in the US, which makes it extremely rare and expensive. More of a dreamlike experience than a challenge.
game-boy__trip-world.article:
Some games we remember not for the challenge they threw at us, but for the feeling they left behind. Trip World is exactly that kind of title — a dreamy, peaceful and visually enchanting piece that stands out on the Game Boy like a rare jewel among stones. Here Sunsoft showed off what they did best: **gorgeous, fluid animation** you would hardly expect from a gray-green display.

From the very first moment it is clear that this is no ordinary platformer. The hero Yacopu can **transform into various forms**, changing how he moves and interacts with the world around him. But the most unusual part comes when you run into enemies — and discover that **some of them do not harm you at all.** Trip World refuses the logic on which the overwhelming majority of action games rest. Instead of constant conflict, it offers space for discovery, observation and almost meditative wandering.

This unusually gentle tone makes it more of a **dreamlike experience than a test of reflexes**. It is not a game you „beat“; it is a game you walk through and let wash over you. Sunsoft were masters of the technical side at the time, and every frame of animation, every fluid movement of the character proves it. Trip World feels as if someone took an animated fairy tale and breathed life into it on a handheld console.

It earned its reputation as a cult rarity partly because of its scarcity. **It released only in Japan and Europe and never officially reached the United States** — and it is precisely this absence that over time turned it into an extremely sought-after and expensive collector's piece. What was originally a regional oversight is today among the most coveted titles in the GB library.

Trip World thus remains quiet proof that a game need not be hard or long to leave a mark. It is a small work of art that fans pass around almost like a secret tip — and one that rewards anyone looking for something truly different on the Game Boy.

**Why play it:** A dreamy, peaceful platformer with gorgeous Sunsoft animation — a rare and beloved piece that offers a poetic experience rather than a challenge.

game-boy__avenging-spirit.teaser: You play a ghost that possesses enemies and uses their abilities. An original idea.
game-boy__avenging-spirit.detail: An original mechanic: you are the ghost of a murdered person and you survive only by possessing enemies and using their bodies and abilities. When the host body runs out of health, you have a few seconds to jump into another one, or you vanish. A port of an arcade game; a cutely dark premise. The main character appeared as a cameo in the modern Shantae.
game-boy__avenging-spirit.article:
Most action games cast you as a hero of flesh and blood. Avenging Spirit, however, has one fundamental catch: you are already dead. You play the **ghost of a murdered person** who survives thanks to a single brilliantly morbid mechanic — he must **possess the bodies of enemies** and use them as temporary vessels and as a source of abilities. It is an idea so original that it is worth trying on its own.

The entire gameplay revolves around this premise. As a defenseless ghost you cannot exist alone for long; you need to slip inside an enemy and take over both his body and his arsenal. Each opponent works differently — one can shoot, another jumps higher, a third is tougher — so you are constantly weighing **which body is worth grabbing right now**. And when a host runs out of health, you have only a few seconds to jump into the next one, or your soul dissolves for good. This race against the clock adds a tense tactical dimension to otherwise straightforward action.

Avenging Spirit is a **port of an arcade game**, and its pace reflects that — brisk, action-focused and about pushing through levels. But the cutely dark premise of a ghost borrowing other people's bodies lends it a distinctiveness that a lot of period platformers lacked. It is not just more running and shooting; it is an idea that changes the way you think about playing.

Interestingly, this game's main character eventually found its way into the modern era too. It appeared as a **cameo in one of the games in the Shantae series**, a lovely nod to a title that would otherwise easily fade among hundreds of other GB games. It is a small thing, but for fans a pleasant bridge between forgotten classic and the contemporary indie scene.

In the end, Avenging Spirit is exactly the type of game worth rediscovering — proof that a creative idea can create an unmistakable experience even on limited hardware. If conventional action games tire you, this possessed expedition offers a refreshing change of perspective.

**Why play it:** The original enemy-possession mechanic turns an ordinary action platformer into an unexpectedly tactical and unforgettable experience with a morbidly clever idea.

game-boy__dr-mario.teaser: A „match-three“ puzzle with viruses; endlessly replayable, ideal for short sessions.
game-boy__dr-mario.detail: A match-puzzle where you drop two-colored „megavitamins“ onto viruses and wipe them out by matching four colors in a row. It emerged in parallel with the Tetris craze and released simultaneously on the NES and GB. The „Fever“ and „Chill“ music are iconic. Excellent two-player versus mode. Still the foundation of its own mini-series today.
game-boy__dr-mario.article:
Mario set aside his plumbing tools, put on a white coat and picked up a syringe — and in doing so gave the world one of the most addictive brainteasers ever to run on a small screen. **Dr. Mario** was born in the studios of Nintendo R&D1 at exactly the time Tetris mania was turning the handheld market upside down, and it cleverly rode the same puzzle wave — but with its own perfectly recognizable character.

The principle is beautifully simple: two-colored „megavitamins“ fall into a bottle and your task is to stack them so that four squares of the same color in a row or column wipe out viruses of that same color. The fewer viruses remain, the tenser the game — the last two or three pieces can hide in the corners and force you into risky combinations. From the plain idea of „match four colors“ comes a game you learn in thirty seconds but never quite beat.

Unlike many clones of the time, Dr. Mario had a distinctive signature in its sound too. The two musical themes — the brisk **Fever** and the more relaxed **Chill** — are among the best that Nintendo's composers ever wrote for the puzzle genre, and they still appear in remixes across the Smash Bros. and Mario series. The game released simultaneously on the NES and Game Boy, so it quickly made its way into living rooms and pockets alike.

Where Dr. Mario truly comes alive is the two-player versus mode. Two players connected by a link cable make each other's lives miserable, filling the opponent's screen stretches nerves to breaking point, and the calm elimination of germs turns into an adrenaline-fueled battle. It is this competitive layer that made the game a party staple and the reason people keep coming back to it for decades.

The phenomenon was so strong that Dr. Mario kicked off its own little series that lives on today in the form of newer versions and mobile adaptations. It is a textbook example of Nintendo's feel for a mechanic that cannot be improved by adding — only by fine-tuning every detail.

**Why play it:** If you want a perfectly polished puzzle for five minutes or five hours and have a friend on hand for a versus match, Dr. Mario is an addictive classic that has not aged a day.

game-boy__kwirk.teaser: A Sokoban by Atlus with humor; pure logic.
game-boy__kwirk.detail: The first internationally released game by Atlus (today famous thanks to Persona). Sokoban-like logic with humor: as a tomato named „Kwirk“ you push crates, rotate panels and overcome obstacles across the floors of a vegetable tower. Clean, gradually escalating logic; there is a mode of randomly generated puzzles for endless playability.
game-boy__kwirk.article:
Before Atlus became synonymous with stylish Japanese RPGs and the Persona series, it set off into the world with a tomato. **Kwirk** was the very first game Atlus released internationally, and instead of demons and urban legends it offered pure, smiling logic — the hero, after all, is an anthropomorphic tomato with a hearty dose of humor.

Mechanically it is a variation on the Sokoban genre: you move across the floors of a kind of vegetable tower, and to reach the exit you have to push crates, rotate panels and overcome holes and obstacles in the right order. Each room is a self-contained puzzle chamber where a poorly executed move can jam the whole solution and force you to think a step ahead. The gradual escalation of difficulty is exactly what you want from a good logic title — it starts gently and soon you have to plan your moves like chess.

Kwirk, however, does not take itself seriously, and that is part of its charm. The slightly goofy tone, the greengrocer setting and the cute protagonist turn an otherwise austere genre into a pleasantly accessible experience. The game also offers two approaches: a story progression through the tower and a mode with randomly assembled puzzles, which practically means an endless supply of new challenges for players who cannot get enough logic.

For the monochrome Game Boy it was the ideal type of game — no demands on color, an audio show or fast reflexes, just you, the grid and your head. It is precisely such titles that made the handheld a great travel companion, when you could solve one room in a queue and another on the bus.

Today Kwirk is mainly a historically interesting curiosity — the first step of a company that later rewrote the rules of the genre RPG — and at the same time an honestly designed logic game that stands on its own.

**Why play it:** Clean, gradually escalating Sokoban logic with a smile on your face and an endless puzzle mode; ideal for anyone who enjoys thinking without time pressure.

game-boy__mole-mania.teaser: A Miyamoto-produced puzzle where you dig underground. An underrated gem.
game-boy__mole-mania.detail: One of the few titles produced directly by Shigeru Miyamoto, and yet almost unknown. As a mole named Muddy you move both above and below ground (two planes) and solve spatial puzzles — pushing black balls, digging tunnels, searching for children. A clever two-plane mechanic; Miyamoto called it one of his favorite games that nobody played.
game-boy__mole-mania.article:
There are games that their own creator speaks of as a gem nobody played — and **Mole Mania** is exactly that case. Behind it stands a name that draws in every fan the moment they see it on the box: Shigeru Miyamoto, one of the few titles he personally oversaw the production of, and yet it stayed in the background of his fame.

You play as a mole named Muddy, who sets out to save his family, and the whole ingenious mechanic rests on a single idea: the world has two planes. You move both on the surface and underground, digging freely between them. This opens up spatial puzzles you will not find elsewhere — you push large black balls, tunnel under them from one side to the other, dig passages beneath obstacles and surface exactly where the solution requires. Switching between „above“ and „below“ changes from a simple trick into a clever logical tool that the game gradually develops into surprisingly complex challenges.

Game Boy R&D1 did meticulous work: the controls are brisk, the presentation adorable, and each new area adds a variable that changes how you think about space. It is not a race against time or a test of reflexes, but a calm, clever challenge that rewards planning and experimentation.

So why does almost no one know the game? It released late in the life cycle of the original Game Boy, when attention was already turning to its color successors, and it never got a big marketing campaign or a sequel to keep its name in the spotlight. Miyamoto himself repeatedly mentioned it as one of his favorite underrated works — and that is a recommendation that carries weight.

Today Mole Mania is exactly the kind of hidden treasure that makes it worth digging through the Game Boy catalog to the very end.

**Why play it:** A clever two-plane puzzle game from the workshop of Miyamoto himself; an underrated gem offering calm, cunning puzzles and the magic of „how did nobody play this.“

game-boy__boxxle.detail: The official portable version of **Sokoban** (1981), the forefather of all „push the crate onto the target“ puzzles. No enemies, no timer — just pure spatial logic, where a wrong move can jam the level and you have to start over. Hundreds of levels of rising difficulty. For lovers of hard brainteasers, a meditative classic.
game-boy__boxxle.article:
Sometimes a single idea — a crate and a target square — is all it takes to create a genre that survives for decades. **Boxxle** is the official portable form of **Sokoban**, a puzzle from 1981 that is the forefather of all games where you push a crate to a designated spot. On the small screen of the Game Boy, this pure idea proved to be perfectly at home.

The rules are ascetically simple: crates stand on a grid and you have to get them onto marked squares. The catch is that a crate can only be pushed, never pulled, so one hasty step can shove a crate into a corner from which there is no way out — and you have to start the whole level over. No enemies, no time pressure, no power-ups. Just space, your foresight and hundreds of levels of rising devilishness.

Boxxle's strength lies precisely in that austerity. Where other games distract with a graphical show, here nothing remains but logic. Each room is a self-contained puzzle you have to solve in your head before you make the first move — and the satisfaction when the last crate finally clicks into place is all the purer.

This type of game was made for a handheld console. Sokoban's monochrome display was entirely sufficient, the game could be put down and picked up anywhere, and one solved level was the ideal dose for a moment of waiting. Boxxle made sure that classic computer logic reached your pocket too.

For lovers of hard brainteasers it remains to this day a meditative, almost zen classic — a game in which time flows differently and where every click means a small victory of reason over chaos.

**Why play it:** Straightforward yet devilishly clever Sokoban logic in its purest possible form; if you love hard brainteasers without stress or distraction, it is a timeless classic.

game-boy__catrap.teaser: A logic game with a time-rewind mechanic — revolutionary for its time.
game-boy__catrap.detail: A logic platformer with a mechanic that was years ahead of its time: **you can rewind time** and fix a wrong move without restarting the level. You control a pair of characters and swap between them to solve puzzles. This „undo/rewind“ mechanic only appeared in the mainstream much later (Braid, Prince of Persia 2003). A visionary title.
game-boy__catrap.article:
Imagine a logic game from 1990 that lets you take time back and fix a wrong move — without restarting, without frustration. Sounds like a feature of modern games? **Catrap** could do it years before it was cool, and it is precisely this vision that makes it one of the most underrated titles on the Game Boy.

At first glance it is a logic platformer: you control a pair of characters you switch between, and your task is to clear each level of enemies and obstacles in the right order. You push blocks, climb, count steps — classic puzzle fun where the sequence of moves matters. But then comes the trick: whenever you make a mistake, you can **rewind time** and go back a move or several moves, instead of starting over from scratch.

Today the „undo“ function feels obvious to us, but at a time when games punished every mistake with a fresh start, it was a small revolution in design. This time-rewind mechanic only broke into wider awareness much later — think of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time in 2003 or the independent sensation Braid. Catrap arrived at a similar idea quietly and more than a decade earlier, on an eight-bit handheld.

Thanks to this, Catrap is not only a clever puzzle game with a pleasantly escalating difficulty, but also a fascinating piece of gaming history. It rewards experimentation — because a mistake costs no more than a few moves back — and thereby encourages you to play with each challenge until you find an elegant solution.

Like so many visionary titles on the Game Boy, Catrap stayed out of the spotlight, and yet it deserves to be mentioned every time the origin of the time-rewind mechanic in games comes up.

**Why play it:** A clever logic platformer with a time-rewind mechanic that was more than ten years ahead of its time; a visionary title as instructive as it is fun.

game-boy__pipe-dream.teaser: Build pipes before the liquid arrives. A simple, stressful addiction.
game-boy__pipe-dream.detail: You lay pieces of pipe on a grid before „flooz“ starts flowing through it, trying to build the longest possible route. It originated on computers and was ported practically everywhere. The „pipe minigame“ mechanic became so iconic that it is used as a hacking minigame in dozens of later games (BioShock made it famous).
game-boy__pipe-dream.article:
The water is already flowing and you are desperately laying more and more pieces of pipe to keep it running — welcome to one of the most stressful and at the same time most addictive puzzle ideas of the eighties and nineties. **Pipe Dream** took the simple idea of building a pipeline and turned it into a reflex-driven race against the clock that engulfs anyone who so much as touches it.

The mechanic is ingeniously understandable: you place randomly arriving pieces of pipe on a grid and try to assemble the longest possible continuous route before a liquid called „flooz“ starts pouring from the outlet. Once the liquid sets off, it flows relentlessly through the pipe you laid — and if it hits a dead end, it is over. So you have to plan ahead, improvise with whatever the game happens to offer you, and make peace with the fact that the perfect route almost never works out. From this springs that characteristic feeling of pleasant tension, where every decision by a single square is a gamble.

The game originally emerged on home computers and was ported practically everywhere — on the Game Boy it found a great home, because it fits precisely into short sessions on the go. A few screens and you realize half an hour has already passed.

The most interesting thing about Pipe Dream, though, is its cultural footprint. The principle of building a pipeline became so iconic that it turned into a fundamental building block of countless „mini-puzzles“ in later games — from hacking and lockpicking minigames to more complex systems. Most famously it was popularized by BioShock, where the „pipe minigame“ became the main way of hacking. Few puzzles from that era left such a broad footprint.

Pipe Dream is thus a rare case of a simple game that became a language — a visual shorthand understood even by players who never played the original.

**Why play it:** A simple yet nerve-wracking and endlessly addictive puzzle whose pipe-building mechanic you know from dozens of later games; the ideal little stressor for your pocket.

game-boy__qix.teaser: Claim territory, dodge the enemy. Abstract, hypnotic.
game-boy__qix.detail: A port of an abstract arcade game from 1981. You claim territory by drawing enclosed shapes while dodging the bouncing „Qix“ and enemies along the edges. The goal is to claim a given percentage of the area. A tense balance between risk (a big claim) and safety. Abstract, hypnotic, timelessly different.
game-boy__qix.article:
There are games that explain their rules to you in five seconds and then hold you at the screen for hours. Qix is exactly such a case. No story, no heroes, no jump-scare bosses — just an empty area, your line and the compulsive urge to claim more than is wise.

The principle is geometrically clean. Your marker moves along the edges of the playing field and draws enclosed shapes. Once you close off a piece of the area, it is yours, and the percentage counter climbs. The goal is to claim a predetermined share of the whole — and therein lies all the devilish charm. You can draw small, safe segments and advance cautiously bit by bit, or sweep across half the screen and risk everything. For across the field bounces the titular „Qix“, a chaotic, undulating entity, and along the edges of your unfinished lines other enemies creep. Until you close the line, you are vulnerable. Every big claim is thus a gamble: the longer the move, the greater the reward and the danger.

Qix originated as an arcade cabinet back in 1981 at the Taito studio and belongs to that rare category of games that are literally timeless, because they rest not on graphics or technology but on abstract mathematical tension. Here we have it in the form of a Game Boy port from 1990, and the monochrome handheld suits this game incredibly well. No colors distract — all that remains is the tension between risk and safety, reduced to pure lines and percentages.

What makes Qix so hypnotic is the rhythm it draws you into. For a while you calculate, waiting for the right moment, tracking the path of the Qix — and then you steel yourself for a risky cut across the open space, your heart leaps as your marker races across the field and you hope you can close the shape before something hits you. It is the pure essence of „just one more round“ gameplay, where every loss is your own fault and every win a small victory over your own impatience.

The game also has its tactical layer, which those who sink into it more deeply will appreciate. What matters is not only how much area you claim, but also how fast you do it — slow, cautious drawing lowers your risk, but an unfinished line can usually be drawn at two speeds, where the slower one brings a higher score for the claimed area. So you learn to read the Qix's behavior, anticipate where the undulating entity will move, and exploit the moments when it draws away for bolder moves. From a simple game of claiming territory comes a duel of nerves and timing.

Qix is in its own way a game outside of time and genre pigeonholes. It is neither a classic platformer nor a logic puzzle in the usual sense — it is an abstract battle for territory that has little parallel even today. If you are looking for a title that will not burden you with story or a tutorial and instead offers you pure, focused gameplay for five minutes or an hour, here it is.

**Why play it:** A timeless abstract arcade game where every move is a gamble between greed and caution — easy to grasp, hard to put down.

game-boy__daedalian-opus.teaser: A pentomino puzzler; peace of mind.
game-boy__daedalian-opus.detail: A rare pentomino puzzle: you fit twelve different five-square shapes (pentominoes) into pre-drawn figures with no gaps. No stress, no clock — pure geometric logic and calm. A curiosity for collectors and puzzle lovers alike; one of the very few purely „pentomino“ video games.
game-boy__daedalian-opus.article:
Some games want to beat you. Daedalian Opus wants to calm you down. At a time when the Game Boy was flooded with action platformers and hard-edged arcades, 1990 saw the release of this unassuming title from Vic Tokai, which offers not a single enemy, not a second of time pressure — just you, a grid, and a handful of geometric shapes.

At its core is the pentomino, a classic mathematical puzzle. A pentomino is a shape made of five squares, and there are twelve distinct varieties. Your task is to arrange these pieces into a pre-drawn figure so that they fit together perfectly, with no gaps and no overlaps. It sounds simple, but as the number of pieces grows and the target shapes get more complicated, you discover that every solution demands patient rotating, flipping, and thinking about space several moves ahead. It is a puzzle in the purest sense of the word — no tricks, just geometry and logic.

Daedalian Opus is a curiosity for several reasons. The pentomino is one of the oldest recreational mathematical puzzles, yet the number of video games that treat it as their main dish is literally a handful. That makes this one of the very few purely „pentomino“ titles ever released, and that alone makes it a point of interest for collectors and for puzzle lovers looking for something off the beaten path.

What you will appreciate about this game is its absolute honesty. There is no score to stress you out, no timer breathing down your neck. You sit with the console, slide the pieces around, and when you finally manage to close off a figure, you get that quiet, satisfying feeling of a problem solved. It is a game ideal for winding down in the evening, for a train journey, or for a moment when you want to clear your head with a single, clearly defined task.

What makes Daedalian Opus especially welcoming is its gradual buildup. The game does not throw you straight into the hardest puzzles — it starts with simple figures and a few pieces, and only gradually adds more complex shapes and less intuitive layouts. In doing so it gently teaches you to think in pentominoes, to recognize which piece goes where, and to anticipate how the remaining gaps will be filled. It is a learning curve that respects the player and lets them grow alongside the difficulty rather than frustrating them. By the end you will be rotating shapes in your head before you ever place them on the grid.

In the context of handheld gaming, Daedalian Opus is proof that the Game Boy was not only a platform for reflex-driven action, but also for quiet, contemplative puzzles. It is not a title that will jolt you with adrenaline — it is more of a repose, a meditation on geometry. And in today's flood of noisy games, such an unassuming, calm puzzler has an unexpected charm.

**Why play:** A rare, purely pentomino puzzle with no stress and no timer — geometric meditation for anyone who wants to clear their head.

game-boy__mario-s-picross.teaser: Nonograms with Mario; if you like logic crosswords, you'll lose hours.
game-boy__mario-s-picross.detail: It brought nonograms (picture crosswords where numbers help you reveal a hidden image) to Western audiences. Nintendo's Mario team oversaw it. It was a success in Japan and got sequels (Japan only); the series then lives on via the 3DS as Picross e. Deductive, addictive, ideal for „one square a day“.
game-boy__mario-s-picross.article:
There is a peculiar kind of game that won't let go of you even after you switch off the console — and Mario's Picross is a textbook example. This game introduced Western audiences to nonograms, logic crosswords in which you deduce a hidden pixel image from the numbers along the sides of the grid. No action, no enemies — just you, the numbers, and the quiet satisfaction of everything clicking into place.

The principle is ingeniously simple and inexhaustible at the same time. The numbers beside each row and column tell you how many contiguous cells are filled and in what groups. From that you must logically deduce which cells to blacken and which to cross out. A single wrong judgment is punished — an incorrect fill eats into your countdown, so the game rewards deliberation over haste. And when the grid finally reveals its picture — a little elephant, a mug, a key — you get that small but genuine sense of accomplishment.

The game was watched over by Nintendo's internal Mario team, and the mascot serves here mainly as the friendly face of the instructions and hints; pickaxe in hand, chisel, hammer — Mario mines images here like a miner of logic. That gave an otherwise abstract puzzle charisma and a brand players knew and bought. Visually the game is clean, legible, and perfectly tuned for the Game Boy's small monochrome screen, where the readability of the grid matters most of all.

In Japan the game was successful enough to earn sequels, which never made it off the islands. More important, though, is what Mario's Picross set in motion: the nonogram (picross) genre took root at Nintendo and lives on to this day — whether as the popular Picross e series on the 3DS or as a fixture of the eShop. This unassuming mid-nineties cartridge is thus something like the forefather of an entire branch of handheld puzzling.

The magic of Mario's Picross lies in the „one square a day“ rhythm that imperceptibly turns into hours. It is a game for the tram, the waiting room, the evening when you want to switch off rather than be wrung out. Deductive, addictive, and surprisingly meditative — exactly the type of title the Game Boy was made for.

**Why play:** If you enjoy logic crosswords and deductive puzzles, this is a clean, polished, and endlessly addictive classic that will make you lose all track of time.

game-boy__arkanoid-doh-it-again.teaser: Breakout refined to perfection; nerves and reflexes.
game-boy__arkanoid-doh-it-again.detail: A portable Arkanoid with support for a special controller; you bounce the ball with a paddle, break bricks, and collect power-ups (laser, paddle extension, multi-ball). Arkanoid (1986) was the one that revived the Breakout genre and added power-ups and bosses (the titular DOH). A reflex-driven, addictive classic.
game-boy__arkanoid-doh-it-again.article:
A ball, a paddle, a wall of bricks — you'd think there was nothing left to invent here. Arkanoid: Doh It Again is proof that refining an old principle to perfection is an art in itself. This portable version of the legendary Breakout descendant takes the simple idea of bouncing a ball and wraps it in a layer of power-ups, bosses, and escalating tension, until the trivial mechanic becomes a test of nerves and reflexes.

You know the basics: with the paddle at the bottom of the screen you bounce a ball to gradually demolish formations of bricks. But Arkanoid added what definitively revived the genre — falling bonuses. A laser that blasts bricks directly, a paddle extension, a slower ball, or the coveted multi-ball that suddenly floods the screen with chaos. Every power-up changes the pace and the tactics, and the decision of whether to risk grabbing a bonus lends surprising depth to an otherwise reflex-based game.

Taito's Arkanoid series stands on solid foundations: the original 1986 arcade machine was the one that resurrected the Breakout genre, gave it a story frame about a spaceship, elevated power-ups into the main draw, and put giant final bosses at the end — the titular enemy DOH. This Game Boy iteration faithfully carries that legacy to the small screen, including support for a special controller for smoother paddle control, which is utterly crucial in this game.

What makes Arkanoid so addictive is its relentless honesty. The game never cheats — every lost ball is your mistake, every cleared level your achievement. That direct link between concentration and result is exactly why players keep coming back to arcade classics of this type for decades. And on a handheld, where it's all about short, intense bursts, the format works even better than at home in front of the TV.

Doh It Again is not a revolution, nor does it want to be. It is the polished essence of one of the purest game principles there is, packaged in pocket form. It is the kind of game where you tell yourself „just one more level“ and wake up an hour later with aching thumbs.

**Why play:** Breakout refined to perfection — a reflex-driven, addictive arcade game for short sessions that will easily swallow an hour of your time.

game-boy__game-and-watch-gallery.teaser: Retro mini-games in two versions (classic + modern). Nostalgia in your pocket.
game-boy__game-and-watch-gallery.detail: A collection of classic Game & Watch LCD games (Gunpei's handheld games from the late 70s and 80s, predecessors of the Game Boy) in both the original and a „modern“ version with Mario characters. A reminder of Nintendo's roots as a toy maker. The series continued with further installments.
game-boy__game-and-watch-gallery.article:
Before there was the Game Boy, there were the Game & Watch — and this collection is both a reverent and playful return to the very roots of Nintendo. Game & Watch Gallery gathers the legendary handheld LCD games that Gunpei Yokoi devised at the turn of the seventies and eighties, and packages them in modern form on the very console that is essentially their direct descendant. It is nostalgia in your pocket, but the kind that can still entertain.

The collection offers the classic LCD titles in two versions each. „Classic“ reproduces the original stark game exactly as it looked on the standalone handheld toys — flat segmented images, plain rules, pure reflex-driven gameplay. The „Modern“ version then dresses the same principles in a coat of real graphics and characters from the Mario world, adding power-ups and bonus elements. So you have side by side a museum exhibit and its contemporary, juicier variation.

Gunpei Yokoi, father of both the Game & Watch and the Game Boy itself, built these games on the philosophy of „lateral thinking with withered technology“ — taking cheap, proven components (LCD displays from calculators) and squeezing maximum fun out of them. The Game & Watch were an enormous commercial success that put Nintendo on its feet in the video game business and foreshadowed the whole era of handhelds. Gallery is therefore more than just a compilation — it is a reminder that Nintendo started out as a maker of toys and clever gadgets.

The magic of these games lies in their directness. No stories, no menus — just an accelerating pace, one wrong move and it's over, an ending that tempts you into an immediate rematch. Right and left, catch falling objects, juggle, firefighters with a trampoline — principles half a century old, and yet instantly understandable and surprisingly gripping. The dual presentation also offers a pleasant comparison of how far game design came in just a few years.

The Game & Watch Gallery series continued with further installments that gradually added more classics, becoming a living archival line of Nintendo. For anyone interested in where modern handheld gaming came from, this is the ideal gateway.

**Why play:** A playful tribute to Nintendo's roots — retro mini-games in two forms, an ideal dose of nostalgia and pure arcade fun for your pocket.

game-boy__harvest-moon-gb.teaser: Farming and calm; the first portable installment of the series.
game-boy__harvest-moon-gb.detail: The first portable installment of the farming series (the original was on the SNES). You sow, harvest, raise animals, and manage your time within the seasons. The GB version has a time limit (you must build the farm up within a given period), unlike the more open-ended later installments. A relaxing counterpoint to action games; the series continues today as Story of Seasons.
game-boy__harvest-moon-gb.article:
While the rest of the Game Boy library fights, shoots, and jumps, Harvest Moon GB hands you a hoe and says: slow down. This first portable installment of the farming series is an oasis of calm in a sea of action — a game about sowing, harvesting, raising animals, and the quiet satisfaction of watching a rundown farm slowly turn into a prosperous holding under your hands.

The daily rhythm is the heart of the experience. You get up, water the crops, feed the chickens and cows, cut the weeds, gather the eggs, and before you know it the sun is setting. The seasons change what you can grow and force you to plan ahead. There is no enemy to defeat — just the soil, time, and your own diligence. Out of those ordinary tasks a surprisingly hypnotic loop is born, one you can easily sink into for hours.

The Game Boy version, though, has one fundamental difference from the later, looser installments: a time limit. You don't farm indefinitely — you get a defined period in which you must raise the farm to a certain level, or else you're finished. That gives the otherwise placid game an unexpected drive and sense of responsibility; every wasted day counts. It is a version of farming with a backbone, where relaxation goes hand in hand with quiet pressure to deliver.

The original Harvest Moon was born on the SNES, and only from there did it head into your pocket.
