Advanced players plan entire family trees across generations to obtain a dream beast with the ideal set of attacks, and it is precisely this depth that turns an otherwise simple concept into a time sink lasting dozens of hours.

The game was created by TOSE in collaboration with Enix, then the publisher of the Dragon Quest brand. It arrived toward the end of the Game Boy era and made full use of the Game Boy Color, giving it clean, colorful graphics and a friendly interface. It bet on what Dragon Quest does best: clear turn-based battles and a difficulty curve that guides the player by the hand without underestimating them. The battles stay readable even on the small screen and the pacing is brisk, which counts double on a handheld.

Culturally it was a clever move. Rather than taking on Pokémon head-on, Enix offered an alternative to players who wanted the same addictiveness but with a different mythology and a style all its own. The slime creatures and other iconic Dragon Quest beings, designed by the hand of Akira Toriyama, got the chance to shine outside the main series and reached an audience that had not yet known it.

Dragon Warrior Monsters spawned a sequel and a whole line of spiritual successors in the Dragon Quest Monsters sub-series, which lives on to this day and remains a very popular offshoot of the brand in Japan. For many Western players it was the very first gateway into a world of monster-collecting RPGs bearing the Dragon Quest name, and it is still remembered as one of the finest titles of its kind on a handheld.

**Why play it:** If you love catching and breeding creatures but want something other than Pokémon, Dragon Warrior Monsters offers a deep breeding system and dozens of hours of experimentation.

game-boy-color__harvest-moon-gbc.article:
There is a genre where the goal is not to defeat an enemy, but to water your field and milk the cow before the sun goes down. Harvest Moon GBC brought its laid-back farming idyll to the small screen of a handheld and proved that even slow, calm play can be incredibly addictive on the go.

The essence of the game is simple and hypnotic at once: you inherit a neglected farm and have to bring it into bloom within a set period. You plant crops according to the seasons, tend animals, chop wood, expand your fields and manage both time and energy. Every day has its rhythm, every season its rules, and the magic lies in how a thriving homestead gradually takes shape out of tiny everyday chores. The day is short and you are constantly weighing what to do first, so even ordinary watering carries strategic weight.

Unlike some of the console entries, this handheld version focuses above all on the farming itself. The goal is to bring a run-down farm back to life and prove yourself in an evaluation of just how good a farmer you have become. Bit by bit you unlock new options, save up for upgrades and watch bare soil turn into a prospering estate. It is this slow but steady progression that makes the game a pleasantly addictive routine.

The Harvest Moon series was born at Victor Interactive (originally under the Pack-In-Video label), and the spiritual father of the concept is Yasuhiro Wada, who wanted to capture the nostalgia of country life and a calm that games had lacked until then. The Game Boy version brought that calm to a black-and-white – or, on the Game Boy Color, colorful – handheld format. It had to simplify and trim some elements known from the console entries, but the core of the simulation, that satisfying business of building a farm day by day, remained fully intact.

The cultural significance of the series is enormous: Harvest Moon practically defined the farming-simulation genre and became a direct inspiration for later phenomena such as Stardew Valley, whose author openly acknowledges the series' legacy. It showed that a game needs neither enemies nor the time pressure of combat to keep a player glued to the screen for hours on end. Contentment and meaningful work turned out to be a surprisingly powerful game engine.

The handheld edition built its own circle of fans precisely because farming was suddenly possible anywhere, whether on a train or under the covers. The series continued across many entries on various platforms and, after complications with the brand's license, its creators later developed it under the new name Story of Seasons. Harvest Moon GBC thus remains a milestone that successfully squeezed calm, building-focused play into the palm of your hand.

**Why play it:** If you are looking for a relaxing, stress-free game where the reward is the growth of your own farm, the handheld Harvest Moon is the perfect companion for long journeys.

game-boy-color__top-gear-pocket.article:
A racing game that literally fits in your pocket yet delivers a sense of speed you would not expect from a handheld. That was Top Gear Pocket, a racer for the Game Boy Color that set out to bring brisk arcade driving from a behind-the-car perspective to the small color screen.

The Top Gear series has its roots in the well-known arcade racers, and this handheld offshoot tried to preserve their spirit. The player tears along the tracks from a view behind the car, overtakes rivals and tries to keep up the highest possible pace through the corners. The emphasis is on brisk, readable driving rather than a realistic driving simulation.

The title arrived at a time when the Game Boy Color was expanding handheld gaming with color, and Top Gear Pocket tried to use that possibility for a livelier depiction of tracks and cars. For players on the move it was a chance to experience a fast arcade racer without having to sit at a home console, which back then was the chief virtue of handheld gaming.

From today's perspective, Top Gear Pocket is part of a long tradition of racing games that tried to strike a balance between instant fun and the technical possibilities of a given platform. On the Game Boy Color it was an attempt to give players a sense of speed and competition in the most accessible form possible.

For lovers of retro racers and Game Boy Color collectors it is a title that recalls how developers reined in the ambitions of big arcade racers within the confines of handheld hardware. It is a piece of the history of portable racing, back when the color screen was only just becoming the standard.

**Why play it:** A brisk pocket-sized arcade racer for the Game Boy Color that offers a sense of speed and competition anywhere on the go.

game-boy-color__street-fighter-alpha.article:
Say Street Fighter Alpha and most players picture colorful, stylized bouts with an expanded roster of fighters. That this branch of the series made it all the way to the Game Boy Color is a small surprise in itself, and at the same time proof of just how popular the Street Fighter brand was in its day. Capcom tried to cram its iconic fighter into a handheld.

The Alpha series, known in Japan as Street Fighter Zero, is a prelude to the story events between the first and second games and delivers brisker, more energetic bouts. The foundation, however, stays true to the roots of the genre. You pick a fighter, face an opponent in one-on-one combat and try to overpower them with a combination of ordinary blows and special moves.

The handheld treatment on the Game Boy Color naturally runs into the limits of the hardware. The smaller screen, limited number of buttons and more modest performance force developers to adapt both the pacing and the scope of what the fighters can do. Even so, it is admirable that the game managed to preserve the legibility of the characters and the basic feel of a fighter on such a small device at all.

Street Fighter Alpha as a whole is prized for its artistic style and a deeper combat system that added new mechanics and characters to the series. With this sub-series Capcom appealed to players craving something between the classic Street Fighter II and the later entries, thereby expanding the world of its iconic brawlers.

For Game Boy Color owners this version was a chance to take a slice of the famous fighter along with them. From today's perspective it is mainly an interesting example of how Capcom stretched its most famous brand across every conceivable platform, including the handheld.

**Why play it:** A pocket-sized take on the stylish fighter Street Fighter Alpha, alluring for series fans craving one-on-one bouts on the go.

game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-minish.teaser: A charming Zelda with a shrinking mechanic; one of the prettiest 2D entries.
game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-minish.detail: The third and final Zelda from Capcom/Flagship. It rests on a shrinking mechanic: the Ezlo cap lets Link shrink to the size of a coin and enter the world of the tiny Minish, where a puddle is a lake and a table a mountain. Beautiful, detailed pixel art and clever puzzles built around the change of scale. This is where Vaati, the recurring villain, first appeared.
game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-minish.article:
What if the hero of the greatest fantasy saga shrank to the size of a coin and a puddle turned into a lake? That is exactly what **The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap** offers, one of the prettiest two-dimensional entries in the whole series and, at the same time, the last Zelda from the workshop of Capcom and the Flagship studio. After the pair of titles Oracle of Ages and Oracle of Seasons, these skilled outside developers were handed a supremely enticing task – and they rose to it with grace.

At the heart of the game is the shrinking mechanic. A talking cap named Ezlo lets Link shrink to the size of a coin and enter the world of the tiny beings called Minish, where every table is a mountain and every puddle a lake. This change of scale is not just a visual trick – it is the backbone of clever puzzles in which the player must think about a single location in two different sizes at once. Hunting for gaps you can only fit through while shrunk, and linking the two worlds together, is immensely satisfying.

Visually it is one of the peaks of handheld graphics of its time. The detailed, artistically rich pixel art on the Game Boy Advance bursts with color and charm, and every location is full of small touches that reward an attentive eye. What is more, the game introduced **Vaati** into the series' mythology – a villain who later became a recurring character – and it sets the Four Sword within a broader story context.

Minish Cap came out in 2004 and to this day counts as one of the most endearing and design-honed 2D Zelda entries. It combines the classic Zelda virtues – exploration, dungeons, the gradual unlocking of abilities – with an original central mechanic that sets the game apart from the others and gives it an unmistakable identity.

For newcomers it is a great and welcoming entry point into the world of Hyrule; for veterans, proof that even in the shadow of the great three-dimensional entries a 2D Zelda could shine. It is a game full of wit, ideas and craftsmanship in every pixel.

**Why play it:** For its original shrinking mechanic, gorgeous pixel art and clever puzzles – one of the most accomplished 2D Zelda entries and a great way into the series.

game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-link-t.teaser: A port of the best SNES Zelda + a multiplayer bonus.
game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-link-t.detail: A port of the best SNES Zelda (1991) plus a brand-new cooperative game, Four Swords – the very first multiplayer Zelda, playable by linking several GBAs. Double the value: the classic plus new content.
game-boy-advance__legend-of-zelda-link-t.article:
Two games on one cartridge, and both exceptional – that is an offer you cannot refuse. **The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past + Four Swords** brought to the Game Boy Advance a port of what many still consider the best two-dimensional Zelda ever, and on top of that added something the series had never had before – multiplayer. For fans of Hyrule it was a double helping of joy.

The foundation of the package is **A Link to the Past**, a 1991 classic originally for the SNES. This game defined the modern Zelda formula: a sprawling world split between Light and Dark, between which the player switches to solve interconnected puzzles, a series of thoughtfully designed dungeons and an iconic arsenal of tools from the hookshot to magic mirrors. Even decades later it is a textbook example of flawless game design, and the GBA port made it accessible to a whole new generation of players on the go.

The real novelty, though, is **Four Swords** – the very first cooperative Zelda in history. By linking several Game Boy Advance consoles, players could go through dungeons together, compete for rupees and cooperate while also throwing sticks under each other's feet. This game planted the seed from which later cooperative Zelda experiments grew, and in 2002 it was a small revolution for a brand that had, until then, been an exclusively solo affair.

The combination of a timeless classic and pioneering multiplayer makes this cartridge an exceptionally valuable package. You get both a game you will fall in love with alone in the quiet of your room and an experience best savored amid laughter with friends beside you. It is an ideal example of how cleverly ported releases could add extra value.

Anyone who does not know A Link to the Past has a unique chance to catch up on one of the greatest gems of the genre. And anyone who knows it by heart gets a reason to return – this time with two or more.

**Why play it:** For the timeless SNES classic in handheld form plus the historically first cooperative Zelda – double the value on a single cartridge.

game-boy-advance__metroid-zero-mission.teaser: A remake of the original Metroid; perhaps the best entry point into the series.
game-boy-advance__metroid-zero-mission.detail: A remake of the original Metroid (1986) built on the Fusion engine. It modernizes everything – controls, graphics, the map – and adds a brand-new closing stretch where Samus loses her suit and has to sneak. Regarded as the best entry point into the series.
game-boy-advance__metroid-zero-mission.article:
Go all the way back to the very beginning and do it over again – better, more beautifully and more cleverly. That is exactly what **Metroid: Zero Mission** achieved, a remake of the very first Metroid from 1986 that is often called perhaps the best gateway into the whole series. Built on the refined engine of the previous game Metroid Fusion, it takes the iconic but, for its era, rough original and modernizes it from the ground up.

The Metroidvania genre – named after this very series and after Castlevania – rests on an interconnected world that gradually opens up depending on the abilities the heroine acquires. Bounty hunter **Samus Aran** explores the planet Zebes, collects suit upgrades, unlocks new areas and defeats bosses. Zero Mission perfects this loop: the controls are brisk and precise, the graphics are generations ahead of the original, and the map is finally clear, so the player does not get lost in a maze of corridors the way they once did.

The most interesting new element, though, is a completely new closing stretch that the original game did not have at all. In it Samus loses her powerful suit and must – vulnerable and all but defenseless – sneak through an enemy base. This stealth sequence lends the story tension and gives Samus, as a character, an unexpected humanity; it is a clever way to freshen up a familiar pattern and surprise even series veterans.

Zero Mission came out in 2004 from the legendary internal studio Nintendo R&D1, the cradle of the whole Metroid brand. It combines respect for the original with the courage to rewrite it where needed, and the result is a game that has not run out of breath even after years. For a newcomer it is ideal in how clearly it teaches the genre's principles without losing depth.

Anyone who wants to understand why the Metroid series inspired an entire genre, and at the same time enjoy polished handheld action with the atmosphere of lonely exploration, should not hesitate. It is a remake as one should look – faithful and bold at once.

**Why play it:** For a beautifully tuned Metroidvania and a cleverly reworked classic Metroid with a gripping new finale – the best entry point into the series.

game-boy-advance__metroid-fusion.teaser: A tighter, more story-driven Metroid full of tension; excellent.
game-boy-advance__metroid-fusion.detail: A more linear, more story-driven Metroid with an element of tension: throughout the station you are pursued by SA-X, a near-indestructible copy of Samus you have to flee from. A darker tone and tight pacing. It launched alongside Metroid Prime, marking the series' return after years.
game-boy-advance__metroid-fusion.article:
Imagine being hunted on an abandoned space station by your own dark double – and being able to do nothing but run from it. That is exactly what **Metroid Fusion** is, a game that in 2002 brought the legendary series back into play in a double release: alongside the 3D revolution of Metroid Prime on the GameCube, this two-dimensional essence of everything that made Metroid great arrived on the Game Boy Advance.

Compared to the freely explorable Super Metroid, Fusion is **tighter and more story-driven**. Samus goes through the BSL station following the instructions of the onboard computer, the map opens up gradually and the pacing is firmly steered. To some it may sound like a step back from freedom, but in reality it gives the game a cinematic drive and a focused atmosphere. Every new section is a little chapter with a point of its own.

The heart of the tension is **SA-X** – a near-indestructible copy of Samus's armor, a living menace that moves around the station independently of you. When you hear it walking around the corner, instinct tells you to hide and stay still. These passages, where the huntress is suddenly turned into prey, rank among the most gripping moments of the whole series and push Metroid closer to survival horror than ever before.

The darker tone is underscored by the superb visuals and sound the GBA was proud of: detailed backgrounds, excellent Samus animation and music that alternates melancholy with anxiety. The combat and movement system stays supple and satisfying – you discover wall-jumps, new gear and secret corridors with the delight of a connoisseur of the genre this series helped found.

Metroid Fusion was created at the internal studio **Nintendo R&D1**, the cradle of the series, and to this day it counts as one of the peaks of the Game Boy Advance library. Its story thread was, moreover, for years regarded as the last entry in the chronology – the sequel Metroid Dread, announced even back then, did not arrive until nearly two decades later and followed on directly from Fusion.

**Why play it:** A tight, gripping and beautifully tuned 2D Metroid whose chases with SA-X will stay in your memory long after you finish it.

game-boy-advance__mario-and-luigi-supers.teaser: A funny RPG with superb combat timing.
game-boy-advance__mario-and-luigi-supers.detail: The first entry in the series, where you control both brothers at once (each has their own button) and battles require action timing – a well-timed press strengthens an attack or blocks a hit. Witty writing (Fawful!) and original dual gameplay. The start of a beloved series.
game-boy-advance__mario-and-luigi-supers.article:
What happens when Mario is robbed of his voice, Luigi is made half a coward, and the whole farce is written by a scenarist who is evidently poking fun at everything, himself included? You get **Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga**, one of the funniest RPGs ever to appear on a Nintendo handheld.

The key idea is brilliantly simple: you control **both brothers at once**, each tied to their own button (A for Mario, B for Luigi). In the field this means mischievous puzzles and combined moves; in battle, the absolute foundation of the fun – **action timing**. A well-timed press at the moment a jump lands or a hammer strikes strengthens the attack, and likewise a timely press lets you block or dodge an enemy hit entirely. Battles are thus not a passive wait for numbers, but an active, almost rhythmic game.

The second draw is the **writing**. Superstar Saga overflows with wordplay, absurd situations and unforgettable villains – above all the utterly insane **Fawful**, a fan icon whose contorted English („I have fury!“) became legendary. The humor here is not decoration but a load-bearing pillar of the whole experience.

The game runs briskly, is visually adorable and full of exaggerated expressions and animation that turn both brothers into a comedy duo without a single intelligible word. Bit by bit you acquire new shared abilities that open up the map and new combat tricks, so the system keeps growing and never grows stale.

Behind the game stood the studio **AlphaDream**, and it was the first entry in the Mario & Luigi series, which subsequently grew into several beloved sequels. Superstar Saga laid the foundation of its formula – the combination of action battles, buddy mechanics and self-assured humor – and to this day ranks among the best a handheld Mario RPG has offered.

**Why play it:** A clever, hilariously funny RPG whose combat timing turns every fight into a little mini-game – and the start of one of the most beloved detours in Mario's world.

game-boy-advance__golden-sun.teaser: An epic JRPG duology with gorgeous spells and puzzles; a GBA legend.
game-boy-advance__golden-sun.detail: A two-part epic saga renowned for its gorgeous, elaborate summon animations (Summons) and the „Djinn“ system – elemental spirits with which you customize the abilities and classes of your characters. The environments are full of environmental puzzles solved with psionics (Psynergy). Both technically and in design it belongs among the peaks of the GBA; together they form a single story (data transfer via password/cable).
game-boy-advance__golden-sun.article:
Few games on the Game Boy Advance could take your breath away like **Golden Sun** – and all it took was a single summoned spell that filled the entire screen with sweeping animation nobody would have expected from a handheld. In 2001 it was literally a technical calling card of what the GBA could do.

Golden Sun is a classic JRPG with turn-based battles, but it excels at two things. The first is the **Djinn** system – spirits of the four elements that you collect, equip and activate. Djinn change the stats, spells and entire classes of your characters, so to a large degree you assemble your own combat style. Their summoning also triggers the aforementioned magnificent **Summons**, some of the prettiest effects of their era.

The second pillar is **Psynergy** – psionic magic that serves not only in battle but permeates the exploration of the world as well. With it you move objects, raise pillars, freeze water or light lamps, and thereby solve a great many **environmental puzzles**. The dungeons are thus not merely corridors to the next battle, but clever logical challenges that make exploration a form of entertainment in its own right.

Behind the game stands the studio **Camelot**, otherwise known mainly for the Mario Golf and Mario Tennis series. Here it showed a completely different face – the ability to tell a sprawling fantasy story and build it on solid RPG foundations with tuned pacing and surprisingly mature themes.

It is important to know that Golden Sun is the first half of a larger whole. The story continues directly in the second entry, **The Lost Age**, with your progress and data transferable via password or a link cable. Together they form a single epic saga and belong among the absolute peaks of the Game Boy Advance library.

**Why play it:** A gorgeous, technically astonishing JRPG whose Djinn system and psionic puzzles rank to this day among the best on the entire platform.

game-boy-advance__golden-sun-lost-age.article:
Where the first Golden Sun ended mid-sentence, **Golden Sun: The Lost Age** picks up seamlessly – and in several respects even surpasses its predecessor. It is the second half of one grand saga, into which you can carry over your progress from the first entry via password or link cable and reap the fruits of everything you gathered.

The Lost Age takes the proven foundations and develops them. The elemental spirits **Djinn** return, customizing the abilities and classes of your characters, as does the psionic magic **Psynergy**, with which you continue to solve **environmental puzzles** scattered across the dungeons and the open world. In this respect the game adds new abilities and more ingenious brain-teasers, so exploration is even richer and more rewarding.

Visually and in design it is again the top tier of the Game Boy Advance. The magnificent summons (**Summons**) fill the screen with effects few would expect from a handheld, and the turn-based battles remain tactical thanks to the constant juggling of Djinn between attack, defense and spells. The world is more sprawling and more open, with an emphasis on sailing and discovery.

Story-wise, The Lost Age is interesting in that it shifts the perspective and deepens the motifs begun in the first game, so the whole duology makes sense only when taken together. Both entries were created by the studio **Camelot**, which here showed its more ambitious, storytelling side.

Together with the first entry, The Lost Age forms one of the most distinctive RPG experiences on the platform – for fans of the genre it is almost mandatory to play through both pieces as a whole.

**Why play it:** The culmination of an epic duology that improves everything good from the first game – more world, more puzzles and a magnificent finale to a single story.

game-boy-advance__pokemon-firered-leafgr.teaser: The definitive remake of the first generation.
game-boy-advance__pokemon-firered-leafgr.detail: A remake of the first generation on the third-generation GBA engine, with modernized graphics, quality-of-life features and a bonus island. The definitive way to experience the original Kanto today.
game-boy-advance__pokemon-firered-leafgr.article:
Return to Kanto, but without the painful compromises of the eight-bit era – that is exactly what **Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen** offer, the definitive way to experience the very first generation of the most famous series in the world today.

It is a remake of the original Pokémon Red and Green/Blue, built on the advanced **third-generation engine**. That means not only more colorful and detailed graphics, but above all a host of **quality-of-life** improvements players came to expect later on: a better interface, smoother controls and mechanics the original games did not yet have. Kanto, Pallet Town and the first 151 Pokémon come alive here in a form that ages far more gracefully than the original.

The series is developed by the studio **Game Freak**, and FireRed/LeafGreen showed how cleverly it can renovate its own classic – preserving the soul and structure of the original journey for badges and the Elite Four, while dressing it in a modern coat. For newcomers it is an ideal entry point; for those who remember, pleasant nostalgia without the frustration.

What is more, bonus content was added – the **Sevii Islands** archipelago, which extends the story and links it to the events of the third generation, so even seasoned trainers got new reasons to explore. Thanks to compatibility with other games of the time, the options for trading and completing the Pokédex expanded as well.

In the end FireRed and LeafGreen rank among the most beloved remakes ever and are today the most accessible way to play the thing that started it all.

**Why play it:** The original Kanto in the best possible form – a first-generation classic stripped of its archaic ills and enriched with modern comforts.

game-boy-advance__pokemon-ruby-sapphire-.teaser: Third generation; Emerald is the most complete version.
game-boy-advance__pokemon-ruby-sapphire-.detail: The third generation introduced Abilities, Natures, double battles and the water-rich Hoenn region. Emerald is the most complete version, featuring the Battle Frontier. A hugely popular era thanks to its finely tuned battle system.
game-boy-advance__pokemon-ruby-sapphire-.article:
A new generation, a new region, a whole new ocean of possibilities — **Pokémon Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald** brought the series to the **Hoenn** region, a land full of water, islands and two feuding teams bent on ruling both land and sea.

The third generation introduced several changes that still shape the series today. Chief among them are **Abilities** — passive traits that fundamentally alter how Pokémon behave in battle — and **Natures**, which influence stat growth and open the door to deeper breeding and competitive tuning. **Double battles** were added as well, turning fights into a more tactical game of pairing up your team.

Hoenn itself is a distinctive region packed with bodies of water, surfing and diving, giving exploration a different rhythm than previous generations. The battles here are so well balanced that this era became one of the most beloved among fans.

Of the three versions, **Emerald** is the most complete. It combines content from both Ruby and Sapphire, refines the story, and above all adds the **Battle Frontier** — a set of demanding combat challenges that turns the game into a paradise for anyone who wants to test their tactics to the bone.

Once again, the series was developed by **Game Freak**, and the third generation is now seen as an important milestone that laid the foundations for modern competitive battle mechanics. For many players, Hoenn remains a matter of the heart.

**Why play it:** A beloved Pokémon era with a finely tuned battle system — and in the form of Emerald with its Battle Frontier, it offers the most complete third-generation experience.

game-boy-advance__advance-wars.teaser: Turn-based strategy in perfect pocket form; fiercely addictive.
game-boy-advance__advance-wars.detail: The Wars series had existed in Japan since the NES, but it was Advance Wars that finally brought it West (ironically it launched just after 9/11, which delayed its Japanese release). Turn-based warfare on hex/grid maps with rock-paper-scissors units and commanders (CO) with unique abilities. Brilliantly accessible yet deep; a pillar of the genre on handhelds.
game-boy-advance__advance-wars.article:
A turn-based strategy game that grabs you by the collar and won't let go until you finish "just one more map" — and then suddenly it's morning. That's the effect of **Advance Wars**, a game that proved the depth of wartime tactics could be crammed onto a pocket console without losing an ounce of its punch.

The Wars series had existed in Japan since the days of the NES, but it was Advance Wars that finally brought it to the **West** in 2001. In an irony of fate, it launched right after the attacks of 9/11, which conversely delayed its home Japanese release — the war theme suddenly felt sensitive, even though the game itself, with its bubbly, almost cartoonish style, is anything but grim.

The core is beautifully clean: on grid maps you command an army of units that interact on a **rock-paper-scissors** principle. Infantry captures buildings and generates income, tanks crush weaker targets, artillery fires from a distance, planes and ships turn the tide of battles. On top of that come **commanders (CO)**, each with a **unique ability** and a special "CO Power" that can turn even a lost match around. This layer gives every map its own character and personality.

The genius of Advance Wars lies in the balance between **accessibility and depth**. You'll grasp the rules within the first missions, but mastery — when to build, when to attack, how to manage your money and when to unleash a CO Power — will keep you busy for dozens of hours. The addictiveness is almost dangerous.

Behind the game stands the studio **Intelligent Systems**, Nintendo's in-house strategist, and Advance Wars rightly became a pillar of the turn-based tactics genre on handhelds. Its clean, polished design influenced a host of other titles and to this day remains the benchmark for what a pocket strategy game should look like.

**Why play it:** A perfectly tuned, fiercely addictive turn-based strategy you'll grasp in minutes and refine for hours — the series' gateway to the West.

game-boy-advance__advance-wars-2-black-h.article:
When the first Advance Wars created a small strategic addiction in the West, the sequel **Advance Wars 2: Black Hole Rising** simply took the proven recipe and cranked it up in every direction. It's the kind of sequel that doesn't want to reinvent the wheel — it wants to spin it faster.

The foundation remains unshakable: on clear maps you command units that work on a **rock-paper-scissors** principle, capture buildings for income, build an army and try to outsmart the enemy. Infantry, tanks, artillery, air force and navy together form a tactical puzzle in which position, economy and timing decide everything.

Once again the most striking layer is the **commanders (CO)** with their unique abilities and devastating CO Powers. Black Hole Rising develops this idea further — it offers new commanders as well as the front-line villains of the Black Hole faction, so battles take on new colors and the player must adapt their strategy to each specific opponent. The campaign is more varied and at times more cunning, with maps that force you to think differently.

Just like the first game, the sequel excels in the balance between **accessibility and depth**. You already know the rules, so you dive straight into the tactical subtleties, and that famous "just one more turn" addictiveness is perhaps even stronger here.

Behind the game once again stands **Intelligent Systems**, masters of turn-based tactics, and Black Hole Rising confirmed that Advance Wars is no one-off miracle but a full-fledged series with firm foundations. For anyone who fell in love with the first installment, the sequel is a natural and welcome next step.

**Why play it:** A bigger, more varied and equally addictive sequel to a superb turn-based strategy — more commanders, more maps and still that irresistible "just one more" pull.

game-boy-advance__fire-emblem.teaser: The series' arrival in the West; tactics with permanent unit death.
game-boy-advance__fire-emblem.detail: The seventh Fire Emblem was the first officially released in the West (the series was popularized by Marth from Smash Bros.). Turn-based tactics with **permadeath** — a fallen unit is gone for good, giving every decision weight. Sacred Stones is more accessible thanks to the option to grind on random maps. Depth of relationships between characters and story.
game-boy-advance__fire-emblem.article:
For a long time, the name Fire Emblem was known in the West only through a single swordsman from Super Smash Bros. — and then at last came the game that explained the legend. **Fire Emblem** for the Game Boy Advance was the first installment in the series officially released outside Japan, and it opened the world of deep turn-based tactics to Western players.

In fact it was the seventh entry in a long Japanese line whose Western popularity was kick-started precisely by **Marth** from Smash Bros. — so much so that Nintendo finally resolved to export the series. And it was a good choice: this game blends strategy with storytelling and characters so deftly that it quickly found a devoted audience.

The heart of the gameplay is **permadeath** — when a unit falls in battle, it's gone **for good**. No revival, no second chance. This single mechanic turns every turn into tense decision-making: risk an attack with a valuable character? Pull back the wounded? Sacrifice someone for victory? Each loss hurts all the more because you've had time to build a bond with the characters.

And it's precisely the **characters and their relationships** that form the second pillar. Bonds form between fighters that show up in both battle and story, and the campaign interweaves tactical missions with a tale of intrigue, betrayal and heroism. The grid battles meanwhile stick to the proven weapon triangle and thoughtful movement across the terrain.

The series is developed by **Intelligent Systems**, and this installment laid the foundations of the brand's Western popularity. Its more accessible sibling **The Sacred Stones** later offered a gentler difficulty curve and the option to grind on random maps, thereby opening the door to less hardened strategists too.

**Why play it:** Deep turn-based tactics in which permadeath gives every decision real weight — and the West's first official encounter with a legendary series.

game-boy-advance__fire-emblem-sacred-sto.article:
Fire Emblem became famous for being beautiful, deep — and merciless. **Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones** however offered something many had wished for: an entry into this tactical legend without the feeling that the game punishes you for every hesitant step.

The core remains faithful to the series. Combat is turn-based on a grid, units work according to a thoughtful weapon triangle, and every move across the terrain matters. And of course the notoriously infamous **permadeath** reigns here too — a fallen unit is gone for good, so every decision to attack or defend carries real weight and emotion. No game teaches you caution so quickly.

The key difference from the previous installment is **accessibility**. The Sacred Stones lets you **grind on randomly generated maps**, so you can strengthen weaker characters and balance the difficulty to your liking. For newcomers to the series this means a far friendlier curve — you can experiment, learn and not be crushed by every mission in the process.

Nor does it lack what makes Fire Emblem so moving: the **depth of relationships between characters** and a story that frames the tactical missions with a tale of the fates of a whole band of heroes. The bonds forming between fighters carry over into battle and into just how much each loss hurts.

Behind the game stands **Intelligent Systems**, and The Sacred Stones is now regarded as one of the friendliest entry points into the series on the Game Boy Advance — a place where even those who were once afraid of its harshness can enjoy the tactical depth of Fire Emblem.

**Why play it:** The most accessible gateway into the world of Fire Emblem — all the tactical depth and weight of permadeath, but with a grinding option that tames the difficulty.

game-boy-advance__castlevania-aria-of-so.teaser: The pinnacle of the GBA Castlevanias; the enemy-soul system is genius.
game-boy-advance__castlevania-aria-of-so.detail: The pinnacle of the GBA Castlevanias. Set in the year 2035, hero Soma Cruz collects the „souls“ of defeated enemies — over 100 abilities that give huge build variability (the Tactical Soul system). Great combat, music (Michiru Yamane) and a plot twist. For many one of the best metroidvanias ever; it received a direct sequel, Dawn of Sorrow, on the DS.
game-boy-advance__castlevania-aria-of-so.article:
The year is 2035, and Soma Cruz, an ordinary high-schooler, finds himself trapped in a castle captured within a solar eclipse. So begins **Aria of Sorrow** — for many players the finest metroidvania Konami ever released, and the crown jewel of the entire Castlevania era on the Game Boy Advance.

At the heart of the game is the brilliant **Tactical Soul system**. When you defeat an enemy, you have a chance to seize its "soul" — and there are over a hundred of them. Each grants you some ability: a passive bonus, a summoned helper, or an active attack. Instead of a rigid inventory, you thus build your own arsenal exactly to suit the play style that fits you. Collecting souls is addictive in its own right and at the same time gives combat meaning even in moments when you already know the castle by heart.

Unlike the previous GBA installments, everything here clicks into place. The controls are brisk and precise, the level design guides you through the castle with the elegant logic of a metroidvania — new abilities open up previously inaccessible corners and you keep returning with the feeling that you're growing. The music was composed by **Michiru Yamane**, the series' resident composer, and her gothic melodies lend the atmosphere exactly the right heft.

The plot moreover offers a twist that cleverly plays with the mythology of the whole saga and with the figure of Soma himself. Aria of Sorrow doesn't hide behind the Belmont name and builds its own story, which fans grew so fond of that it received a **direct sequel, Dawn of Sorrow**, on the Nintendo DS — a rarity in the otherwise fragmented Castlevania chronicle.

Together with Circle of the Moon and Harmony of Dissonance, Aria of Sorrow forms the holy GBA trinity, but even in this company it clearly stands out. It's a title that showed a handheld console could handle a full-fledged, deep and beautiful action-adventure experience without compromises.

**Why play it:** A supreme metroidvania with an addictive soul-collecting system, superb combat and atmospheric music — one of the best titles of the entire GBA era.

game-boy-advance__castlevania-circle-of-.detail: Circle was a GBA launch title, dark (criticized for poorly visible graphics on the unlit screen) with a card-based spell system (DSS). Harmony is faster and more colorful with a pair of interconnected castles. Together with Aria they form the GBA trinity that fans love.
game-boy-advance__castlevania-circle-of-.article:
When the Game Boy Advance hit the market in 2001, one of its launch titles was **Castlevania: Circle of the Moon** — proof that Nintendo's new handheld could do more than just colorful platformers. Konami brought over a full-blooded metroidvania in the style of the legendary Symphony of the Night.

Circle of the Moon is dark, gothic and atmospheric to the bone. That is at the same time its famous weakness: the game was **criticized for poor graphics visibility** on the original, unlit GBA display, where dark scenes were lost in the gloom. But anyone who played on a better-lit panel or later console revisions discovered an impressively somber castle full of detail.

Mechanically the game rests on the card-based **DSS (Dual Set-up System)**. By combining two types of cards you unlock dozens of different magical effects and attacks — from elemental modifications of your whip to summoned helpers. The hunt for rare cards dropped by enemies adds another layer to exploring the castle and rewards persistence.

As a metroidvania, Circle of the Moon offers exactly what you'd expect from the genre: a sprawling, interconnected castle, the gradual acquisition of abilities that open new paths, and the constant urge to explore every corner. The combat is a touch more deliberate than in later installments, but it builds a solid foundation on which the series continued to build on the GBA.

Together with Harmony of Dissonance and Aria of Sorrow, Circle of the Moon forms a trinity that fans love. It's the first chapter in the story of how classic Castlevania was reborn in pocket form — and even with its minor ailments, it's a chapter worth experiencing.

**Why play it:** An atmospheric gothic metroidvania and GBA launch title with an addictive card-based spell system — the cornerstone of the beloved Castlevania trinity.

game-boy-advance__castlevania-harmony-of.teaser: Two more excellent metroidvanias; together with Aria, the holy trinity.
game-boy-advance__castlevania-harmony-of.article:
Between the dark Circle of the Moon and the brilliant Aria of Sorrow stands **Harmony of Dissonance** — the middle installment of the gondola-like Castlevania trinity on the Game Boy Advance, which took a lesson from its predecessor and set off in the opposite direction.

Where Circle of the Moon was dark and at times hard to read, Harmony is **markedly faster, more colorful and more legible**. Konami clearly responded to the complaints about visibility on the unlit display and pushed for a richer, more contrasting palette. The hero's movement is nimble, the combat straightforward, and the game's overall pace is among the most dynamic in the series.

The most conspicuous mechanic is the system of **two interconnected castles** between which you switch. Moving between the two versions of the castle expands the map, opens new paths and gives both the puzzles and the exploration an interesting spatial layer — the best of the metroidvania, where you keep returning and discovering how the individual parts of the world connect.

As part of this "holy trinity" of GBA Castlevanias, Harmony of Dissonance offers everything you'd expect from the genre: the gradual acquisition of abilities, a sprawling tangled castle, and that elusive joy when you finally break through a door that had been teasing you for so long. It's a title fans place without hesitation among the excellent metroidvanias, even though today it's most often remembered in the shadow of its successor.

Anyone who fell in love with Aria of Sorrow and wants another helping of pocket Castlevania will find here a fast, varied and cleverly designed adventure that elegantly rounds out the trinity.

**Why play it:** A fast, colorful and cleverly designed metroidvania with a system of two interconnected castles — a solid part of the beloved GBA Castlevania trinity.

game-boy-advance__mega-man-zero.teaser: Brutally challenging, stylish action; a cult favorite among hardcore players.
game-boy-advance__mega-man-zero.detail: Created by the studio Inti Creates (founded by former Mega Man developers). A brutally challenging, stylish series with Zero, characterized by a performance rating after each mission (the better you play, the more abilities you get). Gorgeous pixel art (designs by Toru Nakayama). Rewards mastery; a cult favorite among hardcore players.
game-boy-advance__mega-man-zero.article:
Forget everything you know about forgiving platformers. **Mega Man Zero** is a series that makes you die, again and again, until you nail every jump and every strike to the millimeter — and it's precisely for this that hardcore players fell in love with it.

Behind the series stands the studio **Inti Creates**, founded by former developers of the classic Mega Man games. The main character is Zero, a metallic warrior with a laser sword, and the whole game is built on **brutal difficulty and style**. The combat is fast, aggressive and demands mastery — the reward for precise play is a deep satisfaction that other action platformers only rarely offer.

Genius lies in the system of **performance rating after each mission**. The better and cleaner you get through a level, the higher grade you receive — and the more likely you are to retain access to new abilities. The game thus actively pushes you to improve, not to lean on crutches and to strive for perfection. It's a design that doesn't coddle but forges a better player.

Visually the series excels. The gorgeous pixel art and distinctive character designs from the hand of **Toru Nakayama** give the series a strong, melancholic identity — a post-apocalyptic world where reploids and humans fight for survival. The aesthetic is stylish, more mature and more serious than you'd expect from the Mega Man brand.

Four installments (2002–2005) form a tight, story-connected whole and together represent one of the most respected action series on the Game Boy Advance. It's not a game for everyone — but for those who crave a challenge and a reward for mastery achieved, it's a small treasure.

**Why play it:** Stylish, uncompromisingly difficult action that rewards mastery — a cult gem for players seeking a genuine challenge.

game-boy-advance__mega-man-battle-networ.teaser: Grid-based action RPG; a huge, addictive series.
game-boy-advance__mega-man-battle-networ.detail: An alternate universe where Mega Man isn't a robot but a „NetNavi“ inside the internet. Battles take place on a 3×3 grid in real time and you build a deck of „Battle Chips“ with attacks — a mix of action and deckbuilding. A huge, addictive series (6 main installments), a phenomenon in Japan with an anime.
game-boy-advance__mega-man-battle-networ.article:
What if Mega Man weren't a combat robot but a program living in the depths of the internet? It's precisely on this idea that **Mega Man Battle Network** rests — an alternate universe in which Capcom took the classic brand and turned it into one of the most addictive action RPGs on the Game Boy Advance.

In this world you're an ordinary boy named Lan, and your partner is a **NetNavi** called MegaMan.EXE, whom you send into the interconnected network to carry out tasks and fight. The story combines everyday life with adventure in cyberspace and builds a surprisingly rich, distinctive world with its own mythology.

The heart of the game is an utterly unique battle system. Fights take place in real time on a **3×3 grid**, across which MegaMan moves, dodges attacks and returns them. Your ammunition meanwhile is assembled from a deck of **Battle Chips** — cards with various attacks and effects that you put together both before each clash and during it. It's a clever mix of an action reflex game and deckbuilding, without any real equivalent.

Building the deck, hunting for rare chips and optimizing your strategy make Battle Network an incredibly **addictive** affair. You collect, combine, tune — and before you know it, hours have vanished. The series comprises six main installments, and each develops the mechanics and story further.

In Japan, Battle Network became a genuine **phenomenon**, accompanied by an anime and a whole multimedia machine. For many players it was a gateway to the RPG genre altogether, and today the series belongs among the most distinctive things the GBA offered from the Capcom workshop.

**Why play it:** An original mix of grid-based action and deckbuilding in a cleverly built cyber-world — a huge, addictive and unmistakable series.

game-boy-advance__super-mario-advance-4-.teaser: The best Mario of all time in portable form.
game-boy-advance__super-mario-advance-4-.detail: A port of perhaps the best 2D Mario game (SMB3, 1988) with improved graphics from All-Stars and e-Reader support — by scanning cards you unlocked bonus levels and items (today available via patches). The pinnacle platformer in your pocket.
game-boy-advance__super-mario-advance-4-.article:
There's a serious debate about which 2D Mario game is the best ever — and **Super Mario Bros. 3** from 1988 stands firmly at the top of it. And this exact giant you can slip into your pocket thanks to **Super Mario Advance 4**.

It's a port that takes the unrivaled level design of the original and dresses it in the **improved graphics from the All-Stars version** on the SNES. Richer colors, cleaner sprites, added voice acting — everything that made SMB3 timeless remains here, just in a prettier coat. The Tanooki suit, flying with the Super Leaf, brilliantly built worlds: this platformer was genius in 1988 and it's genius today.

The most interesting addition was **e-Reader** support. By scanning special cards you unlocked entirely new bonus levels, items and variants — a clever, if slightly impractical, experiment in expanding the game with physical collectible cards. Today this content is available via community patches too, so you won't miss out on anything.

The port is faithful and brisk, the controls precise, and the whole game runs like butter on the GBA. For players who never experienced the original on the NES, it's the ideal way to discover one of the most influential titles in the history of the genre. For veterans, meanwhile, it's a convenient, portable version of a classic you can return to endlessly.

At its core, Super Mario Advance 4 is a celebration of a perfect game. It spoils nothing, only adds — and sends the supreme 2D platformer where it belongs: everywhere with you.

**Why play it:** Perhaps the best 2D Mario of all time in a finely tuned portable form, plus bonus content from the e-Reader — a timeless classic in your pocket.

game-boy-advance__kirby-and-amazing-mirr.teaser: Kirby with an open, interconnected map; a metroidvania flavor.
game-boy-advance__kirby-and-amazing-mirr.detail: An experimental Kirby with an open, interconnected map (one big world instead of linear levels) and co-op of up to four Kirbys controlled by AI or players. An exploratory flavor close to a metroidvania. A refreshing detour from the series.
game-boy-advance__kirby-and-amazing-mirr.article:
A pink blob that swallows everything it comes across is usually synonymous with a laid-back, linear platformer. **Kirby & the Amazing Mirror**, however, breaks this pattern — and sets off on a trip into a world that resembles a metroidvania more than a classic Kirby.

Instead of a series of separate levels, the game drops you into **one large, interconnected world** that you explore freely. The individual areas link up, branch out and connect, so you get a sense of genuine discovery — you return, look for shortcuts and gradually uncover a map divided into mirror kingdoms. It's a refreshing detour that gives the series an entirely different rhythm.

Kirby naturally retains his most famous ability: **copying the traits** of swallowed enemies. Swallow a creature with a sword and you gain a blade, swallow a fiery one and you start spitting flames. This mechanic takes on new meaning in the open world — different abilities open up different paths for you.

Also unique is the **co-op of up to four Kirbys** at once, controlled either by fellow players or by artificial intelligence. You can summon helpers at any time, and their presence lends both exploration and combat a pleasant dynamic. Visually the game is exactly as cute, colorful and welcoming as you'd expect from the brand.

Kirby & the Amazing Mirror is an experiment that paid off: it takes the series' friendly, undemanding soul and combines it with an appetite for discovery. For fans of metroidvanias it's a welcoming gateway to the genre, for Kirby fans a pleasantly unconventional adventure.

**Why play it:** A cute Kirby in an open, interconnected world with a metroidvania flavor and four-hero co-op — a refreshing detour from the series.

game-boy-advance__kirby-nightmare-in-dre.article:
Sometimes the best experience lies in going back to the roots. **Kirby: Nightmare in Dream Land** is exactly such a case — a loving remake of the pink puffball's very first adventure for the Game Boy Advance, dressing the classic in a modern, vibrant coat.

The game builds on the timeless essence of Kirby platformers: you control the adorable hero, who can **inhale enemies** and spit them out as a projectile, or take over their abilities. Swallow a fiery foe and you breathe flames; swallow a sword-wielding fighter and you wield a blade — this copy-ability mechanic gives an otherwise accessible game surprising variety and invites experimentation.

Visually, Nightmare in Dream Land makes full use of the GBA's color display. A rich palette, clean sprites and fluid animation make a stroll through Dream Land a joy for the eyes. In terms of design the game is welcoming and friendly — ideal for younger players and for anyone craving a relaxing, well-tuned platformer without frustration.

The pacing is brisk, the levels inventive and the overall feel exactly what you expect from the Kirby brand: laid-back, warm and full of little ideas. This is not a title that wants to punish you — it wants you to have fun, discover abilities and enjoy its carefree atmosphere.

Nightmare in Dream Land is proof that a good foundation ages slowly. It takes an ancient idea, polishes it to a shine and offers it to new generations in the most accessible form possible.

**Why play:** A brilliantly remade classic with the iconic copy-ability mechanic — an accessible, laid-back and beautiful platformer for everyone.

game-boy-advance__wario-land-4.teaser: Frantic pace, great style; the peak of the series.
game-boy-advance__wario-land-4.detail: The wildest Wario Land both visually and musically (a bizarre soundtrack, grotesque design). The mechanic: you clear a level, grab a switch and then have to sprint back to the exit before time runs out. When hit, Wario transforms (fat, drunk, flattened), which opens up new paths. The peak of the series on a handheld.
game-boy-advance__wario-land-4.article:
If any game on the Game Boy Advance can show what „controlled madness“ means, it is **Wario Land 4**. A bizarre soundtrack, grotesque design and a pace that never lets go — this is the peak of Wario's solo adventures and one of the most distinctive platformers on the entire console.

Wario is no heroic savior; he is a greedy, unscrupulous scoundrel out for treasure. And his game is every bit as quirky as he is. Mechanically it works on a brilliant twist: first you calmly explore a level and find a **switch**, but activating it starts a countdown — and you have to make the **sprint back to the exit** before time runs out. A leisurely exploration suddenly turns into a frantic dash.

The most fun part is how Wario reacts to being hit. He doesn't die — instead he **transforms**. He swells up like a balloon, gets drunk and staggers, flattens out after an impact, bursts into flames. Each state has different abilities and opens up different paths, so „damage“ becomes a puzzle-solving tool. It's an idea so bold and funny it has no equal anywhere else.

Add to that audiovisuals that teeter on the edge of a feverish dream. The **soundtrack** is wild, at times unsettling, at times gripping, and the visual style is grotesquely exaggerated. Wario Land 4 has no interest in being cute — it wants to be memorable, and it succeeds perfectly.

The result is a platformer that combines clever design with unbridled creativity. Pace, style and mechanics all fit together so well that they make Wario Land 4 the peak of the series in handheld form and a little gem in the GBA catalog.

**Why play:** An insanely stylish and inventive platformer where taking damage becomes a tool and the pace never lets up — the peak of the Wario Land series.

game-boy-advance__warioware-inc-mega-mic.teaser: Hundreds of five-second microgames; pure joy.
game-boy-advance__warioware-inc-mega-mic.detail: The birth of the „microgame“ genre: hundreds of 3–5-second minigames race one after another at ever-increasing speed, and you have to instantly grasp what to do (open, dodge, catch). It grew out of an experiment by the Wario Land team. Bizarre humor and aesthetics; it founded a long-running series.
game-boy-advance__warioware-inc-mega-mic.article:
Five seconds. That's all you get to figure out what the game wants from you and manage to do it — dodge, catch, press, open. And then the next one immediately. And another, faster. Welcome to **WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgame$!**, a game that literally invented a new genre.

The concept is radically simple and brilliant at the same time: hundreds of **microgames**, each lasting three to five seconds, come at you one after another in an ever-accelerating stream. You get no instructions — just a single word of a hint and a moment to figure out what's being asked of you. Reflexes, intuition and quick thinking are everything.

The beauty lies in that endless surprise. One moment you're dodging an obstacle, the next you're catching a falling object, picking the nose of a drawn character or completing an absurd task with no obvious logic. **Bizarre humor and aesthetics** — crude drawings, photographs, primitive 3D, all thrown together — turn every attempt into a little show.

The game was born as an **experiment by the Wario Land team** and carries Wario's name precisely for that mischievous, unpredictable nature. An entirely new gaming language was born here: speed, chaos and the pure joy of never knowing what's coming. It's the ideal title for short bursts as well as for group play, where the others have fun watching your confusion.

Mega Microgame$! didn't just found a series that continues to this day — it defined a whole category of games. And yet it retains its freshness even today, because its essence is timeless: pure, distilled fun in its most unadulterated form.

**Why play:** The founder of the microgame genre — hundreds of five-second bits of madness in an accelerating stream, full of bizarre humor and pure joy.

game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-vi-advan.teaser: The best version of possibly the best Final Fantasy.
game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-vi-advan.detail: The best version of the 1994 classic: a new translation, added characters, dungeons and bosses. A story with an ensemble of 14 characters and no single main hero, plus the mad clown Kefka, who — rarely — actually succeeds in destroying the world. The opera scene is legendary. Considered by many the best FF.
game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-vi-advan.article:
There are games that spark endless debates in bars, pubs and on the internet, and Final Fantasy VI is one of them. For a lot of players it is simply the best Final Fantasy ever made — and the 2007 Game Boy Advance version is the best way to reach that legend on a small screen.

The original game from 1994 (released in the West at the time under the confusing name Final Fantasy III on the SNES) was Square's crowning achievement of the 16-bit era. The GBA port by studio Tose under the Square Enix banner brought a new, far more faithful translation, two new dungeons, four new Espers and several bonus bosses. It is essentially the definitive edition — the complete content of the original game plus things fans had awaited for years.

What makes Final Fantasy VI so exceptional is its boldness. It has no single main hero. Instead you juggle an **ensemble of fourteen playable characters**, each with their own story, motivations and personal demons — from the repressed mage Terra to the gambler Setzer to a little boy caring for an abandoned grandfather. The storytelling thus resembles a mosaic of fates rather than a classic tale of a chosen one.

And then there's Kefka. A mad clown who works his way up from an annoying henchman to something rarely seen in video games of that time: **a villain whose plan actually succeeds**. Halfway through the game the world falls to ruin and you have to gather your scattered heroes across a bleak, apocalyptic landscape. This audacity makes VI the most emotionally powerful entry in the series.

The opera scene is legendary too — a pixel songstress on stage, Nobuo Uematsu's music and the moment when a 16-bit console suddenly tugs at your heartstrings in a way no one expected. The combat system with Magicite and the ability to teach characters almost any spell gives you enormous freedom in building your party.

**Why play:** Because it is the peak of classic JRPG storytelling in its most complete portable form — a story that will stay in your head for years.

game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-tactics-.teaser: Deep turn-based tactics; dozens of hours.
game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-tactics-.detail: A looser, more accessible tactics game than the original FFT, set in a version of Ivalice dreamed up by children. A deep job system (over 30 classes tied to races) and a controversial court system (Laws) that limits what you're allowed to do in battle. Hundreds of hours of content.
game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-tactics-.article:
If you ever thought turn-based strategy was dry and inaccessible, Final Fantasy Tactics Advance will convince you otherwise — and it does so with incredible depth hidden beneath a friendly surface.

Studio Square took its cult but rather tough tactics from the first Final Fantasy Tactics and sanded off the sharpest edges. The result, from 2003, is a more accessible but still immensely rich turn-based strategy set in a dreamlike version of the world of Ivalice. And that very framing is brilliant: a group of children finds an old spellbook and wakes up in the fantasy realm they had always longed for. The question of whether such an escape from reality is actually a good thing pervades the whole story.

The heart of the game is a **job system with more than thirty classes**, tied to five playable races. Each unit learns skills by equipping weapons, combines abilities from different professions and grows into exactly the shape you envision. The options for building a party are practically inexhaustible, and experimenting with them is fun for dozens of hours in itself.

The most discussed element, though, is the **system of laws (Laws)**. Before each battle, rules apply that forbid certain actions — for instance using swords, targeting specific enemy types or healing. Break them and you risk a penalty. Some find it annoying, others see in it a brilliant tactical layer that forces you to think differently and improvise. Either way it's the unmistakable signature of this game.

There's a huge amount of content here: hundreds of missions, a combat arena, clan-building, gear collecting and the gradual unveiling of the story about what Ivalice truly is. On the GBA it's one of the most expansive experiences of all — it can easily keep you busy for hundreds of hours and you'll still be discovering new combinations.

Visually the game benefits from a clean, colorful style and pleasant isometric graphics that read wonderfully on a small screen. Hitoshi Sakimoto's music lends the campaign a suitably majestic air.

**Why play:** For the boundless depth of the job system and dozens of hours of tactical thinking in one of the most accessible strategy games ever released on a handheld.

game-boy-advance__sonic-advance-1-3.teaser: The best 2D Sonic outside Sega; fast and snappy.
game-boy-advance__sonic-advance-1-3.detail: After Sega's collapse as a hardware maker, Sonic appeared for the first time on a rival's console. Developed by Dimps (later authors of Sonic Rush). The most faithful 2D Sonic outside the original Mega Drive — fast, snappy, with the classic hunt for Chaos Emeralds. The third game adds a partner system.
game-boy-advance__sonic-advance-1-3.article:
When Sega packed up making its own hardware in 2001, something unthinkable happened: its mascot, the blue hedgehog Sonic, ran off onto its arch-rival's console for the first time in history. And on the Game Boy Advance it was no compromise — it was a small series that showed 2D Sonic still had plenty to offer.

Development was handled by studio Dimps, later famous for the Sonic Rush series, in collaboration with Sonic Team. And it shows at every step: the Sonic Advance trilogy is among the **most faithful 2D Sonic outside the original arcades of the Mega Drive era**. Speed, momentum, loops, springs and that inimitable feeling of building up pace after a long slope — everything is just as it should be.

The classic formula stays intact: you race through levels against the clock, collect rings, hunt for hidden Chaos Emeralds in special stages and, at the end of the zones, clash with Eggman's machines. The first game offers four playable characters including Amy with her own play style, the second adds Cream and her floating abilities.

The third game stretched out the most, though, introducing a **partner system** — you pick a pair of characters whose combination unlocks various tag actions and movement abilities. This opens up exploring and replaying levels with a different approach, giving the series an unexpected replay value.

The graphics are fresh, colorful and full of detail that the GBA handles with ease. The levels are designed to reward both players chasing speed and those who like to explore alternative routes up top and down below. It's just the right balance between adrenaline and a well-tuned platforming feel.

For anyone who grew up with the hedgehog on the Mega Drive, the Sonic Advance games feel like coming home — and for newcomers they're the ideal gateway into why classic 2D Sonic was so beloved.

**Why play:** The best 2D Sonic outside Sega — fast, snappy and faithful to the classics, the ideal dose of the blue hedgehog on the go.

game-boy-advance__astro-boy-omega-factor.teaser: Treasure at full tilt; action that won't let you go.
game-boy-advance__astro-boy-omega-factor.detail: From Treasure (masters of action, authors of Gunstar Heroes) based on Osamu Tezuka's classic anime. It combines a beat 'em up with shmup elements and surprising narrative depth (time loops, new endings after repeated playthroughs). A gem both visually and in gameplay; underrated.
game-boy-advance__astro-boy-omega-factor.article:
When you say a licensed game based on an anime, most players picture a soulless quick cash-in. Astro Boy: Omega Factor is the exact opposite — and behind it stands a name that commands respect in action circles: Treasure.

Studio Treasure, masters of Japanese action and authors of the legendary Gunstar Heroes, set out in 2003 to adapt a classic work by Osamu Tezuka, the founder of modern manga. And they didn't take it lightly. Omega Factor is a loving tribute to Tezuka's oeuvre that brings in dozens of characters from his sprawling universe, not just from Astro Boy himself.

In terms of gameplay it's a **masterful blend of genres**. The core is a brisk beat 'em up where Astro punches and kicks hordes of enemies, but Treasure interlace it with passages reminiscent of a shmup, where you hurtle through the air spraying the screen with fire. The fights are fast, readable and full of ideas — exactly the kind of action that won't let you go.

The biggest surprise, though, awaits in the story. Omega Factor hides a **time-loop mechanic**: after the first completion a new layer of narrative unlocks, where with newly gained abilities you travel back in time and change characters' fates to avert a tragedy. What at first glance seems an ordinary action game thus becomes a story with unexpected emotional depth and meaningful replay value.

Visually the game is a gem. Detailed sprites, fluid animation and colorful backgrounds show what the GBA can do in the hands of true craftsmen. Treasure, as always, pushes the hardware where others give up, and the result still looks spectacular years later.

And yet Omega Factor remained one of the most underrated games on the console. It didn't get the attention it deserved, and today it's something of a hidden gem that enthusiasts swear by. If you like action with an idea and a soul, it's a must.

**Why play:** Treasure at full tilt — a genre blend of action and shooting with a surprisingly deep story about time, loss and hope.

game-boy-advance__drill-dozer.teaser: Game Freak outside Pokémon; you drill through the levels, original.
game-boy-advance__drill-dozer.detail: A rare title from Game Freak (authors of Pokémon) outside their main series. You control a girl named Jill in a mech with a giant drill, with which you drill through walls, turn gears and solve puzzles. The cartridge had rumble (vibration). A juicy drilling feel; original.
game-boy-advance__drill-dozer.article:
Game Freak is a name the overwhelming majority of players associate exclusively with Pokémon. But now and then the studio allowed itself a detour away from its monstrous gold mine — and Drill Dozer from 2005 is the best demonstration that it can do something completely different too.

You play as a girl named Jill, who squeezes into a mech equipped with a giant drill and sets off for revenge and for a stolen treasure. The whole game rests on one brilliantly simple idea: **you have a drill for everything**. You drill through walls, crush enemies, turn gears and locks, spin propellers and climb upward — drilling here is movement, attack and puzzle-solving all in one.

The magic lies in how tangibly the whole thing works. The drill can be shifted into different gears, so you tune between speed and power depending on the situation. The feeling when you bite into an obstacle, build up revolutions and finally gnaw your way through to the other side is unexpectedly satisfying — Game Freak squeezed the most out of this single mechanic.

The technological cherry on top was that the **cartridge contained a vibrating rumble module**. While drilling, the game buzzed pleasantly in your hands and the physical feel of drilling through was heightened even further. On the GBA it was a rare gimmick that pushed the game closer to actually holding a running machine.

The levels are cleverly designed — they combine platforming action with exploration and puzzles into which the drill is worked in a little differently each time. Visually the game is colorful, striking and full of the distinctive character Game Freak never lacked.

Drill Dozer stayed rather off the main radar, but among connoisseurs it counts as an original and heartfelt title of a kind that rarely came to the console. It's proof that even the creators of one of the most successful gaming phenomena had the urge to really play around with an idea.

**Why play:** An original platformer built on a single, beautifully tuned drilling mechanic — Game Freak outside Pokémon in its best form.

game-boy-advance__mother-3.detail: The third entry in the EarthBound/Mother series by Shigesato Itoi, never officially released in the West (there is an acclaimed fan translation that arose as a protest and a proof of demand). It combines bizarre humor with unexpectedly dark, mature themes (death, loss, industrialization) and a rhythmic combat system (combos in time with the music). For many one of the best stories in the medium.
game-boy-advance__mother-3.article:
Some games become legends not because of sales or marketing, but because of how deeply they burrow under people's skin. Mother 3 is exactly such a case — a title the West never officially got, and yet it built up a cult here that many a blockbuster series might envy.

The third entry in the Mother series (known in the West as EarthBound) came out in 2006 in Japan only. Behind the script stands Shigesato Itoi, an essayist, copywriter and distinctive storyteller whose authorial fingerprint is felt in every line. Because the game never got an English version, fans translated it themselves — and there arose an **acclaimed fan translation that is to this day regarded as a textbook example of community work** as well as a quiet protest and proof that there was enormous demand for the game.

At first glance Mother 3 is a cute, slightly loopy JRPG full of bizarre humor, talking animals and absurd situations. But beneath that playful shell hides a surprisingly **dark and mature story** about death, loss, family and what unstoppable industrialization does to an idyllic world and its people. The game masterfully and unabashedly handles the shift from a smile to a lump in your throat.

The combat system adds a distinctive idea: it's **rhythmic**. You can chain attacks into combos by pressing the button in time with the background music. The better you hit the tempo, the longer the series of hits you chain — which turns ordinary turn-based battles into a little music game and at the same time forces you to listen to the great soundtrack.

It is precisely this union of unexpected emotional power, quirky humor and melancholy that makes Mother 3, for many players, one of the best stories ever created in video games. It's not an action spectacle or a technical miracle — it's storytelling that gets to you.

**Why play:** For one of the most powerful and moving stories in the history of the genre, hidden behind a cute facade and rhythmic battles.

game-boy-advance__klonoa-empire-of-dream.detail: The first handheld Klonoa, more puzzle than action: in 2.5D you lift and throw enemies to solve puzzles and reach inaccessible places. A charming style and Klonoa's made-up language. For fans of the series and of clever platformers.
game-boy-advance__klonoa-empire-of-dream.article:
Klonoa is a bit like a secret handshake among platformer fans — those who know it love it, and those who don't are missing a lot. Empire of Dreams from 2001 was this adorable character's first adventure on a handheld console and at the same time a lovely surprise for anyone who likes a platformer that engages the brain.

Here Namco took its dreamlike mascot — a cat-like creature with huge ears and a cap — and placed it in a **2.5D world that focuses more on puzzles than on action**. Klonoa's main trick remains: using a wind ring he inflates enemies into a bubble, grabs them and can throw them, hurl them or jump off them higher than he could reach on his own.

And it's around this single mechanic that the whole game revolves. Every level is really a little brain-teaser: you have to correctly grab and throw an enemy to reach an inaccessible platform, unlock a path or clear an obstacle. It's clever, well-tuned and gradually escalates into inventive situations that force you to think about space.

The magic of Klonoa, though, doesn't lie only in the gameplay. The series has an unmistakable atmosphere — a charming, slightly melancholy visual style and characters who speak a **made-up language** that lends the whole world a fairy-tale, dreamy mood. It's cozy, warm and a bit like an interactive animated fairy tale.

On the GBA the game ran splendidly: colorful, clean and clear, with level design tailored to portable play in smaller bites. Empire of Dreams may not be as sweeping as the series' console entries, but as a pocket portion of Klonoa and clever brain-teasers it works great.

For fans of the series it's a pleasant chapter, for lovers of puzzle-platformers an underrated gem that deserves more attention than it ever got.

**Why play:** An adorable and clever puzzle-platformer with an unmistakable dreamy atmosphere — ideal for fans of the series as well as lovers of ingenious brain-teasers.

game-boy-advance__boktai-sun-is-in-your-.teaser: Stealth action using real sunlight (the original had a solar sensor). A Konami curiosity.
game-boy-advance__boktai-sun-is-in-your-.detail: Hideo Kojima's boldest experiment: the cartridge contained a **real solar sensor** and the game reacted to real sunlight, with which you charge your weapon against vampires — you had to play outside in the sun. In emulation the light is set in software. Stealth action with breaking the day cycle. A curiosity that was never repeated.
game-boy-advance__boktai-sun-is-in-your-.article:
Imagine a video game chasing you outside into the sun. Literally. That it's not enough to just sit on the couch, but that you have to take the console out into the garden, because otherwise you simply won't get any further. This is exactly what Boktai: The Sun Is in Your Hand pulled off — and to this day it's one of the boldest experiments ever created.

Behind this crazy idea from 2003 stands none other than Hideo Kojima, the creator of Metal Gear, with his team under the Konami banner. And their move was utterly unexpected: **the cartridge contained a real solar sensor**. The game thus reacted to real sunlight falling on the console, and with that light you charged your main weapon — a solar gun against vampires.

The logic was brilliantly straightforward: you're a vampire hunter and your enemies can take only as much as vampires in folklore can — that is, the sun kills them. But to actually crumble them to dust, you had to expose them to direct light, which the game literally demanded of you outside on a bright day. Playing Boktai thus became dependent on the weather, the time of day and the season.

The game itself is a thoughtful **stealth action with RPG elements**, where you sneak through dungeons, avoid enemies and solve puzzles involving the manipulation of light and shadow.
