The day-night cycle here isn't mere scenery but a full-fledged mechanic you have to understand and use. Kojima's sense for ideas and atmosphere shows at every step.

In today's emulation the intensity of the sun is thankfully set in software, so you can enjoy the game even in a basement at midnight — although this takes away a bit of that original, physical magic. Boktai simply belongs among the curiosities that, with their connection between the real world and the game, **were never repeated**.

It's a title that's valued today more as a bold experiment and proof of Kojima's untamed imagination than as a mass-market game — and that's exactly why it's worth getting to know.

**Why play:** For a unique experience where the real sun influences the gameplay — Kojima's boldest experiment and a curiosity the likes of which will never be made again.

game-boy-advance__gunstar-super-heroes.teaser: A Treasure run & gun; pure action ecstasy.
game-boy-advance__gunstar-super-heroes.detail: A sequel/reimagining of Gunstar Heroes by Treasure. A pure action barrage full of ideas, bosses and effects pushing the GBA to the max. For fans of intense shooting.
game-boy-advance__gunstar-super-heroes.article:
If there's a studio that can wring pure action ecstasy out of a handheld, it's Treasure. And Gunstar Super Heroes from 2005 is the best proof — a barrage of ideas and explosions that pushes the GBA to the very edge of what it can do.

In it Treasure returns to its cult Gunstar Heroes from the Mega Drive era, a classic of the run & gun genre that connoisseurs revere to this day. Super Heroes is neither a direct sequel nor a plain rehash — it's more of a **reimagining** that takes the spirit of the original and recasts it into a new, snappy and modern-leaning form adapted to the handheld console.

The principle stays brutally straightforward and addictive: you run, jump and shoot with everything you've got. But beneath that simplicity hides an enormous **variety of situations** — Treasure is famous for not letting you rest for a moment. No sooner do you get used to one style of play than the game throws you into a passage with a different viewing angle, a different pace or a completely new idea.

The absolute highlights are, as always, the **bosses**. Treasure turns them into little spectacles — giant opponents that change forms, flood the screen with projectiles and force you to read their attacks and find weak spots. Each such encounter is a standalone experience and the main reason players keep coming back to this game.

Visually it's one of the flashier titles on the console. A ton of sprite effects, explosions and detail show just how deep into the hardware Treasure managed to reach. The pace is high from the very first moment and the game never lets up until the end.

Gunstar Super Heroes isn't a long epic — it's a concentrated dose of adrenaline you blast through in one breath and keep coming back to for the joy of pure action and boss fights.

**Why play:** For concentrated action ecstasy and superb bosses from Treasure — a run & gun that pushes the GBA to the max.

game-boy-advance__ninja-five-o.teaser: A cult, rare action game with grappling; a collector's gem.
game-boy-advance__ninja-five-o.detail: A cult rarity that fuses ninja swordplay with Bionic Commando-style grappling — you swing on a hook and slash with your blade. Fluid action, highly rated, but it shipped in tiny numbers and today it's a pricey collector's item. Emulation is the best way to experience it.
game-boy-advance__ninja-five-o.article:
There are games whose price on the collector's market tells a story all by itself — and Ninja Five-O is one of them. This action platformer from 2003 shipped in such small numbers that over the years it became one of the most expensive and sought-after titles in the entire Game Boy Advance library.

But fans don't worship it just for its rarity. Ninja Five-O is above all a **superbly playable action game** that cleverly combines two ideas: sword combat in the spirit of classic ninja games and **grappling à la Bionic Commando**. Your ninja carries a hook you can latch onto ceilings or platforms, swinging across chasms, over enemies, or shortcutting your way through a level.

And the magic lies precisely in that swinging. Once you catch the rhythm, movement turns into a fluid, almost dance-like flow — you slash hostages free with your liberating blade, swing through the air, and land exactly where you need to. It's the kind of control that takes a little practice, but once you master it, it delivers an unmistakable sense of freedom and command.

The levels blend action, a touch of platforming agility, and hostage rescue, all while keeping the pace brisk and the combat system clear. The game earned high marks from those lucky enough to play it — sadly, thanks to the small print run, there weren't many of them.

That very rarity makes Ninja Five-O a double-edged legend: on one hand a celebrated gem, on the other a title that few can get their hands on in its original form without seriously deep pockets. For the average player, that leaves **emulation as by far the most sensible route** to finally experiencing this underrated classic and finding out why it stirs up so much fuss.

It's a reminder that quality and availability don't always go hand in hand — and that some of the best games of their era stayed hidden purely because too few of them were ever made.

**Why play:** For fluid ninja action with addictive grappling — a cult rarity best enjoyed today through emulation.

game-boy-advance__car-battler-joe.teaser: RPG + cars; an unusual combination that works.
game-boy-advance__car-battler-joe.detail: From the Ancient studio (Yuzo Koshiro). An unusual mix: RPG progression where you build and upgrade a battle car, take on quests, and fight in arenas and an open world. An original combination you won't find anywhere else.
game-boy-advance__car-battler-joe.article:
What if someone told you that the most original action RPG on the Game Boy Advance isn't about swords and magic, but about building your own battle car and heading out into the desert? **Car Battler Joe** is exactly the kind of quiet gem most players missed and that enthusiasts now pass around as a secret tip.

Behind the game stands the **Ancient** studio, home of composer and developer **Yuzo Koshiro**, a name every lover of the Streets of Rage soundtrack knows. Publishing was handled by **Natsume**, and the result is a title that toys with genre boundaries perhaps more boldly than many a big AAA production of its time. Instead of leveling up a character, you build and fine-tune a machine: you swap out engines, armor, weapons, and chassis, and every battle becomes partly a question of how cleverly you've assembled your car.

The gameplay itself rests on an intriguing blend of RPG progression and arena combat. You take on jobs, explore a more open world, and test in duels whether your configuration holds up against opponents. There's a chunk of classic "grind and upgrade" in there, but because the rewards are new parts and rebuild options, the loop stays surprisingly addictive. Battles demand both reflexes and tactics, since the driving and aiming are active rather than turn-based.

Visually the game benefits from the pleasantly colorful, clean graphics the GBA could deliver and from a legible design that never overwhelms. It's no technical showstopper, but a craftsmanlike, honest game that knows what it wants to be. That very confidence makes it a piece that ages better than plenty of flashier contemporaries.

Today **Car Battler Joe** is more of a collector's and fan affair than a hit everyone knows, which makes it all the more rewarding for those who enjoy uncovering overlooked ideas. It's proof that the handheld gave rise to creative hybrids the big platforms didn't dare attempt.

**Why play:** If you want an RPG you haven't already played in a thousand variations and enjoy tinkering together your own machine, this is a little treasure off the beaten path.

game-boy-advance__mr-driller-2-ace.article:
Drilling has never been this tense. **Mr. Driller** is a series that took a simple idea — dig your way down through colorful blocks as deep as you can — and turned it into one of the snappiest and most addictive puzzle experiences you could have on a handheld.

The foundation comes from **Namco** and is ingeniously simple: you keep falling deeper, clearing clusters of same-colored blocks and watching two things. First, the falling blocks that can crush you, and second, your dwindling oxygen supply, which you top up by collecting air capsules on the way down. It's a constant decision between speed and caution, and it's precisely this small but relentless ticking time pressure that turns every descent into a little adrenaline race.

On the Game Boy Advance the series found its ideal home. Short, intense play sessions fit handheld gaming perfectly — you play a round at the bus stop or in a queue and immediately want another. The colorful, cartoonish style with the cute mascot Mr. Driller lends the game an unmistakable mood that contrasts with just how demanding and nerve-wracking it can get when the oxygen meter nears zero.

The title's magic lies in how quickly you grasp the rules and how long it takes to truly master them. A beginner sees only falling blocks, while a seasoned player reads whole chains and plans which block to remove so the column collapses in their favor without burying them. That depth beneath a simple surface is exactly what separates ordinary time-fillers from great puzzle games.

Mr. Driller belongs to those series that need no grand story or flashy graphics to keep you glued to the screen. A perfectly tuned loop is enough, and here it works splendidly.

**Why play:** The ideal handheld puzzler for short moments and long evenings alike — simple rules, a high skill ceiling, and an addictiveness that's hard to walk away from.

game-boy-advance__polarium-advance.article:
Black and white, one rule, endless possibilities. **Polarium Advance** is proof that the best logic games get by with a minimum of colors and a maximum of ideas, and that a simple mechanic can keep you at your console longer than you'd care to admit.

The principle is elegant: before you is a grid of black and white squares, and with a single unbroken stroke you flip their color. The goal is to arrange each row so it's uniform, because only such rows disappear. It sounds trivial, but once the playing field fills up and you have to plan one clever move that triggers a cascade, the game turns into a real brain-teaser where every move counts.

On the Game Boy Advance the title presents itself in a clean, minimalist style that suits the game's essence — no needless distractions, just you and the grid. This visual modesty is entirely deliberate and underscores that this is about pure thinking. The game alternates a puzzle mode with pre-built brain-teasers, where you look for the single correct solution, and a freer mode reminiscent of endless stacking, so both fans of calm puzzles and those chasing high scores will find something for them.

Polarium's magic lies in that "aha" moment when you suddenly see how a single move dissolves several rows at once. It's the kind of satisfaction familiar to fans of the best puzzle games, and here it comes in doses precisely measured for handheld play. Easy to learn, hard to truly master.

Among the GBA's puzzle titles, this is one of the more elegant and less overexposed ideas, deserving more attention than it got.

**Why play:** For anyone who loves clean logic puzzles with no frills — instantly understandable, yet with a depth that rewards patient planning.

game-boy-advance__denki-blocks.teaser: A trio of solid logic games for the in-between moments.
game-boy-advance__denki-blocks.detail: A trio of logic games for the in-between moments. Mr. Driller (you drill your way down and watch your oxygen) is snappy and colorful, Polarium is about flipping black-and-white squares, and Denki Blocks is about sliding colored blocks. Solid brain-teasers.
game-boy-advance__denki-blocks.article:
Three brain-teasers, one shared magic — the knack of grabbing you for five minutes and not letting go for an hour. **Denki Blocks!** is the name hiding an honest logic game on the Game Boy Advance whose principle is to slide colored blocks around the playing field so they join up into the required shapes.

The trick is that you can't move one piece in isolation. When you push a block in one direction, all the other blocks of the same color move with it until they hit an obstacle. What looks at first like trivial shuffling thus becomes a spatial puzzle where you have to think ahead and reckon with each move affecting the whole group at once. This single elegant mechanic carries the entire game and offers surprising depth.

What's lovely about games of this kind is how gently they start and how imperceptibly they ramp up. The first levels teach you the rules in a moment, but later you catch yourself pondering over a single screen, mentally replaying sequences of moves in reverse. No stress from a countdown, just the pure joy of finding a solution — exactly the kind of relaxing yet clever gaming that shines best on a handheld.

Denki Blocks! belongs to the fine tradition of the British puzzle school that gave rise to a whole array of catchy brain-teasers. Visually the game is simple and clear, because it's not about effects here but about the idea and its hundreds of variations. It's precisely the quantity and inventiveness of the levels that separates a shallow time-filler from a full-fledged puzzle.

On the GBA, which teemed with puzzle games, Denki Blocks! holds its ground thanks to a clean, well-tuned mechanic and how considerately it leads the player from simple to properly tricky puzzles.

**Why play:** If you love logic games you can think over at your leisure, this is the ideal companion for the in-between moments — a simple rule, plenty of tricky levels, and a pleasant sense of accomplishment from every solved puzzle.

game-boy-advance__goodboy-galaxy-ish.article:
Every now and then someone takes long-abandoned hardware and creates a game on it more beautiful than many a period original. **Goodboy Galaxy** is exactly that case — a modern indie platformer designed to run on a real Game Boy Advance, even though the world moved on to far more powerful machines long ago.

As a modern indie title for the GBA, this game falls into a fascinating phenomenon of the current scene, where passionate creators write new games for classic consoles. It's not a nostalgic imitation but a full-fledged platformer that harnesses the best the handheld can do while adding a sensibility and design maturity that comes from today's understanding of the genre. The result is a project standing with one foot in the golden era of the GBA and the other in the contemporary indie world.

With platformers of this kind it's always crucial how the game controls and how the character's movement "feels" in your hands, and this is exactly where modern indie titles often excel, because their creators grew up on the genre's best representatives. So you can expect snappy exploratory gameplay, colorful environments, and an attention to detail in animation and level design that's typical of this new wave of GBA games.

The cultural significance of such projects goes beyond their scope. They're proof that a platform the manufacturer wrote off long ago lives on thanks to a community that refuses to let it sleep. For collectors and retro fans it's a small celebration — a new physical game for an old console is a rarity today, a joy to hold in your hand.

Goodboy Galaxy represents the very best of the independent spirit: love for the medium, craftsmanlike care, and the courage to bet on hardware no "sensible" person bothers with anymore. And that's exactly why it's worth attention.

**Why play:** For platformer lovers and retro enthusiasts who want to experience how new, beautiful, and honestly designed games can still be made on the old GBA.

game-boy-advance__anguna.teaser: A homebrew RPG/action game; likable community projects.
game-boy-advance__anguna.detail: Community titles of the contemporary GBA scene. Anguna is an action RPG/metroidvania originally developed as a hobby project, a likable testament to a living homebrew community.
game-boy-advance__anguna.article:
Sometimes the best way to understand the golden era of handheld RPGs is to reach for a game made not by any big studio, but by an enthusiast in their spare time. **Anguna** is exactly such a title — a homebrew action RPG with metroidvania elements that started as a hobby project and became one of the likable symbols of the living home-brew scene around the Game Boy Advance.

The game combines two genres that go together beautifully. From action RPGs it takes real-time combat, collecting gear, and the gradual strengthening of the hero, while from the metroidvania it takes an interconnected world that opens up to you as you gain new abilities. You return to previously inaccessible places, discover secret passages, and piece the map together bit by bit — precisely the loop of discovery and reward that makes people love the genre.

What's most valuable about a homebrew project is exactly what it represents. It came about not for profit or marketing plans, but from a pure desire to create something and understand how the console works inside. Anguna is thus more than just a game — it's a message that the community around the GBA is still active and that people are willing to invest their time in new content for hardware that officially retired long ago.

With titles of this kind it's fair not to expect the polish of big productions, but to appreciate the idea, the atmosphere, and the very fact that they exist. Anguna offers exactly what you'd expect from an adventurous action RPG — exploration, combat, and a sense of progress — in a package that breathes the honest enthusiasm of its creators.

For anyone interested in what gaming beyond the official catalogs looks like, Anguna is the ideal entry point into the world of homebrew creation.

**Why play:** A likable window into the living GBA homebrew community and, at the same time, an honest action RPG with metroidvania exploration for those who enjoy discovering things off the mainstream.

game-boy-advance__broken-circle.article:
Story-driven adventures were a rarity on the Game Boy Advance, which makes any title that bets on storytelling and atmosphere over action all the more intriguing. **Broken Circle** is an adventure game built on exactly what makes adventures adventures — immersion in a story and exploring the world step by step.

With the adventure genre, what matters most is always the mood and the way the game draws you into its world. Instead of reflexes and quick fingers, curiosity and the appetite to uncover what lies behind the next door are what count. You move through environments, piece connections together, and progress by understanding the world around you — precisely the kind of calmer, more contemplative gaming that forms the counterpoint to fast action games.

On a handheld like the GBA, adventures represented both an interesting challenge and an opportunity. The limited power and small display forced creators to focus on the essentials — atmosphere, environment design, and clarity. Where the big consoles could afford to lavish detail, a handheld adventure had to captivate through its idea and storytelling. That makes titles of this kind interesting pieces for players who prefer substance over effects.

Broken Circle fits into the broader tradition of adventure games whose magic lies in the feeling that you're part of some larger story and your task is to unravel its threads. It's gaming you don't rush and that rewards attention to detail.

For fans of the genre, every adventure on a platform where so few appeared is a welcome change of pace and proof of the diversity of the Game Boy Advance library.

**Why play:** For lovers of story-driven adventures seeking calmer, contemplative gaming with an emphasis on atmosphere and exploration instead of action and reflexes.

game-boy-advance__tactics-ogre-knight-of.article:
Before Final Fantasy Tactics conquered the world, there was a series that defined this kind of tough, grown-up turn-based strategy — and **Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis** is its proud representative on the Game Boy Advance. For genre connoisseurs it's one of those titles passed along as a solid tip.

The Tactics Ogre series came from the workshop of creators whose signature you'll recognize across a whole range of genre classics, and Knight of Lodis brings their characteristic style to the handheld. Awaiting you is an elaborate system of turn-based grid battles where terrain, elevation, unit positioning, and their classes all matter. You build an army, develop your soldiers' jobs, and in every clash you plan your moves ahead, because good positioning and use of the environment decide things more often than raw strength.

But Tactics Ogre was never content with mechanics alone. The series became famous for its mature, serious storytelling about war, duty, and loyalty, and Knight of Lodis honors that tradition. The story of a knight in a foreign land has its own atmosphere and weight, which means the battles aren't just a dry exercise but part of a larger narrative you care about. This combination of depth and story is exactly what ranks the series among the most respected in the genre.

On the Game Boy Advance, which was extraordinarily rich in tactical RPGs, Knight of Lodis holds a firm place precisely thanks to its legacy and honest execution. It's a game for patient strategists who'll appreciate a title that gives them nothing for free and rewards them for thoughtful advancement.

For anyone who has taken a liking to turn-based strategy and wants a glimpse at the genre's roots, this is an essential stop.

**Why play:** For lovers of demanding turn-based strategy with a mature story — the classic Tactics Ogre signature in handheld form, rewarding thoughtful play.

game-boy-advance__rebelstar-tactical-com.article:
Imagine turn-based tactics in the spirit of UFO: Enemy Unknown, but condensed into your pocket on the small screen of the Game Boy Advance. That's exactly what **Rebelstar: Tactical Command** is — a game that honors its ancestors with unusual fidelity. No wonder: behind its spiritual lineage stands the tradition of British turn-based strategy, a name every fan of the genre knows and one that reaches all the way back to the roots of the X-COM series.

The core of the game is pure turn-based tactics. You command a small squad of fighters on a square grid, manage action points, take cover behind obstacles, and calculate firing angles and hit probabilities. Every move carries weight, every lost character hurts. That's precisely the kind of tension that makes turn-based games so addictive — slow, deliberate, with the constant risk that a single mistake sends your whole turn down the drain.

On the handheld of the day this was a rarity. The GBA was home mainly to platformers, action games, and RPGs, but pure, hard turn-based tactics for more grown-up tacticians was more of an exception. **Rebelstar** fills that gap with unprecedented depth: this is no simplified pocket variant, but a full-fat tactical experience that doesn't coddle the player it respects.

Visually it bets on clarity — an isometric view, clear icons, a readable environment. That's essential in a turn-based game, because the player must understand the battlefield situation at every moment. The story framework adds motivation, but the real star remains the combat, where tactical cleverness pays off far more than reflexes.

Today it's a title more for connoisseurs seeking honest tactics on the go who aren't afraid of the challenge. If you like thoughtful battles where every move counts, **Rebelstar: Tactical Command** will reward you with a depth few would expect from a handheld game.

**Why play:** For hardcore turn-based tactics in the spirit of X-COM that you can take anywhere — demanding, thoughtful, and surprisingly deep.

game-boy-advance__star-wars-new-droid-ar.article:
Luke's lightsaber, the sands of Tatooine, and an army of droids rolling across the galaxy — **Star Wars: The New Droid Army** bets on the power of the most famous film brand of all time and packs it into an action game for the Game Boy Advance. For Star Wars fans it was a chance to take a piece of that galaxy along on their travels.

In gameplay terms it's an action adventure with a top-down and isometric perspective, where you lead a hero through enemy ranks. You wield a lightsaber, block and slash, gradually cutting through waves of droids and using the Force as well. The mix of close combat and abilities gives the game pace and an effort to offer something more than simple button-mashing.

The GBA was a grateful home for the Star Wars brand — the machine's power allowed for decent graphics and music echoing the iconic film themes. Atmosphere is key here: familiar environments, familiar enemies, and musical echoes lend even simple missions the right "galactic" flavor.

It's fair to say this is a licensed title whose ambition was to please fans and offer solid action on the go, not to redefine the genre. But that's exactly how it fulfills its role — anyone craving a serving of Star Wars on a small screen gets exactly what they expect.

Today it's more of a collector's curiosity for lovers of the brand and the history of handheld games. As part of the vast family of GBA titles from the Star Wars universe, it demonstrates just how strongly this license shaped the handheld gaming landscape of the early millennium.

**Why play:** If you want a serving of Star Wars action in your pocket and don't mind licensed straightforwardness, it offers familiar atmosphere and lightsaber slashing on the go.

game-boy-advance__star-wars-episode-iii-.article:
Anakin Skywalker's fall into darkness ranks among the most dramatic moments of the entire saga — and **Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith** tries to forge that epic tragedy into action on the Game Boy Advance. The film source gives the game a clear direction: to guide the player through a story every fan knows by heart.

In gameplay terms it's a top-down action game built around lightsaber duels. You slash, block, chain attacks, and use Force abilities against waves of enemies. The handheld version focuses on the most enticing parts of the source material — the duels and the battle chaos of the Clone Wars — and packs them into a pace suited to gaming on the go.

The game's release accompanied the film's premiere, making it a classic simultaneous licensed title meant to extend the cinema experience onto the handheld as well. Meanwhile the GBA version had to flex its muscles: presenting iconic environments and musical themes within the limits of the handheld hardware, which it manages thanks to colorful, legible graphics.

As with most film adaptations, the game aims chiefly at fans who want to relive Episode III's key moments with their own hands. It's no revolution in the genre, but an honest serving of lightsaber duels and action from a world millions of people across generations love.

Today it's an interesting document of a time when a handheld game came out alongside every big film. For collectors and the nostalgic it's one more piece in the mosaic of the enormous Star Wars gaming family on the Game Boy Advance.

**Why play:** For fans of Episode III who want to experience Anakin's fall in the form of snappy action and lightsaber duels on a handheld console.

game-boy-advance__star-wars-trilogy-appr.article:
What if the original Star Wars trilogy came to life as a classic platformer? That's exactly what **Star Wars Trilogy: Apprentice of the Force** attempts — a game that propels the player through the iconic moments of Episodes IV, V and VI in a side-scrolling view on the Game Boy Advance. It's a loving stroll through a galaxy that generations of viewers know by heart.

The gameplay foundation is a platformer with action elements: you jump, slash through enemies with a lightsaber and wield the Force. The side-on perspective gives the game a brisk pace and a traditional platforming rhythm, into which duels and occasional action sequences are woven, all nodding to famous scenes from the films — from Tatooine through Hoth to the final showdown.

The GBA was ideal for this kind of game. Side-scrolling platformers were its bread and butter, and Apprentice of the Force uses that strength of the console to tell a story the whole world knows. Familiar settings and musical motifs serve as a constant reminder of which universe you're moving through.

This is a licensed title that leans on nostalgia and recognizability rather than genre innovation. Its strength lies precisely in that combination of proven platforming mechanics and a beloved source material — the fan gets to revisit the trilogy's most famous moments while jumping and dueling along the way.

Today it's a pleasant nostalgic stop for anyone who loves both Star Wars and classic handheld platformers. Among the many GBA titles set in the Star Wars universe, it holds a special place precisely because it returns to the roots of the whole saga.

**Why play:** For fans of the original trilogy who want to experience its most famous scenes as a snappy handheld platformer with a lightsaber.

game-boy-advance__mario-kart-super-circu.article:
When Nintendo brought its racing legend to a handheld, many doubted that four buttons and no analog stick could ever handle controlled drifts. Mario Kart: Super Circuit swept those doubts away before the engines even quieted at the starting line. This game proved that the joy of drifting, banana peels and shells fits right into the palm of your hand.

Mechanically, Super Circuit stands firmly on the foundations laid by its predecessor Super Mario Kart on the SNES. The isometric view returns, using the pseudo-3D Mode 7 technique, which the Game Boy Advance handled surprisingly smoothly. The heart of the fun is the power-slide: hold the jump button in a corner, the kart breaks into a drift, and with the right timing you earn a short burst of speed. Add the classic set of items, four cups and three difficulties measured in engine sizes (50cc, 100cc, 150cc).

Development was handled by Intelligent Systems in collaboration with Nintendo, a team with a deep knowledge of the brand. The game launched as one of the first major titles for the Game Boy Advance in 2001, shortly after the console's release, and instantly became one of the reasons to pick up the handheld. Nintendo also added a bonus that became legendary: on top of twenty new tracks, the cartridge hides all the circuits from the original SNES game, unlockable by collecting coins.

It's this nostalgic layer that makes Super Circuit a bridge between generations. For many players it was the very first portable Mario Kart, and it defined expectations for the series' handheld entries for years to come. Multiplayer via link cable allowed races of up to four players, and a single cartridge was enough for the basic multiplayer game.

Critics welcomed the game warmly, and commercially it was a huge success, ranking among the platform's best-selling titles. Today Super Circuit is also available on newer devices through Nintendo Switch Online, so you can enjoy its retro charm legally without an original cartridge.

**Why play:** It's a pure-blooded handheld Mario Kart with great controls and a generous bonus in the form of the complete set of SNES tracks.

game-boy-advance__warioware-inc-mega-mic.article:
Press! Dodge! Sneeze?! WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgames! is a game that, within a few seconds, hands you a command whose failure stings — and then immediately serves up another, even more absurd one. It's one of the most original things Nintendo has ever released, and to this day it has no equal in the way it turns chaos into perfect entertainment.

The entire concept is built on so-called microgames. Instead of classic levels, the game throws hundreds of five-second challenges at you, each with a single simple objective, often expressed by a single word on screen. One moment you have to jump, the next dodge, the next perhaps pick your nose. The microgames come one after another, the pace gradually speeds up, and you must instantly read the situation and react on instinct. The controls are limited to the D-pad and a button, so all the challenge lies in the speed of recognition and your reflexes.

Behind the idea stands a team around Nintendo and a producer who had previously worked on the Mario Artist series and Wario titles. The game came out in 2003 and gave birth to an entirely new brand, in which the main antihero Wario collects money by forcing his friends to make crazy mini-games. The visuals are deliberately fragmented, mixing pixel art, photographs and cartoon characters, which perfectly underscores the sense of unpredictability.

Culturally it was a small revolution. WarioWare showed that a game doesn't need long levels or an elaborate story to keep you glued to the screen. This philosophy of short, addictive loops foreshadowed much of what would later dominate mobile gaming. The series grew with a number of sequels on the GameCube, Nintendo DS, Wii and Switch, each installment experimenting with the controls of the given console.

Critics showered the game with praise for its inventiveness and the sheer joy of playing, and to this day it ranks among the most acclaimed original concepts on the Game Boy Advance. It's a title that works just as well for five minutes on the bus as for an evening full of laughter with friends passing the console around, trying to beat each other's score.

**Why play:** If you want to experience the most creative and craziest idea on the GBA, WarioWare will sweep you away with an avalanche of five-second challenges you simply can't tear yourself away from.

game-boy-advance__mega-man-zero-2.article:
The blue bomber isn't waiting here. In Mega Man Zero 2, the reins are taken by Zero, a warrior with a lightsaber, and right from the first minutes it's clear this will be one of the most demanding platformers of its time. Capcom created a game here that doesn't forgive mistakes and rewards precise play all the more.

The gameplay system is built on a classic action platformer with running, jumping and shooting, but adds the trademark angle of the Zero series: besides the classic blaster, you fight up close with the Z-Saber lightsaber and gradually acquire more weapons. Central to it all is the form system — the so-called Elves and forms — thanks to which Zero upgrades his abilities according to your playstyle, changes attack properties and gains new skills. The game also grades your performance in each mission, which pushes players to improve and play cleanly.

Behind the series stands Inti Creates in collaboration with Capcom, and the distinctive artistic style of the characters belongs to artist Toru Nakayama. The second installment came out in 2003 and built on the success of the first Mega Man Zero, smoothing out many of the original's rough edges and making the ability system more accessible. The story continues in a bleak world where Zero defends both humans and reploids against forces that seek to destroy them.

Visually the game ranks among the best the GBA offered in the genre: detailed pixel animation, fluid combat and impressive boss fights. The Zero series is revered among fans today precisely for its difficulty and the depth of its combat system, which rewards an aggressive yet thoughtful style of play.

The four-part Zero line later received the complete Mega Man Zero/ZX Legacy Collection, thanks to which these classics are available on modern platforms, including the option to soften the difficulty for new players. For many devotees of the Mega Man brand, it's precisely the Zero era that represents the peak of action platformers on a handheld console.

**Why play:** A demanding, stylish and exceptionally satisfying action platformer for players craving lightsaber combat and a hard but fair challenge.

game-boy-advance__mega-man-battle-networ.article:
What if Mega Man didn't race across platforms but fought inside computer networks? Mega Man Battle Network 3 takes this bold idea to perfection and offers one of the most beloved entries in the entire sub-series. It's an RPG, action game and card game rolled into one, wrapped in a cyberpunk world of an interconnected future.

The heart of the game is combat on a grid measuring three by six squares. You control the network warrior MegaMan.EXE, move around your half of the field and attack using so-called Battle Chips — chips you draw both before and during battle from your own assembled palette. Each chip represents a different attack or ability, so building your own collection and strategically assembling your deck is just as important as real-time reflexes. This combination of instant action and deck-building keeps the battles feeling fresh even years later.

The series was handled by Capcom, and the third installment came out in 2003, released in two versions, White and Blue, which differ in the available chips and some content elements, similar to Pokémon. Outside of combat, the game alternates between exploring the real world, where you unravel plots surrounding the schoolboy Lan, and the internet dimension of the Net, full of long corridors, puzzles and hidden treasures.

Battle Network 3 is often singled out among fans as the peak of the series, whether for its polished combat system, the abundance of content, or its legendary punishing hidden bosses. The cyberpunk theme of an interconnected world, where battles take place inside appliances and networks, brilliantly captures the era's fascination with the internet at the turn of the millennium.

The entire Battle Network line received the collected release Mega Man Battle Network Legacy Collection, which made all the installments accessible to modern players and even revived online battles. For many players this series was a gateway to both turn-based and action RPGs, and Battle Network 3 remains its most brightly shining point.

**Why play:** An addictive mix of grid-based action and battle chip collecting in a cyberpunk world, one of the most acclaimed installments in the entire series.

game-boy-advance__final-fantasy-i-and-ii.article:
Where it all began. Final Fantasy I & II: Dawn of Souls brings to the Game Boy Advance the pair of titles that, back in 1987, launched one of the most famous brands in gaming history. And it's not a mere dry port, but a carefully polished release that finally lets these ancient classics age with grace.

The first Final Fantasy is a textbook turn-based JRPG: you assemble a party of four heroes, choose their jobs such as warrior, black mage or thief, and set out to save a world ruled by four elements. The second installment introduces an unconventional growth system, where characters don't improve through classic levels but by how often they use a given ability or weapon. Both games combine world-map exploration, descending into dangerous dungeons and random turn-based battles in which you choose each character's actions.

The original titles were created by Square (today Square Enix) under the leadership of Hironobu Sakaguchi, for whom the first Final Fantasy was meant to be his last game before ending his career — hence the name Final. Instead, a phenomenon was born. The 2004 Dawn of Souls version added improved graphics and music, a reworked interface, new bonus dungeons and bosses tied to later entries in the series, delighting seasoned fans as well.

The cultural significance of these games is hard to overstate. The first Final Fantasy helped define the genre of Japanese RPGs, established recurring motifs like crystals, black-and-white magic and character jobs, and paved the way for dozens of sequels and spin-offs. The second installment then boldly experimented with storytelling and themes of sacrifice and rebellion, making it a fascinating detour.

Dawn of Souls is today considered one of the best ways to discover these roots of the series, thanks to friendlier difficulty balancing and translation quality. For anyone who wants to understand where all those later megahits came from, this cartridge is the ideal starting point into a world that launched an entire legend.

**Why play:** The most approachable way to play the roots of the entire Final Fantasy series in a polished form with bonus content and improved balancing.

game-boy-advance__sonic-advance.article:
The blue hedgehog finally defects to enemy territory. Sonic Advance was Sonic's first adventure on a Nintendo console, and after years of a fierce console war it was an almost unthinkable event. What's more, it turned out great: this is a fast, colorful and truly Sonic-worthy platformer.

The gameplay stays faithful to the classic 2D entries from the Sega Mega Drive. You hurtle through levels full of loops, springs and steep slopes, collect golden rings that protect you from harm, and try to blast through the levels as fast as possible. Four playable characters are available: besides Sonic, also Tails, Knuckles and Amy, each controlling a little differently and having their own abilities, which gives a reason to play through the game repeatedly.

Development was handled by Dimps in collaboration with Sonic Team, and the game came out in 2001, at a time when Sega had just abandoned making its own hardware and become a publisher on other platforms. Sonic Advance thus symbolically launched a new era in which Sega's famous mascot began appearing on the devices of its former archrival. For fans it was a small miracle.

Visually the game elegantly transfers the classic Sonic style to a smaller screen, with fluid animation and a brisk pace that the GBA hardware handles without a stumble. Special stages hidden behind collecting rings and Chaos Emeralds add a challenge for those who want to see the true ending and get everything out of the game.

Sonic Advance received a warm reception as proof that classic 2D Sonic still has something to offer, and it spawned two direct sequels. For many players it was a return to the roots of the series at a time when 3D Sonic was still finding its footing. It's a lovely reminder of why the blue hedgehog once became an icon.

**Why play:** A fast and faithful 2D platformer that brings classic Sonic to a handheld Nintendo and offers four distinct playable characters.

game-boy-advance__sonic-advance-2.article:
Just when you think Sonic can't go any faster, along comes Sonic Advance 2 and shifts into a higher gear. This sequel bet everything on pure, dizzying speed and created one of the most breakneck experiences the blue hedgehog has ever offered on a handheld console.

The basic principle remains a platformer: running, jumping, collecting rings and battling the evil Doctor Eggman. But the second installment dramatically ramps up the pace and designs the levels to reward you for blasting through them at full throttle without stopping. A new playable character, Cream, joined with her chao Cheese, alongside the return of Sonic, Tails, Knuckles and Amy. Each character controls differently, so replays make sense.

Development was once again handled by Dimps in collaboration with Sonic Team, and the game came out in 2002. It arrived at a time when Sega had fully embraced the role of publisher on other platforms, and Sonic Advance 2 confirmed that the hedgehog's move to Nintendo hardware wasn't a one-off affair but a long-term direction.

A characteristic element of this game is the emphasis on acrobatic tricks and maintaining maximum speed, where Sonic lights up at sufficient pace and becomes almost unstoppable. This philosophy turns the game into an adrenaline ride, albeit at the cost of some passages needing to be memorized first. Collecting the seven Chaos Emeralds is this time tied to finding hidden special rings in each level, an infamous challenge.

Sonic Advance 2 earned a reputation as one of the fastest 2D Sonics ever, and fans remember it to this day for its energetic momentum and catchy music. For fans of the series it's a mandatory stop among the blue hedgehog's handheld entries and proof that speed never gets old.

**Why play:** A lightning-fast 2D platformer that pushes Sonic's pace to the max and adds the new character Cream with inventive abilities.

game-boy-advance__sword-of-mana.article:
The legend returns to its beginnings. Sword of Mana is a remake of the game many in the West know as Final Fantasy Adventure, the first installment of the famous Mana series. On the Game Boy Advance it received a complete overhaul and transformed into a beautiful action RPG that combines fast-paced action with a fairytale atmosphere.

Unlike the turn-based RPGs of the time, battles in Sword of Mana take place in real time. You move around the world, slash enemies with a weapon of your choice, and combine attacks with magic and special abilities. The game offers a character upgrade system, blacksmithing crafting and item collecting, plus the series' signature element of interchangeable weapons, each of which also has its own use in the environment for solving puzzles. You can experience the story as either a hero or a heroine, which slightly changes the narrative's point of view.

Behind the game stands Square Enix, and it came out in 2003 as a generous reconstruction of the 1991 original. The developers significantly expanded the story, redid the graphics into the rich and colorful style typical of the GBA era, and filled the world with new characters and content. The music was composed by Kenji Ito, the longtime composing mainstay of the Mana series, whose melodies lend the game a dreamy and melancholic tint.

The Mana series occupies a special place in the world of Japanese RPGs thanks to its emphasis on real-time action and cooperative play, made famous by the later Secret of Mana. Sword of Mana, as a remake of the very first installment, offers a look at where this esteemed line began, while presenting it in a modern and accessible form.

Even though opinions on the difficulty and balance vary among players, Sword of Mana remains a favorite choice for anyone who loves sweeping action RPGs with the lightness of a handheld console. It's a calm, atmospheric journey full of forests, castles and ancient secrets, ideal for slow exploration.

**Why play:** A charming action RPG and remake of the very first installment of the Mana series, with fast real-time combat and a fairytale atmosphere.

game-boy-advance__rhythm-tengoku.article:
Imagine someone shoving a handheld console into your hand and saying: now you mustn't watch the screen with your eyes, but with your ears. That's exactly how **Rhythm Tengoku** works, one of the boldest and most infectious rhythm titles ever released on the Game Boy Advance. The game bombards you with short mini-games in which the only thing that matters is the correct timing of a button press to the beat.

The mechanic is seemingly trivial, and that's precisely where its genius lies. You'll handle most actions with a single A button (or the D-pad), but the rhythm you have to hit is often deliberately hidden, syncopated, or the game strips away the visual cue after a while and leaves you to rely solely on your hearing. The individual mini-games have utterly crazy, surreally Japanese premises, and each has its own melody that burrows into your head for the whole day.

The developmental context is the most interesting thing about the entire game. Behind the project stands the famous musician and producer **Tsunku** in collaboration with the team around Kazuyoshi Osawa at Nintendo, that is, the people who later also stood behind the WarioWare series. It's no coincidence that **Rhythm Tengoku** shares that hectic structure of short challenges with WarioWare. The game came out in Japan in 2006 as one of the last major titles for the GBA, at a time when the successor Nintendo DS already reigned.

Culturally it's a cornerstone of the entire later Rhythm Heaven series (Rhythm Paradise in Europe), which on the Nintendo DS, Wii and 3DS grew into hundreds of thousands of copies sold worldwide. The original Game Boy version, however, never officially left Japan, which made it a little legend among collectors and import fans, one long tended to in the West through fan translations.

The graphic style is also characteristic: a clean, flat cartoon aesthetic with bold colors and minimalist characters, which became the visual signature of the entire series. The game proves that the limited GBA hardware could offer an experience that stands and falls on design and music, not on technical spectacle.

**Why play:** If you want to understand where the perfectly tuned Rhythm Heaven series came from, you have to start right here with the addictive, funny and ear-pleasing original.

game-boy-advance__mario-vs-donkey-kong.article:
The famous rivalry between the plumber and the giant gorilla, which began all the way back in 1981 in the arcades, received a modern and unexpectedly clever form on the Game Boy Advance. **Mario vs. Donkey Kong** casts you as Mario, who chases Donkey Kong after the thief robs the Mini-Mario toy factory. The result is a fresh mix of puzzle game and platformer that plays with the legacy of an arcade classic.

The gameplay is built on a two-phase level structure. In the first part you collect a key and use it to open the door to an elevator, while having to figure out how to get past moving platforms, switches, conveyor belts and colored toggles. In the second part you then lead the miniature Mini-Mario toy figures safely to the finish. Mario also commands a surprisingly rich repertoire of movement, including flips, handstands and throwing his own body, which makes the game both a brain-teaser and a test of dexterity at once.

The game was developed by Nintendo and came out in 2004. It conceptually follows the older Game Boy title Donkey Kong from 1994, which even back then transformed a simple arcade template into an extensive puzzle adventure. **Mario vs. Donkey Kong** carried this idea further with the GBA's fully colored graphics, fluid animation and thoughtful design of progressively harder levels.

The cultural significance of the title lies in the fact that it kick-started an entire standalone sub-series. It was followed by a number of sequels, primarily on the Nintendo DS, where the focus shifted to controlling a swarm of Mini-Mario figures with the touch pen, and in 2024 Nintendo returned to the original game with a well-made remake for the Switch. This proves how strong and viable an idea the original GBA version brought.

Thanks to its combination of accessibility and gradually increasing difficulty, the game ranks among the best-rated puzzle titles of its time on a handheld console. It offers dozens of levels, bonus phases and so-called expert worlds for players who want to push their skill to perfection.

**Why play:** It's an intelligent blend of platformer and brain-teaser that honors the arcade roots of the series while offering pleasantly challenging fun for dozens of hours.

game-boy-advance__lego-star-wars-video-g.article:
When two global brands joined forces in 2005 — LEGO bricks and the Star Wars galaxy — a phenomenon was born that redefined what a family action game could look like. **Lego Star Wars: The Video Game** retold the plot of the new prequel trilogy with unmistakable humor, where heroes and villains alike are assembled from plastic bricks and death means merely crumbling into a pile of pieces.

The heart of the game is cooperative action with light puzzle elements. You move through levels, thrash enemies with a lightsaber or blasters, collect studs (brick coins) and take apart and reassemble objects from the environment to get further. The key is switching between characters with different abilities, whether it's a Jedi with a saber and the Force, a droid able to hack a terminal, or a small character squeezing through a narrow crawlspace. The Game Boy Advance version had to adapt the content to weaker hardware, so it offered its own perspective and adjusted design compared to the big console releases.

Behind the game stands the British studio **Traveller's Tales** in collaboration with the publisher then known as Eidos, and later LucasArts and TT Games. It was this first installment that laid the foundations of the enormous LEGO games line, which grew with dozens of titles based on Indiana Jones, Batman, Harry Potter, The Lord of the Rings and Marvel.

The cultural impact is hard to overstate. **Lego Star Wars** showed that a licensed game need not be a rushed cash-in, but cleverly designed entertainment for children and their parents alike, full of references and jokes for fans of the films. The series gradually became one of the best-selling gaming brands ever and fundamentally helped the LEGO business itself.

The handheld GBA version fulfilled an important role: it let you take the galaxy far, far away with you on your travels at a time when there were no smartphones full of mobile games yet. Even with the technical compromises, it retained that light, undemanding and smiling style that became the hallmark of the entire line.

**Why play:** It's the start of the legendary LEGO series, a fresh and funny take on the prequel trilogy that will entertain Star Wars fans and the youngest players alike.

game-boy-advance__lego-star-wars-ii-orig.article:
If the first LEGO Star Wars won players' hearts with its take on the prequels, its sequel headed straight for the holy of holies. **Lego Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy** brings the classic trilogy of episodes IV, V and VI into the world of plastic bricks, the stories that entire generations grew up on. And it does so with an even bigger dose of humour and charm than its predecessor.

The gameplay foundation stays true to the proven recipe: cooperative action, smashing and rebuilding the environment, collecting studs and switching between characters with different abilities. The great draw of the original trilogy is its iconic moments, from the escape from the Death Star to the battle on the icy planet Hoth all the way to the duel in Jabba's palace. The Game Boy Advance version once again scaled the scope to fit the handheld's hardware, but it kept that playfulness and easy accessibility.

Development was handled once again by **Traveller's Tales** and the game came out in 2006. Compared with the first instalment, the sequel brought a host of improvements: richer vehicle-driving options, a more elaborate character system and more room to explore. The team clearly learned from the reception of the first game and honed the formula that, in a lightly tweaked form, still powers LEGO games to this day.

The cultural significance of this instalment lies in how it cemented LEGO Star Wars as a fixture. The original trilogy is sacred material for fans, and turning it into a cute brick parody without losing respect for the source was a daring feat. The game is full of visual gags, characters hamming it up and little references that delight connoisseurs of the films.

The GBA release had its purpose here too: it offered a portable version of the experience for players on the move and complemented the big console editions. Together with the first instalment, both titles were later combined into the collector's compilation LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga, closing the arc around the entire original set of six episodes.

**Why play it:** The classic Star Wars trilogy in a mischievous brick coat, full of humour and iconic scenes, ideal for playing together across generations.

game-boy-advance__bionicle-game.article:
At the turn of the millennium, the Danish brand LEGO took a gamble on something completely new: the dark mythology of the Toa warriors, masks of power and the island of Mata Nui. The **Bionicle** line became a huge media franchise, so a video game adaptation could hardly be missing. **Bionicle: The Game** brought this world of heroes and elements to the handheld Game Boy Advance as well.

The game is a mostly action-driven affair in which you take on the roles of the individual Toa and make your way through levels inspired by the brand's story. Each hero is tied to a particular element, fire, water, ice, stone, air or earth, and the environments and the way you move through them differ accordingly. The GBA version uses a two-dimensional perspective and puts the emphasis on combat, overcoming obstacles and pushing forward through varied locations.

The game was published by Electronic Arts and came out in 2003, at a time when Bionicle was at the peak of its popularity and the sets were selling in enormous numbers. The adaptation was meant to bring players closer to a story that until then had been told mainly through comics, animated films and set packaging. At the same time, the GBA version had to squeeze an ambitious world into the constraints of the handheld's eight-bit to sixteen-bit era.

Bionicle's cultural significance is considerable: it was one of the projects that commercially saved LEGO in the early 2000s and showed that the brick brand could build its own original fictional world with deep mythology. For many players born in the nineties, the Toa masks and the duel with Makuta are still a powerful nostalgic memory.

The video game version is therefore above all a ticket into this world for fans who wanted to live out their heroes' stories actively rather than just watch them. Even though it belongs among the licensed titles of its time, on the portable console it filled the role of a pocket adventure tied to a beloved toy saga.

**Why play it:** For nostalgic fans of the brick Toa, it is an interactive trip into the mythology of the island of Mata Nui, right in your pocket.

game-boy-advance__drome-racers.article:
Speed, futuristic tracks and a stable of luxurious racing cars, all of that is promised by **Drome Racers**, an arcade racing game that also made it to the Game Boy Advance. The name refers to a fictional world of tracks called the Drome, and the game bets on adrenaline-fuelled driving rather than realistic simulation.

The gameplay principle is a pure arcade race. You get behind the wheel, set off onto a track full of bends and jumps, and try to overtake your opponents. The GBA version uses a flattened, so-called pseudo three-dimensional perspective typical of racing games on this console, where the scenery rushes towards you and you focus on hitting the ideal line. The emphasis is on instant fun, gradually unlocking tracks and competing for the best times.

**Drome Racers** originated as part of the LEGO brand of the same name, which combined racing-car sets with a gaming world. The game was published by Electronic Arts in 2002. The GBA version is a port of a concept that also existed on more powerful platforms, adapted to the technical capabilities of the handheld.

The title's cultural context is closely tied to the wave of LEGO licensed games from the early 2000s, when the Danish company was intensively expanding its theme into video games across genres, from action through racing to adventure. **Drome Racers** is thus one of the fragments of that era when LEGO was searching for the best way to translate its brands onto the screen.

On the Game Boy Advance, the game fits into the rich tradition of handheld racing titles that had to balance a sense of speed with limited hardware. For players who enjoyed undemanding, fast racing without complicated settings, it was an accessible choice for the road.

**Why play it:** Brisk arcade racing from the era of LEGO licences, ideal for short, adrenaline-fuelled runs on a handheld without any unnecessary fuss.

game-boy-advance__lego-racers-2.article:
Racing with cars built from bricks had a solid fan base at the turn of the millennium, so it comes as no surprise that the LEGO Racers brand got a sequel in handheld form too. **Lego Racers 2** brings this colourful racing fun to the Game Boy Advance with an emphasis on family accessibility and playfulness.

The gameplay is arcade racing, in which you tear around tracks and try to outrun your opponents. A big theme of the LEGO Racers brand was always the ability to build and customise your cars out of pieces, which gave the game that typical creative layer. The GBA version handled the races in two dimensions, or rather in the pseudo three-dimensional view common to this console, and focused on brisk, easy-to-grasp driving.

The game was published by Electronic Arts in 2001 as a sequel to the successful first LEGO Racers. While the versions for more powerful platforms offered a more open environment and more options, the handheld GBA edition had to condense the concept into the constraints of portable hardware and focus on the very essence of racing.

Culturally, **Lego Racers 2** belongs to the period when LEGO was experimenting with its own gaming brands before the great success of the LEGO Star Wars series and other film licences from Traveller's Tales arrived. It is thus a witness to a time when the shape of brick video games was still being sought and when original LEGO themes without big film licences still dominated.

For players, the game was a pleasant, undemanding pastime with a theme that children knew well from playing with real bricks. The combination of building and racing gave the title its own identity among the many other arcade racing games on the market.

**Why play it:** Colourful family racing with a brick flavour, undemanding fun for younger players as well as nostalgic fans of the original LEGO video games.

game-boy-advance__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater.article:
The skateboarding series that literally dominated the gaming world at the turn of the millennium made it to the smallest screens too. **Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2** is one of the most acclaimed skating games ever, and its conversion to the Game Boy Advance proved that the spirit of this legend could be squeezed into a handheld too.

The gameplay principle rests on chaining tricks and building combos. Within a time limit you ride through the levels, complete objectives, collect the letters SKATE, hunt for hidden items and try to rack up the highest possible score. The key novelty that the series introduced precisely with the second instalment on consoles was the manual, a two-wheel ride that lets you link individual tricks into endless chains. The GBA version rendered this system in an isometric view adapted to the capabilities of the handheld hardware.

The original **Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2** was developed by **Neversoft** and published by Activision in 2000. The game is to this day considered one of the highest-rated titles in history and ranks among the top-rated games ever according to review aggregators. The soundtrack full of punk and hip hop became cult and defined the sound of an entire era.

The cultural impact of the series was enormous. Tony Hawk's Pro Skater helped popularise skateboarding among young people around the world and turned the name of real skateboarder Tony Hawk into a global brand. The games sold in tens of millions of copies across platforms and inspired an entire genre of extreme sports titles.

The handheld GBA version had a clear purpose: it offered the core pillars of the gameplay, chaining tricks and collecting scores, wherever you happened to be. Even with the technical compromises of the isometric view, it kept that addictive principle of chasing the highest possible combo, thanks to which players keep coming back to the series.

**Why play it:** A handheld version of one of the highest-rated skating games of all time, an addictive chase for the perfect combo that you can take anywhere.

game-boy-advance__banjo-kazooie-grunty-s.article:
The wicked witch Gruntilda returns from defeat, and this time she decides to take her revenge before the bear Banjo and the bird Kazooie have even had a chance to meet her. Banjo-Kazooie: Grunty's Revenge throws you into a story set in the past, and right from the start it promises what the series did best on the Nintendo 64: collecting, exploring and colourful humour condensed into handheld form.

The game keeps the core of the collectathon platformer that made the original famous. You make your way through interconnected worlds, collect musical notes, Jiggy puzzle pieces and other trinkets, solve small puzzles and gradually unlock new areas. Banjo and Kazooie once again work as a well-oiled duo with their own moves, which makes moving through the levels varied and more inventive than in an ordinary jumper. Everything is translated into an isometric top-down view that proved itself on the GBA and made it possible to preserve the full-bloodedness of the 3D original even on a small display.

The development context is interesting here. While the original instalments were made by Rare for Nintendo, this portable spin-off was developed by Rare in collaboration with external development and came out in 2003 under the THQ banner, at a time when Rare was already moving under Microsoft's wing. Grunty's Revenge is thus among the last titles under this brand that still came out on Nintendo hardware.

Culturally, it is an attempt to bring the magic of big console collectathon platformers into the handheld era, when the Game Boy Advance was proving that pocket gaming did not have to mean concessions in depth. For fans of the bear with a backpack and the cheeky feathered companion, it was a welcome way to repeat the proven formula on the move, even if on a more intimate scale than the big originals. The bet on an isometric view and less sprawling worlds was a logical concession to the hardware, yet the spirit of the series remained recognisable at first glance.

It is also interesting to place the game within the wider goings-on around the brand. After Rare's departure to Microsoft, the fate of Banjo and Kazooie on Nintendo platforms became uncertain, and it was precisely the GBA titles that represented the last chapter Nintendo got with these heroes on its hardware. In hindsight, Grunty's Revenge carries the touch of a small farewell to the era in which the two partners were synonymous with first-rate 3D platformers.

Although it never reached the fame of its console siblings, Grunty's Revenge remains an honest handheld version of a genre that is finding its admirers again today. For collectors and lovers of the classic duo, it is a lovely full stop at the end of the era when Banjo and Kazooie were among the icons of their time, and proof that even on a small display you could build an adventure with a character of its own.

**Why play it:** If you like collectathon platformers and wanted to carry Banjo and Kazooie in your pocket, this is their portable adventure in the proven style.

game-boy-advance__street-fighter-alpha-3.article:
That a full-fat arcade fighting game could fit into a handheld console without powerful buttons and with a tiny display? In 2002 Capcom proved just the opposite. Street Fighter Alpha 3 Upper is a port of an acclaimed instalment of the Alpha series (Street Fighter Zero 3 in Japan) to the Game Boy Advance and ranks among the most ambitious fighting games ever released on the platform.

At the heart of the game is a system of three fighting styles, the so-called -isms: A-ism offers classic charging and multi-level super combos, X-ism is cleaner and harder with strong single-level supers, and V-ism rests on the so-called Custom Combo, in which the player assembles their own chains of strikes. This choice fundamentally changes the pace and strategy of each fight and makes Alpha 3 one of the mechanically deepest 2D fighters of its era. Added to that is a huge roster of characters, genuinely unusually extensive for a handheld console.

The Upper version originally arose for the arcade board and Dreamcast as a tuned, expanded revision of Alpha 3 with additional fighters and balance tweaks. Capcom then ported it precisely to the GBA, where it managed a devilishly difficult job: getting two planes of detailed sprite animation and dozens of moves into hardware that on paper was not up to it. The result was technically impressive for its time, though concessions in fluidity and sound were inevitable.

Culturally, Alpha 3 is part of the golden fund of the Street Fighter series. The Alpha line fills the story space between the first instalment and Street Fighter II and is to this day valued by the community of competitive players for its depth. With the port to the GBA, this depth became accessible for the first time to those who had neither an arcade cabinet nor a home console.

Today it is a title that reminds us how far the ambitions of handheld ports reached at the turn of the millennium. It is not the ideal version of the game, that you will find on more powerful platforms, but as proof of what the GBA could pull off, it is remarkable.

**Why play it:** Mechanically one of the deepest 2D fighters of its time in a handheld rendition, ideal for Street Fighter fans who want the Alpha system on hand at any moment.

game-boy-advance__tekken-advance.article:
Tekken was always synonymous with 3D combat on big consoles, where characters intertwine in fluid polygon animation. Tekken Advance from 2001 is therefore a small miracle: Namco's three-dimensional fighter ported to the Game Boy Advance, handheld hardware without native 3D acceleration, and yet with an effort to preserve the soul of the series.

Namco borrowed the characters and combat foundation from the console Tekkens and adapted them to the GBA's buttons. The characteristic four-button system, where each button controls one limb, had to undergo simplification, but the essence remained: juggling the opponent in the air, chaining strikes and an emphasis on timing. The game bets on fast, readable fights and a compact roster of familiar fighters, among whom faces like Kazuya, King or Yoshimitsu are not missing.

In terms of development, it was one of the first attempts to get a fully fledged 3D fighter onto Nintendo's new handheld shortly after its launch. Namco was at the peak of its arcade fame at the time and Tekken was one of its crown jewels, so bringing the brand to the GBA made commercial sense, even though the technical compromises were considerable. Visually the game resembles more a two-dimensional rendition with a 3D-inspired camera than a genuine polygon engine.

Culturally, Tekken Advance is mainly an interesting footnote in the history of the series. It shows the era's effort by manufacturers to get big console brands into your pocket at any cost, before the arrival of more powerful handhelds enabled more faithful conversions. For collectors and Tekken fans it is a curiosity worth knowing.

In the end it is a playable, brisk fighter whose greatest asset is its very existence: a Tekken you could have in your backpack long before handheld 3D fighters became commonplace.

**Why play it:** A curious but surprisingly brisk attempt to bring 3D Tekken to the GBA, a draw especially for series fans and collectors of period ports.

game-boy-advance__gradius-galaxies.article:
There are series that defined an entire genre, and Konami's Gradius undoubtedly belongs among them. Gradius Galaxies, released in 2001, brings this legendary horizontal shooter to the Game Boy Advance and proves that the classic shmup formula works in your pocket too.

The heart of the game is the famous upgrade system, the so-called power-up bar. For destroyed enemies you collect capsules that move an indicator along the bottom bar, and at the right moment you choose what to activate: ship speed, missiles, double shot, laser, protective Options or a shield. This manual management of your arsenal is what sets Gradius apart from the competition, because it forces the player to think about when to invest and when to save. Galaxies adds to this the series' typical volcanic, organic and mechanical levels and battles with mighty bosses.

In terms of development, it is interesting that Galaxies was created primarily for the Western market as a distinct instalment outside the main numbered line, and in Japan it came out under the name Gradius Generation. With this Konami wanted to offer fans a fully fledged new Gradius on the GBA launch wave, not a mere port of an older title. The result is a game that honours tradition while standing on its own feet.

Culturally, Gradius recalls an era when arcade shooters were a measure of a player's skill and when a game was judged by how far you fought your way through. The series' notorious difficulty is also legendary, where a single hit means losing most of your collected equipment, which turns every cautious advance into a tense gamble.

On the GBA, Gradius Galaxies ranks among the best that the horizontal shooter genre offered on the platform. It is pure, addictive action for players who enjoy a challenge and gradual improvement.

**Why play it:** A fully fledged handheld Gradius with the iconic upgrade system, one of the best horizontal shooters on the GBA for lovers of demanding arcade action.

game-boy-advance__iridion-ii.article:
The second attempt is often the one where a studio finally hits the mark. Iridion II from 2003 is a textbook example: where the first instalment stumbled, this follow-up shooter from Germany's Shin'en Multimedia showed what brisk handheld action should look like.

Unlike the first Iridion, which was a classic horizontal shooter, the sequel shifts to a vertical and half-isometric view and bets on dynamic movement across the screen. The player collects three types of weapons that can be upgraded separately, and juggling between them according to the type of enemies forms the tactical layer of the game. The pace is fast, there are lots of enemies and the emphasis lies on smooth, arcade-styled action with bonus collecting.

Shin'en built a reputation as a technical master on the GBA. Its games were famous for how they squeezed the maximum out of the Game Boy Advance hardware, whether it was graphics or sound based on their own audio engine. Iridion II, both visually and audiovisually, belongs to what the platform could boast about, and to this day it is prized among connoisseurs as the studio's technical showcase.

Culturally, it is a title that recalls the golden era of smaller but ambitious European developers who made games on Nintendo's handhelds with care and craftsmanlike integrity. Shin'en later continued on Nintendo's other platforms and remained a respected name.

Iridion II is thus a lesser gem for shooter fans looking for something fast, tuned and visually above average on the GBA. It is not the best-known title in the library, but all the more pleasant a discovery.

**Why play it:** A technically polished shooter from the masters at Shin'en that shows what the GBA can do, ideal for players longing for fast arcade action.

game-boy-advance__mario-tennis-power-tou.article:
What if tennis were not just about hitting the ball but about your own journey from klutz to champion? Mario Tennis: Power Tour from 2005 combines arcade tennis with the Mario series and a surprisingly deep RPG mode that turns a handheld sport into something addictive.

The gameplay foundation builds on the proven formula of the Mario Tennis series by Camelot: colour-coded strokes, topspin, slice, lob and smash, and above all a system where you strengthen a well-timed shot. Added to this is a story mode in which you create your own character enrolling in a tennis academy. Training, matches and gradually raising stats give the game an RPG dimension that ordinary sports titles lack, and it motivates you to play one match after another.

In terms of development, Power Tour builds on Mario Tennis for the Game Boy Color, which introduced the same combination of tennis and character growth. Camelot, Nintendo's go-to studio for Mario sports games, thus took its idea to a more elaborate form on the GBA. The Mario characters here serve as a link to the wider world of Nintendo, but the centre of gravity of the experience lies on your own career.

Culturally, Power Tour fits into the long tradition of Nintendo taking simple sports and enriching them with its own layer of depth and humour. The Mario Tennis series became a fixture and Power Tour ranks among its most valuable handheld instalments precisely thanks to its extensive career mode.

For a player looking for a sport on the GBA that lasts longer than a few matches, this is the ideal choice. The combination of brisk tennis and gradual character growth holds you to the screen surprisingly long.

**Why play it:** Arcade tennis with an addictive RPG career mode from the specialists at Camelot, a sport that offers far more than just individual matches.

nds__new-super-mario-bros.article:
After more than fifteen years, Mario returned to where he belonged: the two-dimensional world of solid platforms, question-mark blocks and jumping turtles. New Super Mario Bros. from 2006 was the first classic 2D instalment since the days of the SNES console, and for an entire generation of players it meant their very first encounter with the way Mario was played in the eighties and nineties.

The genius of the game lies in how cleverly it combines the old with the new. The controls remain purely platforming and honed to perfection over decades, but the environment is rendered in a delicate 2.5D style, where the characters and enemies move like three-dimensional models along a two-dimensional track. New abilities were added, the most striking being the giant Mega Mushroom, after eating which Mario grows to monstrous proportions and literally smashes through an entire level, and conversely a miniature mushroom that shrinks him and opens up hidden little paths.

Development was handled by the internal studio Nintendo EAD, the same people who stood behind the main instalments of the series. The game came out on the Nintendo DS, whose lower touchscreen served to display the map and stored items, while the main action ran on the upper screen. A simple two-player battle over a wireless connection was also available.

The title's cultural significance is enormous: it proved that the classic 2D platformer is not a museum exhibit but still an immensely sellable and entertaining format. New Super Mario Bros. became one of the best-selling games on the Nintendo DS ever and ranks among the most successful titles in the entire history of the brand. Its success kicked off a whole new subseries that continued on the Wii, 3DS and Wii U consoles.

Thanks to how accessibly the game is built, even a complete newcomer can handle it, and yet it offers enough hidden challenges, three star coins in each level and secret paths to entertain even seasoned veterans as well. It is a textbook example of design that works at every skill level.

**Why play it:** A flawless modern 2D platformer that revived classic Mario for a new generation and still ranks among the best on the DS.

nds__mario-kart-ds.article:
If there is a single reason people still keep a working Nintendo DS around for just one game, it is most likely Mario Kart DS. This 2005 racing installment was the first in the series' history to let you compete against real opponents from around the world over an internet connection, turning a casual session in front of the screen into a global racing phenomenon.
