Visually the game is a notch richer, and the bosses are even more spectacular — giant alien forms that fill half the screen and demand precise targeting of weak points.

As with Contra, it shines best in two-player co-op. Advancing together through the storm of enemy fire, sharing weapons, and coordinating movement make it a great experience for two — though even solo it offers a serious challenge for players who like a game that pushes them to improve.

Super C is exactly the sequel fans wished for: more of the same, only sharper. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it perfects the run & gun recipe and remains one of the most honest action titles on the NES.

**Why play:** A polished sequel to Contra with everything that made the original great — tough run & gun action, excellent co-op, and spectacular bosses.

nes__ninja-gaiden.teaser: Cinematic cutscenes on the NES + brutal pace; a milestone.
nes__ninja-gaiden.detail: It brought cinematic, anime-style cutscenes between levels to consoles — storytelling that was groundbreaking for 1988. Brutally fast ninja action with wall climbing. Notoriously demanding (especially the final stretch). Influential for the entire genre and the later 3D reboot.
nes__ninja-gaiden.article:
Instead of throwing you straight into the action, **Ninja Gaiden** first sets the story in motion — and does so cinematically, in a way consoles in 1988 practically didn't know. Between the levels, animated, anime-style cutscenes unfold, with detailed shots, dramatic cuts, and a tale of the revenge of the ninja Ryu Hayabusa. For its time it was a small revolution in how a game could tell a story.

When you set down the controller after the cutscene, action awaits that is every bit as intense as the story. Tecmo created a lightning-fast ninja platformer here in which Ryu climbs walls, leaps from wall to wall, and cuts down enemies with his katana and throwing techniques picked up along the way. The movement is nimble and elegant, but the environment is merciless — enemies reappear the moment you shift the camera, and a single mistimed jump can knock you back whole sections.

It was precisely the difficulty that became legendary. The game's final stretches rank among the hardest the NES had to offer: the last bosses, being sent back to the start of a level after death, and precise timing that forgives not even the slightest hesitation. For many players, beating Ninja Gaiden remains a badge of honor to this day.

This game's influence reaches far beyond 1988. The combination of cinematic storytelling and fast, technical action inspired entire generations of action titles, and the franchise itself later received a highly acclaimed 3D reboot that introduced Ryu Hayabusa to a new generation as one of the toughest fighters in the genre.

So Ninja Gaiden is a double milestone at once — as a pioneer of video-game storytelling and as a test of reflexes that still challenges even seasoned players today.

**Why play:** A pioneer of cinematic cutscenes on consoles and brutally fast ninja action — a storytelling milestone and a merciless test of reflexes in one.

nes__punch-out.teaser: Boxing as a reflex puzzle; hasn't aged.
nes__punch-out.detail: Boxing conceived as a reflex puzzle: every opponent has a learnable pattern you must read and counter. The original version featured the licensed Mike Tyson as the final boss (replaced by Mr. Dream after the contract expired). Charismatic characters; hasn't aged a day.
nes__punch-out.article:
Boxing as a game of brute strength? Forget it. Nintendo's **Punch-Out!!** proved in 1987 that the ring can actually be a puzzle — and that the most important muscles in boxing are the ones that govern perception and memory. This game elevated the fistfight into an elegant riddle of reflexes.

As the diminutive Little Mac, you step up against a lineup of charismatic, wildly caricatured opponents — from Glass Joe through King Hippo to Bald Bull. Each of them has their own fixed pattern of attacks and movements. Your task isn't to swing away blindly, but to **read** that pattern: to notice a tiny twitch of an eye, the tilt of a shoulder, or some other warning sign that gives away where the blow is coming from. Then, in a split second, you dodge, block, and land your fist exactly where your opponent is exposed. It's a dance of reading and reaction, not a slugfest.

The opponents are designed with such a feel for character that they burn themselves into memory — their animations, taunts, and dance moves make them icons that fans recognize to this day. The gradual discovery of how to outwit each one gives the game a great rhythm: every new boxer is a small standalone puzzle you have to crack by trial and error.

The original version bore a subtitle with a licensed name — **Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!** — with the final boss being the real Mike Tyson at a time when he was among the most feared boxers in the world. After the licensing contract expired, he was replaced in later editions by the fictional character Mr. Dream, but Tyson's presence in that opening version made the game a phenomenon of its era.

Unlike many titles of its era, Punch-Out!! has practically not aged. Its principle of reading the opponent is so clean and timeless that you'll gladly fire the game up even today.

**Why play:** Boxing conceived as a brilliant reflex puzzle — charismatic opponents, timeless gameplay, and a piece of boxing history in the form of Mike Tyson as the final boss.

nes__battletoads.teaser: Notoriously the hardest NES game; a challenge for masochists.
nes__battletoads.detail: Rare's answer to the Ninja Turtles, notorious for its extreme difficulty — the third level, the „Turbo Tunnel“ (a hoverbike race with obstacles you must memorize), is an internet symbol of frustration. Varied level styles and co-op (with notoriously problematic friendly fire). A memetic classic.
nes__battletoads.article:
There are games that will give you a hard time, and then there's Battletoads — a game that wants to break you. For an entire generation of NES players it became synonymous with pure, cunning, at times downright sadistic difficulty, and that's exactly why it lodged itself in memory more deeply than hundreds of more polished titles.

At first glance it's a classic beat 'em up in the style that was in vogue back then thanks to the success of the Ninja Turtles — three amphibian heroes, green skin, a lightly mutant vibe, and humor. But the studio **Rare**, then at the peak of its technical prowess, refused to be boring. Every level mixes in a different style of play: one moment you're pummeling enemies with fists that comically transform into giant hammers at the instant of impact, the next you're sliding down ropes, climbing walls, or fighting your way through a snake tunnel.

And then comes the **Turbo Tunnel**. The third level, a hoverbike race in which walls, holes, and obstacles loom up before you at ever-increasing speed. It's not a test of reflexes, it's a test of memory — you have to learn the exact placement of every barrier by heart, because a single mistake means instant death. Decades after its release, this level became an internet symbol of gaming frustration, a meme and a badge of honor all at once.

Two-player co-op paradoxically makes things worse. The friendly fire here is infamous: your partner can accidentally (or on purpose) drag you across the entire screen, quickly turning a friendly party into an argument on one couch. Many pairs never got past certain sections, and it's precisely these shared defeats that today rank among the platform's most fondly remembered experiences.

Battletoads is something of a paradox: a game most players never finished, and yet almost everyone knows it. Its technical inventiveness, animations, and cheeky personality made it a cult classic whose name, even decades later, is spoken with both a smile and a shudder.

**Why play:** If you want to experience the legendary NES difficulty firsthand and understand where half of gaming's frustration memes come from, Battletoads is a must — just brace your nerves.

nes__bionic-commando.article:
What if a platformer had no jump? This single, daring question makes Bionic Commando one of the most distinctive action titles on the NES — a game that takes away your most basic ability and hands you something far more interesting in its place.

The hero, you see, can't jump. His only means of moving upward and across chasms is the bionic arm — a grappling hook you use to latch onto platforms, swing over enemies, and literally pull yourself through the world. It sounds like a limitation, but it actually changes the entire logic of play. Instead of mindless hopping, you have to plan every grab, judge the trajectory, and perceive space in a completely different way than in an ordinary platformer.

The structure is likewise unconventional. You advance across a map divided into areas that you move between, communicate with units over the radio, and infiltrate enemy bases. This layer of tactics and espionage atmosphere gave the game a pleasantly more serious, military flavor for its time, one that set it apart from the more colorful competition.

The graphics are snappy, the music catchy, and the combat system — a combination of shooting and skillful swinging — rewards those who learn to control the arm instinctively. At first you'll hang helplessly in place and plunge into chasms, but once the mechanic gets into your blood, movement becomes unexpectedly fluid and satisfying.

Bionic Commando is exactly the kind of game that stands on a single bold idea and carries it through to the end. That's precisely why it earned a reputation as a hidden gem of the NES library, and its hook became a model for a whole host of later games.

**Why play:** For the unforgettable feel of movement based purely on the bionic hook — once you get used to the absence of a jump, you won't want anything else.

nes__crystalis.teaser: A post-apocalyptic action RPG; ambitious and beloved.
nes__crystalis.detail: A post-apocalyptic action RPG (a world after a nuclear war in the year 2097) with fluid top-down combat, chargeable elemental swords, and spells. Often compared to Zelda, but with its own identity and a deeper RPG system. Highly regarded and underappreciated; it got a (controversial) GBC remake.
nes__crystalis.article:
The world ended in nuclear fire, and you awaken from a hundred-year sleep into a post-apocalyptic landscape where technology and magic have collided into one wondrous world. So begins Crystalis — an action RPG that to this day ranks among the most ambitious and at the same time most underappreciated titles on the NES.

The story unfolds after a devastating war in the year 2097, and from the very start it breathes a distinctive atmosphere: the ruins of civilization, nature come back to life, tribes and mysterious towers. Here the studio **SNK** blended a top-down action combat system with fluid controls that in many respects recalls the Zelda series, but it charts its own course. You have at your disposal swords of the four elements, which can be charged for stronger attacks, along with a set of spells and a gradually growing arsenal.

Against purely action-based clones, Crystalis sets itself apart with a deeper RPG layer. Your character gains experience, grows stronger, learns new incantations, and so combat carries weight — it's not just swinging a sword, but the gradual building of a hero capable of facing ever more dangerous threats. The chargeable elemental swords also force you to think about which element to deploy against which enemy.

On the NES the game excels both technically and in design: a vast world to explore, a decent amount of text and storytelling, fluid animations, and a soundtrack that burrows into memory. It's no wonder Crystalis built up a devoted fan base that to this day calls it one of the console's best but little-appreciated works.

The game later received a remake on the Game Boy Color, which is, however, controversial among fans — it changed the story and the atmosphere, and for many the original remains the clearly better version.

**Why play:** For a post-apocalyptic world full of ideas and the combination of action with a real RPG — Crystalis is a quiet gem of the NES that deserves far more attention.

nes__final-fantasy.teaser: The beginning of a legend; the roots of the entire JRPG genre.
nes__final-fantasy.detail: The game that saved the failing Square (hence „Final“) and became the foundation of the biggest JRPG franchise. It defined the genre's conventions: choosing and combining the party's classes, side-view turn-based combat, an epic quest with a twist in time. Hironobu Sakaguchi bet everything on a single card and won.
nes__final-fantasy.article:
When the founding team at the studio **Square** was putting together its last chance in 1987, no one suspected that a name was being born that would go on to carry dozens of games across generations of consoles. The word „Final“ sounded like a farewell back then — instead it became the beginning of one of the greatest legends of the gaming industry.

Final Fantasy arrived with a simple but powerful idea: assemble your own party of heroes and lead them on an epic quest to save the world. At the start the player chooses and combines classes — fighter, black and white mage, monk, and others — and each combination fundamentally changes the style of play. The turn-based combat shown from the side, where your foursome faces off against the enemies, became one of the defining conventions of the entire JRPG genre.

For its time it was a remarkably sprawling adventure: you explore the world map, sail ships, fly an airship, and gradually uncover a story that isn't afraid even of a twist in time. This ambition, combined with the atmospheric music of composer Nobuo Uematsu, gave the game a depth few expected on consoles.

Legend has it that Square was on the brink of collapse at the time and Hironobu Sakaguchi bet everything on a single card. The game's success saved the studio and launched a franchise that to this day ranks among the most important in the whole field. The game reached the West in 1990 and helped open the door there for Japanese RPGs.

Today Final Fantasy is above all a historical milestone — the root from which the entire tree of modern JRPGs grew. To play it is to return to the basics, to the moment when the rules that still hold today were being written.

**Why play:** For an encounter with the roots of the entire JRPG genre and with a game that literally saved Square and founded an immortal franchise.

nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.teaser: The building blocks of the JRPG; the third game was a phenomenon in Japan.
nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.detail: The building blocks of the JRPG from Yuji Horii (design) and Akira Toriyama (characters, creator of Dragon Ball). The third game introduced a class system and a day/night cycle; in Japan it was such a phenomenon that its sale flooded the streets. The fourth introduced a chapter structure with multiple protagonists. In the West they were released as „Dragon Warrior“ due to a trademark dispute.
nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.article:
In Japan the story goes that when the third game came out, the streets filled with people heading off for their copy — a phenomenon so powerful that legends of schoolchildren and queues weave around it. Dragon Quest, released in the West at the time as Dragon Warrior, wasn't merely a game but a genuine cultural event.

Behind the series stand two names that together created the magic. Designer Yuji Horii gave the genre a comprehensible, accessible structure, and the artist Akira Toriyama, creator of Dragon Ball, dressed the world in unmistakably friendly, iconic characters and enemies. This combination made the Japanese RPG into something that could reach the masses.

**Dragon Warrior III** pushed the series fundamentally further. It introduced an elaborate class system, where the player assembles a party and changes its professions, and brought in a day and night cycle that changed both the world and the possibilities. It was a grand adventure whose scope and freedom astonished in 1988 and turned it into a national event in Japan.

**Dragon Warrior IV** then set off in a different direction — toward storytelling. It divided the game into chapters, each of which follows a different protagonist before the story lines converge. This structure gave the characters room and personality and foreshadowed the emphasis on storytelling that became typical for the JRPG.

By the way, the name „Dragon Warrior“ in the West didn't come about by chance — the original name Dragon Quest couldn't be used there due to a trademark dispute, and so the series long bore a different name than in the rest of the world.

**Why play:** To understand what the entire JRPG genre stands on — these installments laid the cornerstones, from the class system to chapter-based storytelling.

nes__tetris.teaser: The two best puzzle games on the console.
nes__tetris.article:
Some games age, others remain eternal — and Tetris belongs to that second, rare category. The falling tetrominoes, the filling playfield, and that unmistakable melody made it one of the purest and most perfect gaming ideas of all time.

Almost everyone knows the principle today: variously rotated combinations of four blocks fall from above, and your task is to rotate and slot them so they form solid rows. Every filled row vanishes and frees up space, but the pace speeds up inexorably. The genius of it is that you grasp the rules in a few seconds, but you spend a lifetime seeking mastery of them.

The NES version offers exactly what you'd expect from a home console — comfortable controls on a big screen, a clean presentation, and catchy music that makes it easy to lose track of time. It's the ideal game for a short break and for marathons alike, when you just keep telling yourself „one more try“.

Tetris has gone down in history as one of the most influential and successful games ever, and became a symbol of the entire puzzle genre. Its simple beauty transcends the boundaries of platforms, age, and languages — it works for absolutely everyone.

That's precisely where its strength lies: it needs no story, no characters, no effects. All it takes is falling blocks and your urge to assemble the perfect row.

**Why play:** Because Tetris is timeless puzzle perfection — one of the best games ever made, and on the NES it's in an ideal form for endless play.

nes__dr-mario.article:
What does a plumber do when he doesn't feel like playing with pipes? He cures viruses. Dr. Mario took the famous hero, dressed him in a white coat, and sent him into battle against colorful microbes — and the result is one of the most addictive puzzle games on the NES.

The principle is brilliantly simple and yet deep. Two-color pills fall from above into a bottle, and you rotate and stack them so that four of the same color in a row or column destroy the matching viruses. The bottle is full of colorful little critters, and your task is to wipe them out to the last one — except that new pills fall ever faster and space keeps running out.

The two-player variant is what makes Dr. Mario immortal. Duels side by side, where you make each other's lives difficult, can unleash passions and joy as fierce as any racing game. It's the kind of title the whole family easily takes turns at.

The music also contributes to the overall charm — the catchy tracks „Fever“ and „Chill“ burrow into memory and are themselves among the console's iconic melodies. The controls are instant and precise, so you quickly settle into a smooth, almost hypnotic rhythm of stacking.

Dr. Mario showed that Nintendo can turn even its mascots into the foundation of a great puzzle game, and it became a permanent part of its puzzle legacy, followed by further installments across consoles.

**Why play:** For instantly graspable but hard-to-put-down puzzle fun — and above all for the two-player duels that will put friendships to the test.

nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.teaser: Pure logic in an adorable package; jewels of the genre.
nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.detail: A puzzle series that a young Satoru Iwata (later president of Nintendo) worked on at HAL. You push blocks, wipe out enemies and solve one screen at a time — brilliantly designed puzzles that ramp up steadily. Based on the Japanese Eggerland series. Some of the finest puzzles on the NES.
nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.article:
No rush, no reflexes — just you, a single screen and a puzzle that looks innocent until you start racking your brain. Adventures of Lolo is pure logic wrapped in a cute coat, and it ranks among the very best the genre offered on the NES.

The series grew out of the Japanese Eggerland line and its premise is elegantly simple: you control the round blue hero Lolo, collect hearts on every screen, dodge enemies, push blocks and cleverly use the environment to reach the exit. Each room is a self-contained puzzle with a single correct solution you must uncover before you make an irreversible move.

The beauty of this series lies in its perfectly measured difficulty curve. You start with trivial tasks, but every new screen introduces fresh elements, combinations and pitfalls. The game never cheats you — everything you need is right in front of you, you just have to figure it out. That moment when the solution to a seemingly impossible room finally clicks is pure joy.

The development at **HAL Laboratory** involved a young Satoru Iwata, the later legendary president of Nintendo. Thanks in part to his contribution, the series has that distinctive blend of friendliness, cleverness and precise design that HAL's other titles would later become famous for.

The trio of games offers dozens upon dozens of well-thought-out puzzles and together they form a little puzzle textbook. It is ideal entertainment for calm evenings when you want to put your head to work, not your fingers.

**Why play:** For brilliantly designed, gradually escalating puzzles in an adorable package — some of the best logic games of the entire NES era.

nes__kickle-cubicle.teaser: Another great puzzle for your brain-teaser evenings.
nes__kickle-cubicle.detail: Kickle freezes enemies and builds ice bridges across chasms. Wario's Woods is famous as the very last licensed NES game in North America (1994, long after the SNES arrived) — an action puzzler where Toad lines up enemies and bombs. Both are clever logic games.
nes__kickle-cubicle.article:
Freeze an enemy into a block of ice and build a bridge across a chasm out of it — that is the idea Kickle Cubicle is built on, one of those lesser-known but all the more delightful logic games on the NES.

You control the grinning hero Kickle, who has one crucial ability: his breath turns enemies into ice blocks. He can then push these blocks around, use them to fill holes and build himself a path across the level. The goal is to collect the hidden items scattered on each screen and open the exit, with every room a self-contained puzzle requiring the right sequence of steps.

The charm of the game lies in the combination of cute, colourful graphics and a surprisingly thoughtful level design. What looks like a children's trifle can keep you genuinely busy — you have to work out where and when to freeze an enemy, how to position the ice bridges and how not to block yourself in. It is pleasantly contemplative logic without needless stress.

Kickle Cubicle belongs to the kind of titles that can easily get lost among the big names on a console, but that all the more reward anyone who gives them a chance. It offers exactly that calm, puzzle-solving fun you can spend a long evening with, never feeling that the game is cheating you.

If you enjoy puzzle games whose main asset is a clever idea and its clean execution, this icy classic deserves a place in your library.

**Why play:** For the original mechanic of freezing enemies and building ice bridges — clever, calm logic in an adorable package for laid-back puzzle evenings.

nes__wario-s-woods.article:
Wario's Woods holds one indisputable distinction: it is famous as the very last licensed game ever released for the NES in North America, in 1994 — long after its successor the SNES had already taken the throne. In its own right it feels like a charming farewell to an entire era.

Unlike most puzzle games, you do not stack or rotate blocks falling from above. Instead you directly control the character Toad, who moves around the playfield, picks up and shifts enemies and bombs, and lines them up so that the right combination destroys them. This action-driven, spatial perspective makes Wario's Woods an unconventional and refreshing entry in the genre.

The task is to clear the screen by joining enemies and explosives into rows and columns, while more critters keep dropping in from above. The blend of action-based movement and logical planning creates a pleasantly hectic rhythm — you have to think and react nimbly at the same time, a combination you won't meet in more static puzzlers.

And of course Wario is on hand as the antagonist, giving the game just the right playful, slightly mischievous atmosphere and the colourful presentation typical of Nintendo. It is a title that keeps an infectious energy and that „one more try“ pull.

Its historical context lends it a special charm: to play Wario's Woods today is to touch the last official moment of a famous console, the full stop after an era that defined home gaming.

**Why play:** For its unconventional action puzzling, where you yourself push enemies and bombs — and for its symbolic status as the very last licensed NES game in North America.

nes__kid-icarus.detail: Built on the same engine as Metroid and by the same team, but with Greek mythology and vertical climbing. Pit collects upgrades and climbs toward the sky. Difficult and underrated in its day; it only gained cult status and a comeback with the Uprising installment (3DS) and appearances in Smash Bros.
nes__kid-icarus.article:
From Greek mythology Nintendo borrowed a winged hero and sent him into hell — not downward, though, but upward. **Kid Icarus** ranks among the most challenging and, at the time, most underrated titles of the early NES, yet it grew out of exactly the same workshop and at the same time as the legendary Metroid.

That is no coincidence. The game was created at Nintendo R&D1 and runs on an engine related to Metroid's, only instead of the claustrophobic corridors of planet Zebes it offers a vertical climb toward the heavens. The hero Pit, an archer with angelic ambitions, climbs upward screen by screen, collecting upgrades and hearts he spends at merchants. That climbing is itself a mechanic: falling off the bottom of the screen means death, so every jump is a little drama.

What makes the game stand out is its uncompromising difficulty and its structure. Vertical stretches alternate with side-scrolling dungeons complete with maps and bosses, changing the pace and the demands on the player. Pit starts weak and vulnerable, but as the game goes on he grows strong enough that at the summit he faces the goddess of darkness herself. That arc — from helplessness to triumph — is part of why fans remember the game.

For many years Kid Icarus was more of a footnote in Nintendo's history, a curiosity in the shadow of the big brands. The comeback came later and grandly: thanks to Pit's presence in the **Super Smash Bros.** games and especially the modern installment **Kid Icarus: Uprising** on the 3DS, the brand gained a new cult status and a whole generation of new fans who traced their way back to the original.

Today the eight-bit original is regarded with respect — as a tough, ambitious game that took mythology seriously and did not go easy on players. It is a title for those who love a challenge and are not afraid to die.

**Why play:** A demanding, atmospheric platformer from Nintendo's golden era that stands at the roots of the metroidvania and today is finally reaping its deserved respect.

nes__blaster-master.teaser: Tank + on-foot, two play styles; ambitious hybrid.
nes__blaster-master.detail: An ambitious hybrid: you drive the SOPHIA tank in a side view and step out on foot into top-down caves (switching between two play styles). An interconnected, explorable world à la metroidvania. Great music and technical work from Sunsoft. It got a modern sequel (Blaster Master Zero).
nes__blaster-master.article:
Step out of the tank and go into a cave on foot — few eight-bit games gave the player such freedom of movement as **Blaster Master**. This is no ordinary platformer but an ambitious hybrid of two gaming worlds fused into a single interconnected adventure.

At its core is the SOPHIA tank, in which you roam sprawling levels from a side view — jumping, climbing walls, collecting upgrades that give the tank new abilities and open up previously inaccessible areas. But when you hit a door to the underground, you step out of the vehicle and continue on foot in a top-down view, in caves full of enemies and bosses. That switch between two distinct play styles was bold for its time and still works surprisingly smoothly today.

The world of Blaster Master is interconnected and explorable in a way that foreshadows the metroidvania genre — a new ability means a new route, a return to old places and the gradual uncovering of the map. The game is further driven by the craftsmanship of **Sunsoft**, one of the NES's technical elite: it looks great, moves smoothly and the soundtrack has swagger.

The story of a boy searching for his lost frog, which turns into a fight against mutants, is of course just a pretext — and in the West it got a different flavour than in Japan. But that hardly matters. What counts is the feel of playing: that moment when you first climb a vertical wall in your tank, or when you tensely head out on foot into an unknown cave.

Blaster Master earned a cult reputation and got a modern sequel, **Blaster Master Zero**, which dusted off the original concept for a new generation and confirmed that the tank/on-foot switching idea ages well.

**Why play:** A technically polished hybrid of action, exploration and metroidvania from the masters at Sunsoft — one of the most inventive games on the NES.

nes__little-samson.teaser: A rare, technically top-tier platformer; a collector's grail.
nes__little-samson.detail: Released at the very tail end of the NES in a tiny print run, so it is today one of the most expensive NES titles of all (a complete copy runs into the tens of thousands). You play four characters with different abilities (a boy, a dragon, a mouse, a golem) that you switch between. Technically top-tier and excellent to play — emulation is the only reasonable path.
nes__little-samson.article:
There is a handful of cartridges collectors crave like a holy grail — and **Little Samson** is one of them. It came out at the very tail end of the NES era in 1992, at a time when the world had long since turned its gaze to sixteen-bit consoles, and so it sold desperately few copies.

The result? Today it ranks among the most expensive NES titles of all, and a complete, well-preserved copy sells for the equivalent of thousands of dollars. But the price tag should not overshadow what matters: Little Samson is, in purely gameplay terms, an absolutely outstanding platformer, one of the most technically advanced titles of the entire eight-bit generation.

Its gameplay rests on a clever idea of four playable characters you switch between freely during play. The titular Samson can climb walls and ceilings, the dragon Kikira flies and breathes fire, the mouse Gamm slips through narrow gaps, and the stone golem Ko can soak up enormous punishment. Every level thus becomes a little puzzle: which character to deploy, where it pays to risk the dragon and where it is better to send in the durable golem.

The graphics are detailed and colourful, the animation smooth and the level design thoughtful — you can tell the creators at **Takeru** knew exactly where the NES's limits were and pushed them to the max. The soundtrack and overall craftsmanship hold to the same high bar.

The sad truth is that owning an original is unrealistic for most people today — the physical cartridge simply costs a fortune. Emulation is therefore not only a reasonable but practically the only way to play this gem at all. And it is worth it: beneath the legend of rarity hides a genuinely great game.

**Why play:** A technically top-tier platformer with four characters, now a legendary collector's grail — but one that thoroughly deserves attention on its own gameplay merits.

nes__sweet-home.article:
Before Resident Evil existed, there was **Sweet Home** — and anyone who knows the history of survival horror knows what a fateful role this eight-bit game played. It was created as a game tie-in to the Japanese horror film of the same name and became the direct blueprint from which Capcom later drew when building its famous horror series.

At first glance Sweet Home is an RPG with turn-based battles, but its true face is deeply horrific. Five filmmakers enter the haunted mansion of a deceased painter and begin uncovering its dark secrets. The game dissolves tension and fear into its mechanics in a way that was utterly unusual on the NES: characters can die permanently, and when they die, their story and abilities are gone for good.

Key is the system of five characters, each carrying a unique item — a lighter, a key, a camera, a vacuum, a first-aid kit — essential for solving puzzles and overcoming obstacles in the mansion. The player splits the group up and reunites it, because some doors and threats require specific equipment or several people. That tension, when you separate a vulnerable character from the group, is pure horror.

Blood, corpses and terrifying imagery pushed the boundaries of what the NES could dare to show, and that is precisely why the game never officially released in the West. It can be played in English only thanks to a fan translation the community lovingly created to make this pivotal piece of gaming history accessible.

The DNA of Sweet Home is visible today in every survival horror that uses limited resources, item puzzles and an atmosphere of fear instead of direct action. It is the root of the whole genre.

**Why play:** The forefather of survival horror and the direct inspiration for Resident Evil — an atmospheric horror RPG that, thanks to a fan translation, the West can finally play too.

nes__gimmick.teaser: A Sunsoft gem with physics and phenomenal music; rare.
nes__gimmick.detail: A technical gem for the twilight of the NES: advanced physics (you throw a star you can even ride and bounce off walls) and one of the best NES soundtracks ever, because the Japanese cartridge contained a special sound chip (FME-7). Difficult and rare; revered by connoisseurs, it got a modern remaster release.
nes__gimmick.article:
When a Japanese cartridge contains its own sound chip, you know the creators meant business. **Gimmick!** is Sunsoft's swan song on the NES and at the same time one of the most refined technical gems of the entire eight-bit era — a game that looks and sounds as if it mistook which generation it belonged to.

A visually adorable title in which you control the green creature Yumetaró, it hides a surprisingly deep and challenging game beneath its sugary shell. The central mechanic is a star the hero conjures above his head and throws — except this star obeys advanced physics. It bounces off walls, you can keep it in the air, ride it like a platform and combine jumps so it carries you to places you otherwise couldn't reach. Mastering these physics separates ordinary players from masters.

And then there is the sound. The Japanese version of the cartridge contained a special **FME-7** sound chip, thanks to which the game has one of the best and richest soundtracks ever heard on the NES. The tracks have a depth and melodiousness that simply outgrows the possibilities of the standard hardware.

Gimmick! is, however, also seriously tough and rare. It came out late and only in Japan (and to a limited extent in Scandinavia), so the original is a collector's rarity today. All the more is the game revered by connoisseurs, who see in it a perfect example of what an experienced studio could squeeze out of the NES when it cared neither for budget nor for the market.

Thanks to modern remaster releases Gimmick! is fortunately no longer the privilege of a handful of collectors — it has reached a wider audience that can finally appreciate its physics, its music and its unexpected difficulty.

**Why play:** An adorable but hard platformer with genius star physics and one of the best NES soundtracks — a technical peak of the era, now available outside the collector's vaults too.

nes__shatterhand.teaser: Underrated tough action; a great soundtrack.
nes__shatterhand.detail: Underrated tough action where a cybernetic hero fights with his fists and collects robot helpers summoned with combinations of icons. Excellent music (Natsume were masters of NES sound). A solid, forgotten gem.
nes__shatterhand.article:
Fists instead of guns, robots instead of henchmen — **Shatterhand** is exactly the kind of honest, uncompromising action that has been unjustly forgotten. Studio **Natsume** poured all its skill in here and created one of the best-playing and best-sounding action platformers on the NES.

The cybernetic hero fights his way through enemy bases mostly with his bare fists, which gives the game a pleasantly raw, punchy feel — no shooting from a distance, but tough close-quarters combat. The game is hard and does not go easy on you, but the controls are precise and fair, so you feel your defeats as your own mistake, not a cheat.

The most inventive mechanic is the robot helpers. By collecting icons marked A and B in certain combinations you summon different types of robots that fly around the hero and support him with fire or a strike. The right icon order unlocks stronger variants, so it pays to experiment and build the most useful companion for yourself. This layer adds a depth you wouldn't expect from otherwise straightforward action.

Where Shatterhand truly excels is the sound. Natsume were among the absolute masters of NES audio, and this game's soundtrack proves it — energetic, melodic tracks that drive the action forward and stay in your head long after you turn the console off.

Even so, Shatterhand remained in the shadow of more famous titles and to this day is more of a tip for the initiated. It is a forgotten gem that everyone who loves tough, well-tuned eight-bit action deserves to discover.

**Why play:** An underrated, tough action platformer with an inventive system of robot helpers and an excellent soundtrack from the masters at Natsume.

nes__mighty-final-fight.article:
Take the gritty arcade brawler **Final Fight** and convert it into a cute chibi style on the plain old NES? It sounds like a recipe for disappointment — and yet **Mighty Final Fight** is one of the loveliest and best-executed beat 'em ups on the eight-bit console.

Instead of a faithful port the NES hardware couldn't have handled anyway, the creators chose a different approach: they redrew the characters into cute, big-headed chibi proportions and rebuilt the game from the ground up to fit the console's capabilities. The result is a brisk, colourful beat 'em up that keeps the spirit of the original — Haggar, Cody and Guy fight through the city streets and pummel gangs of enemies — but adds its own juice.

Unlike the straightforward arcade templates, a progression element works here on top of that: defeated enemies give you experience, your character levels up, learns new strikes and grows stronger. That gives the game a pull and a reason to keep going that pure brawlers often lack.

Each of the three playable characters plays differently — Haggar is a slow powerhouse, Guy fast and nimble, Cody balanced — so the choice of fighter changes the pace and style of play. The animations are surprisingly fluid and the humorous, exaggerated visuals give the whole scrap a lighthearted, playful touch.

Mighty Final Fight came out late in the NES's life and is proof of how well developers learned to handle the console toward the end of the generation. For fans of the genre and the Final Fight series alike, it is a little gem worth discovering.

**Why play:** A cute chibi reinterpretation of an arcade legend with RPG progression and three distinct heroes — one of the best beat 'em ups on the NES.

nes__river-city-ransom.teaser: Beat 'em up with RPG progression and humour; a cult favourite.
nes__river-city-ransom.detail: An innovative mix of beat 'em up and RPG: you pummel gangs, but with the money from them you buy food and books that permanently raise stats and unlock new strikes. An open city, humour, co-op. Part of the Kunio-kun series; influential and cult.
nes__river-city-ransom.article:
What if a beat 'em up turned into an RPG? **River City Ransom** posed this question back in 1989 and answered it so cleverly that we still feel its influence today. This is not just another brawler — it is an open city where every punch pays off.

The foundation is, of course, the fighting: the duo of scrappers Alex and Ryan brawl their way through the city streets, pummeling gangs of youths. But defeated enemies leave money behind, and you spend it in shops scattered around the city. Food, books, potions — all of it permanently raises your stats and, best of all, unlocks entirely new combat strikes and special techniques. Little by little you grow from a weak youth into an unstoppable pummeling machine.

The city is open and explorable, you can move around it freely, hunting for shops and secret spots. That gives the game an unusual freedom and depth that linear brawlers never knew. Add to that the disarming humour, the slightly cheeky tone and the option to go through the entire city in two-player co-op — the fun multiplies.

River City Ransom is part of the sprawling Japanese **Kunio-kun** series by studio **Technōs**, which spawned dozens of sports and action spin-offs. This particular installment, though, became the most beloved and cult-revered in the West.

Its DNA — the combination of action with RPG progression, spending money on permanent upgrades, an open world — is found in countless later games. River City Ransom was simply timeless and inspiring in a way no one expected in 1989.

**Why play:** A genre-defining combination of beat 'em up and RPG with an open city, humour and co-op — an influential cult favourite that ages remarkably well.

nes__startropics.teaser: A Zelda-like from Nintendo for the West only; a nostalgic gem.
nes__startropics.detail: A Zelda-like adventure developed by Nintendo exclusively for the West (it never released in Japan). A young man named Mike, wielding a yo-yo as a weapon, searches for his kidnapped uncle on tropical islands. A famous puzzle required dipping the enclosed letter in water to reveal a code — a renowned example of „feelies“.
nes__startropics.article:
There is a Zelda-like adventure from Nintendo itself that never officially released in Japan — and you may never have heard of it. **StarTropics** was developed exclusively for the Western market and to this day ranks among the most endearing and nostalgic NES exclusives.

The story follows a young man named Mike, who sails to tropical islands to visit his archaeologist uncle — only for the uncle to vanish, kidnapped by mysterious forces. Mike sets off to find him, and his main weapon is, believe it or not, a yo-yo. This unusual weapon gives the battles a distinctive rhythm and charm that sets the game apart from other action adventures.

In gameplay terms StarTropics mixes exploration of villages and islands from a top-down view (à la Zelda) with dungeons full of puzzles, traps and battles. In the dungeons you also move across a grid of tiles, which adds a tactical touch — you have to think about where to step, because some tiles collapse or hide traps. The mix of exploration, action and puzzles is held together by a lovely tropical atmosphere and storytelling.

Most famous, though, is one particular puzzle. At a certain point the game required a code the player could obtain only by dipping the enclosed paper letter in water — only then did the hidden numbers appear on it. This physical „feely“ element, linking the box to the game, became a legend and, for emulation, understandably a nightmare for many a player.

StarTropics is remembered today with great affection as an unexpectedly personal, Western chapter in Nintendo's history — an adventure that deserves more attention than it usually gets.

**Why play:** A charming Zelda-like adventure with a yo-yo and a tropical atmosphere, developed by Nintendo for the West only — a nostalgic gem and a piece of gaming curiosity.

nes__recca-summer-carnival-92.teaser: A crazed bullet-hell shmup that pushed the NES hardware past its limits. A legend among collectors.
nes__recca-summer-carnival-92.detail: Created for a Japanese game competition, it is famous for how insanely it pushes the NES — more objects and bullets on screen than should have been possible, at bullet-hell pace. It was released in a tiny print run in Japan only, which makes it legendarily rare. A technical marvel among shmup collectors.
nes__recca-summer-carnival-92.article:
The NES was never supposed to be able to do this. The first time you boot up **Recca: Summer Carnival '92**, you feel as though the console might give up at any second — there are simply more enemies, projectiles and explosions on screen than eight-bit hardware was ever meant to handle. And yet it works, at a bullet-hell pace that bends the very laws of what was technically possible on the NES.

Recca was created for the Japanese Summer Carnival game competition, and that is the key to its character: it is a pure show of force, a demonstration of just how far the hardware can be pushed. The screen literally drowns in bullets and explosions, the pace is merciless, and the game demands both quick reflexes and the ability to read the chaos. For an eight-bit shooter, it delivers an experience you would have expected a generation or two later.

From a technical standpoint, Recca remains an object of admiration and study to this day. The developers at **Naxat Soft** found ways to work around the NES's limits on sprite counts and redraws, squeezing out a visual density you will not find anywhere else on the platform. As a lesson in understanding those limits — and in breaking them — it is a textbook case.

The game, however, shipped in an absolutely minuscule print run and in Japan only, tied to that competition. As a result it is legendarily rare today, and the original cartridge is among the most sought-after and expensive treasures in shmup collecting. For most players, then, emulation is the only sensible way to experience this technical marvel.

Recca: Summer Carnival '92 remains something of a myth among shmups — proof that talented programmers could coax miracles even out of an aging NES.

**Why play it:** A crazed bullet-hell shmup that pushed the NES hardware past its limits — a technical legend and a collector's holy grail whose sheer intensity you will not experience anywhere else on eight-bit.

nes__micro-mages.article:
Imagine taking a full-fledged platformer, cramming it into a mere 40 kilobytes, and having the result still rank among the best today's NES scene has to offer. That is exactly what Micro Mages pulled off — a project by the German studio Morphcat Games that became something of a textbook demonstration of what can be wrung out of the eight-bit Nintendo when the authors truly understand the hardware.

At the game's core is a brisk, precisely tuned platformer in which, as a little mage, you climb up a crumbling tower full of traps, monsters and cleverly designed passages. Jumps, wall bounces and pinpoint landings form the basis of a movement system that clicks within a few seconds. The game is built for smooth pacing and repetition, so death never frustrates enough to stop you wanting to try again right away.

What truly sets Micro Mages apart is its co-op. Up to four players can play at once on a single screen — an absolutely exceptional and technically demanding feat on the NES. Climbing the tower together, tossing each other up, blocking one another and occasionally knocking a friend down by mistake turns the experience into raucous fun reminiscent of the best moments of couch multiplayer.

The development context is fascinating in its own right. Morphcat Games not only released the game on a real cartridge but also documented their techniques in public materials on how to fit into extremely limited memory. That made Micro Mages a reference title for a whole new generation of creators developing for the NES decades after the end of its commercial era.

Culturally, it is one of the proofs that the eight-bit platform did not end as a collector's curiosity, but that around it lives a vibrant, technically skilled community capable of creating a game that would not embarrass any period title. For owners of modern retro hardware and emulators alike, it is the ideal entry ticket into the world of contemporary homebrew.

**Why play it:** A superbly controllable platformer with outstanding multiplayer for up to four players and technical execution that bends the possibilities of the NES.

nes__lizard.article:
Sometimes it happens that a new game for an old console feels more convincing than many a period original. Lizard is exactly such a case: a sprawling adventure for the Nintendo NES that blends platforming action with exploration and an ingenious mechanic built on a single, seemingly simple idea.

That idea is shoes. The main character can slip small lizards into various kinds of footwear, with each pair granting different abilities and opening new paths through an interconnected world. Ordinary walking thus becomes both a puzzle and a tool of discovery, as the player constantly ponders which combination to use to get further or uncover a hidden corner.

Lizard also does not follow the path of linear progression. The world is open to exploration, full of detours, secrets and moments where you decide for yourself where to go. This freedom gives the game an adventurous flavor rarely found in period NES titles, underscored by artistically inventive, at times dreamlike graphics.

In terms of development, this is a homebrew title created long after the end of the console's commercial life, yet it was also released in physical form on a cartridge. That makes it one example of how far the ability of contemporary authors to work with eight-bit hardware has advanced — creating a game with its own identity rather than merely a tribute to the old days.

Culturally, Lizard fits into the broader stream of the independent NES scene, which proves that a platform decades old can still host distinctive, creative works. For players who enjoy exploration and unconventional mechanics, it offers a pleasantly refreshing experience off the beaten path.

**Why play it:** An original adventure with an inventive shoe mechanic and an open world, showing the NES from an unexpectedly creative side.

nes__witch-n-wiz.teaser: Accomplished community titles; proof that the NES is alive.
nes__witch-n-wiz.detail: Accomplished community titles from the contemporary NES scene (puzzle-platformer, Tetris-like puzzle, platformer). Proof that the NES is today's liveliest homebrew platform — the tools and community are so mature that games comparable to period releases are being made.
nes__witch-n-wiz.article:
Is the Nintendo NES a long-dead platform? Witch n' Wiz is one of many proofs that the opposite is true. This puzzle-platformer comes from the contemporary community scene and ranks among the titles whose quality and polish could comfortably stand comparison with period games from the eighties and nineties.

In play terms, it is a thoughtful combination of puzzles and platforming movement. Instead of random action, the game relies on deliberate reasoning: each room is a small logical challenge where you must work out the right order of steps, use the environment and think through the consequences of your moves. Progress is divided into manageable segments, so the game nicely rewards patience and experimentation.

Witch n' Wiz stands out above all for how cleanly it is designed. The controls are intuitive, the difficulty rises smoothly, and the individual puzzles are built fairly, so when you fail, you know the mistake was on your side. That is crucial in puzzle games, and it is precisely here that the experience and instinct of the authors from today's homebrew community show.

Developmentally, the title fits into the wave of games being created for the NES in recent years thanks to sophisticated tools and an active community. It is precisely the availability of these tools and shared knowledge that is so great today that the NES may be the liveliest homebrew platform of all, one on which games comparable to period production are being made.

Culturally, then, Witch n' Wiz represents the phenomenon of an old console becoming a full-fledged creative platform for new authors. For fans of puzzle games and for those who want to see how far today's NES scene has come, it is a rewarding and cleverly designed piece.

**Why play it:** A fair, polished puzzle-platformer that is living proof of how strong and creative today's homebrew scene around the NES is.

nes__curse-of-possum-hollow.article:
Action-adventure on the eight-bit Nintendo has its own unmistakable charm, and The Curse of Possum Hollow manages to bring it back to life even today. This NES game bets on a blend of exploration, combat and gradual uncovering of the environment — the very recipe that once defined an entire era of adventure titles on this platform.

The player sets out into a mysterious world that must be explored bit by bit, solving obstacles within it and fighting a way forward. Here the action-adventure genre means it is not just about reflexes but also about orientation in the environment, finding routes and a sense of discovery. It is precisely this mix of action and exploration that keeps the player on edge and compels a return to places previously passed by.

Visually and in atmosphere the game draws on what the eight-bit hardware can do: bold color palettes, legible sprites and a compact world that feels cohesive. The platform's limitations thus become a style-defining element rather than a handicap, and they underscore the title's distinctive mood.

The Curse of Possum Hollow is the work of today's independent NES scene — a community of authors creating for this console long after the end of its commercial era. Many of these games are released on physical cartridges as well, thereby carrying on the original distribution format and appealing to collectors and enthusiasts of real hardware.

Culturally, it is another piece in the mosaic proving that the NES remains a living platform. For players who favor adventure titles with a retro touch but want to experience something new, it is an enticing offer that links nostalgia with fresh content.

**Why play it:** An action-adventure in the spirit of classic NES titles, combining exploration and combat with the atmosphere of a living homebrew scene.

nes__nebs-n-debs.article:
A space platformer for the Nintendo NES that looks as though it rolled off a period assembly line, yet was created much later. Nebs 'n Debs is a brisk action game that demonstrates on eight-bit hardware just how much energy and imagination can be packed into a seemingly simple genre.

The foundation is classic platforming action: jumping, dodging enemies and overcoming traps across levels. The game emphasizes precise movement and pacing, so every jump and every landing carries weight. As a result it maintains that pleasant balance between challenge and fun that the best NES platformers always had.

What makes Nebs 'n Debs stand out is its technical execution. The game exploits the NES's capabilities with a feel for detail, whether in smooth scrolling, colorful environments or legible animation. The result feels period-authentic and polished at once, testifying that the authors know both the possibilities and the limits of the platform well.

Developmentally it is a title from the contemporary homebrew scene which, like many others, was also released on a physical cartridge for real NES hardware. It thereby carries on the original distribution model and becomes part of a community that keeps the eight-bit console alive decades after its peak.

Culturally, Nebs 'n Debs illustrates that the NES today is not merely an object of nostalgia but also a platform for new creation. For lovers of fast platformers it is a pleasantly accessible piece that offers a period gameplay feel without coming across as archaic.

**Why play it:** A brisk space platformer with finely tuned controls and period-faithful execution, ideal for fans of classic NES action.

nes__from-below.article:
Falling blocks and a ticking clock: puzzle games of this type have the power to pull you in for hours on end, and From Below for the Nintendo NES brings that addiction back to the eight-bit screen. It is a puzzle title built on a clear principle and quick decisions — precisely what makes puzzle games so addictive.

In play it revolves around stacking and clearing elements, where you must react to a changing situation and plan ahead. The pace gradually speeds up, so what you manage calmly at first later forces you into split-second decisions. It is exactly this escalation of pressure that is crucial in puzzle games, and From Below works with it deliberately.

The title's magic lies in its accessibility. You grasp the rules in a moment, but mastering them at a higher level takes practice and foresight. This low barrier to entry and high skill ceiling are the mark of a well-designed puzzle game, one you will gladly return to for a better score.

From Below comes from today's independent NES scene, which gives the eight-bit console new life through modern tools and an active community. Similar titles are often released in physical form as well and prove that the arcade-puzzle genre feels right at home on this hardware even after decades.

Culturally, the game joins the proofs that the NES remains a fertile platform for creators and players alike. For fans of puzzle games seeking a quick, catchy challenge in a retro coat, it is a rewarding choice for both short and longer sessions.

**Why play it:** A catchy arcade puzzler with simple rules and rising pace that reminds you why puzzle games are so addictive.

nes__operation-wolf.article:
You step into the jungle, aim at the screen, and the world around you turns into a continuous barrage. Operation Wolf on the Nintendo NES is the home makeover of one of the most legendary arcade hits of the eighties, and even in its living-room form it keeps its raw, adrenaline-fueled DNA: you are a lone commando who must fight through a series of missions, free hostages and gradually smash an enemy operation across confusing terrain.

At the game's core is continuous horizontal scrolling, where the image slides on its own and you aim at targets with a movable cursor. On the NES, aiming was handled either by the classic controller combination or by the Zapper light gun, which was what really gave the game its true arcade stamp. The mechanic is brilliantly simple yet merciless: enemies dash out of the undergrowth, throw grenades, vehicles and helicopters roll in, and you must decide in a fraction of a second whom to take down first. Ammunition and lives are not infinite, so every shot carries weight and panic is your greatest enemy.

The original arcade machine from Taito, released in 1987, was groundbreaking above all for its controls. Built into the cabinet was a so-called positional gun styled as an Uzi submachine gun, which did not respond to light like ordinary light-gun pistols but instead sensed the position of the barrel. That allowed continuous fire and the feeling that you were really hosing the screen with bursts. This detail made Operation Wolf an instant sensation in arcades and defined an entire subgenre of arcade shooters, later followed by games such as Cabal, Beast Busters and the later rail shooters.

The home conversions, meanwhile, were enormous, and the NES version was among the more important ones because it brought the arcade experience into living rooms. Operation Wolf received ports to a whole array of systems of its time, from the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amiga computers to the PC Engine. It was precisely this ubiquity that made the title one of the best-known symbols of the militaristic action of the late eighties, when pop culture lived on films like Rambo — and Operation Wolf rode that wave perfectly.

The game's cultural footprint is unmistakable today. Operation Wolf is regularly cited as one of the milestones of the light-gun genre and as a title that showed intense, cinematic action can work even in a simple arcade form. For many players it was their first contact with shooting at the screen, and the memory of the Uzi's rattle and the enemies dashing out is etched into memory to this day.

On the NES the game had its specifics dictated by the console's hardware. The creators had to squeeze arcade action into the more modest capabilities of the eight-bit Nintendo, so the NES version comes across as somewhat more intimate than the blazing cabinet from the arcade. Even so, it kept its drive toward the goal, and in combination with the Zapper it offered home audiences something they had until then known only from arcades: real gun-aiming at the television screen. It was precisely this accessibility of the console conversion that formed an important piece of the puzzle, thanks to which Operation Wolf reached players who never made it to the arcade machine.

**Why play it:** For the raw, uncompromising adrenaline of eighties action and for the nostalgia of the days when all you needed was a gun, a screen and steady nerves.

nes__excitebike.article:
A few seconds are all it takes to understand why Excitebike etched itself into the memory of an entire generation of eight-bit players. The motorcycle races from left to right, dirt ramps and bumps pile up ahead of you, and with every jump you must judge the landing angle and the moment to hit the turbo before the engine overheats. It is pure, instantly understandable fun that grabs you at once and does not let go.

The game was made in Nintendo's workshop and was one of the titles that accompanied the launch of the Famicom console and later its Western release as the NES. Behind the design stands Shigeru Miyamoto — the same creator who gave the world Mario and Donkey Kong. Excitebike showed that even on limited hardware you could make a dynamic racing experience with a sense of speed and timing, where it is not about the finish line at any cost but about a smooth mastery of the track.

Mechanically the game rests on two things: working with the turbo and controlling the bike's tilt in the air. If you land badly angled, the rider wipes out and you lose precious seconds. The other rider and rivals on the track serve as obstacles that are easy to crash into. A great rarity for its time was the track editor, where players could build their own circuit from ramps, puddles and accelerators.

Excitebike's cultural footprint is unexpectedly long. The game received revivals and sequels across the decades, among them Excitebike 64 on the Nintendo 64 and the digital Excitebike World Rally. The track-editor motif and the characteristic starting run appear repeatedly in other Nintendo projects as nostalgic references.

Today Excitebike plays just as well as it once did. It is an example of how little it takes for a timeless game design when the rules are clear and the controls reward precision. A few minutes with a retro emulator or the original console are more than enough to understand why this motorcycle has held onto its cult status.

**Why play it:** An instantly graspable racing gem with a brilliant emphasis on jump timing and turbo that entertains even after decades.

nes__prince-of-persia.article:
One hour. That is how much time you have to fight your way from the dungeon up to the princess, held captive and threatened by the evil vizier Jaffar. Prince of Persia on the NES brings the famous cinematic platformer to Nintendo's eight-bit console and proves that a story of a race against time worked on any platform.

Jordan Mechner designed the original in 1989 with an emphasis on realistic character animation. Using a technique resembling rotoscoping, in which he transferred the filmed movement of a real person into the game, he achieved a fluidity of motion that was astonishing for the time. The prince runs, jumps, climbs and duels with a weight and inertia that give every step real risk. On the NES this animation carried over remarkably well.

The gameplay combines precise platforming sections with sword fights and deadly traps. Retracting blades, pits and vanishing tiles lie in wait at every step, and a single mistake means death. Added to that is the tension of the constantly running time limit, which turns each level into a puzzle where you must balance caution and speed. Sword duels demand timing of attacks, parries and retreats.

Prince of Persia is among the most ported games of its era, and the NES version is one of the many forms in which this classic reached players. The series later turned into one of the flagship brands of Ubisoft thanks to the three-dimensional Sands of Time trilogy, but the whole myth began with this anxious platforming run through the palace.

Today the eight-bit version is an interesting comparison with the other ports. It shows how strong the core game concept was, having survived conversion to so many different machines. For fans of the series and lovers of demanding platformers alike, it is a piece of gaming history that deserves attention.

**Why play it:** The eight-bit incarnation of the founding legend of cinematic platformers. A tense race against time where every mistake counts.

nes__bubble-bobble.article:
Two little dragons, endless bubbles and a hundred rounds full of enemies to trap. Bubble Bobble on the NES brings one of Taito's most beloved arcade classics to Nintendo's home console, and with it all the charm and surprising depth that made the game immortal.

You control the little dinosaur Bub, who can spew bubbles. When you catch an enemy in a bubble and pop it, you destroy the enemy and collect fruit or treasure. The whole game takes place on a single screen, and each of the many dozens of rounds is really a small puzzle in motion. What matters is the timing of your jumps, when you release the bubble, and the clever use of space. On the NES, moreover, two-player co-op works splendidly and is the heart of the whole experience.

Taito created Bubble Bobble in the mid-eighties and hit upon a flawless formula. The magic lies in the contrast between the adorable graphics and the harsh difficulty of the later rounds. The game became famous for its secrets and especially for the true ending, which you unlock only if you complete all one hundred rounds in two-player co-op. That made Bubble Bobble one of the first games to genuinely celebrate playing together at one screen.

The game's success gave rise to a whole family of titles including Rainbow Islands and Parasol Stars, and the little dragons Bub and Bob became iconic Taito mascots. Bubble Bobble influenced countless later arcade platformers and is still re-released today in modern collections and compilations.

The NES version is among the sought-after ones because it captures the game's original spirit well and co-op works excellently on it. It is pure joy of play — addictive and accessible, yet with enough hidden content for those who want to dig deeper.

**Why play it:** Addictive, instantly understandable and even better with two. Bubble Bobble on the NES is one of the finest co-op arcade games of its time.

nes__double-dragon.article:
The Black Warriors gang has kidnapped Marian, and only two brothers, kung-fu masters, can fight their way through the city streets to get her back. Double Dragon on the NES brings the legendary beat 'em up from Technos Japan to the eight-bit console and became one of the defining titles of the street-brawler genre.

The 1987 original rewrote the rules of arcade brawlers. It brought a rich repertoire of punches, kicks, throws and grapples, plus the ability to pick up weapons like a whip, a barrel, a knife or a rock and turn them against enemies. You advanced through levels full of ever-tougher opponents to the bosses at the end of each chapter. This formula laid the groundwork for later classics such as Final Fight and Streets of Rage.

The NES version earned a peculiar reputation. Because of the console's technical limitations, the game had to sacrifice the classic arcade-style co-op in which two players go through the story together. Instead, the NES port offered a solo campaign complemented by a separate competitive two-player mode and by an experience system where defeating enemies unlocks new punches and techniques. That gave the version its own distinctive identity.

Double Dragon became one of the most significant gaming brands of the eighties and grew into several sequels, an animated series and a live-action film. Its name became synonymous with arcade brawling and inspired an endless line of imitators. For many players it was the very first game in which they grasped the appeal of progressing through levels and dispatching enemies arriving in waves.

Today the NES version is interesting precisely for its differences from the arcade original. It is a distinctive take on the classic that is worth getting to know, whether you are a fan of the series or discovering the roots of the whole genre.

**Why play it:** The founder of the street-brawler genre in a distinctive eight-bit form with its own progression system and a competitive two-player mode.

nes__rainbow-islands.article:
This time you're not spewing bubbles, but rainbows. Rainbow Islands is a direct sequel to the beloved Bubble Bobble and brings its colorful, inventive idea straight onto Nintendo's eight-bit console. The little dragons have turned back into the boys Bub and Bob, and their new weapon and moving platform alike are vibrant, multicolored rainbows.

The gameplay principle is brilliantly simple yet deep. You create rainbows that serve at once as a weapon against enemies and as bridges you climb up. When you smash a rainbow above you, it falls down and can strike opponents beneath you. Unlike the statically conceived Bubble Bobble, here you progress upward, and the goal of each level is to reach the top, ideally before the rising water catches up with you.

Taito released Rainbow Islands at the end of the eighties, and the game became famous for its imaginative rainbow mechanic and its wealth of hidden secrets. Collecting colored diamonds in the correct order unlocks bonuses and secret endings, making the game a deeper experience than it might first appear. Thematically, each island offers a different setting, from an insect world to a toy kingdom, which brings the game to life visually.

Rainbow Islands became one of the pillars of the so-called Bubble Bobble series and, together with Parasol Stars, formed a trio of titles that Taito's little dragons hold as their family lineage. The game is prized for its combination of accessibility and surprising depth, and it still appears in retro collections and compilations to this day.

The NES version brings this colorful gem to a console where, despite technical limitations, it retains its distinctive playability and charm. For fans of Taito as well as lovers of clever arcade platformers, it's a title worth discovering.

**Why play it:** An inventive sequel to Bubble Bobble with a brilliant rainbow mechanic. A colorful, addictive platformer full of secrets to uncover.

nes__pac-man.article:
The yellow disc with an insatiable appetite for dots became one of the most iconic characters in the history of the entertainment industry, and the version for the Nintendo NES brought this arcade phenomenon right into living rooms. Pac-Man is the pure essence of arcade gameplay: a maze full of dots, four colored ghosts chasing you, and large energizers in the corners which, once eaten, flip the roles so that you can gobble up the ghosts for a while.

The original arcade machine was created by the Japanese company Namco and designed by a team led by Toru Iwatani, who wanted a game suitable even for a female audience at a time when shooters ruled the arcades. Inspiration from a pizza with a slice cut out gave rise to the shape of the main hero. The home conversion for the eight-bit Nintendo Entertainment System had to make do with weaker hardware and lower resolution, so the graphics are cruder than in the arcade, but the core of the game stayed faithful.

Pac-Man's magic lies in a simplicity you grasp in a second but only truly master after hundreds of games. Each of the four ghosts has its own behavior pattern, so experienced players can predict their movement and weave through the maze with surgical precision. Between levels there are short humorous animations, so-called intermissions, which in their day felt like little rewards for the player's persistence.

Pac-Man's cultural impact is enormous. The character appeared on T-shirts, in cartoon series, and in popular music, becoming a symbol of the golden era of video games from the early eighties. The franchise gave rise to dozens of sequels and variations, from Ms. Pac-Man to modern 3D versions, and the labyrinth-with-pursuers motif itself influenced countless other titles.

On the NES you can play Pac-Man as a comfortable home variant of a classic known even to people who never cared about video games. It's a title that works across generations and where just a few seconds are enough for even a complete beginner to grasp the rules.

**Why play it:** An immortal arcade classic you'll understand instantly and keep coming back to for that perfect chase through the maze.

nes__mega-man.article:
A blue robot in a helmet who can steal the abilities of the enemies he defeats. That's an idea so simple and brilliant at once that it grew into one of the most enduring gaming brands ever. And it all began right here, with the first installment of Mega Man on the NES.

The key mechanic remains iconic to this day: the game doesn't force you to progress linearly, but instead offers you a choice of several levels capped by a boss, a so-called Robot Master. After defeating him, you gain his weapon, which you can then use against other enemies. This creates a clever game of rock-paper-scissors, where discovering the right order of bosses is a puzzle in itself: each Robot Master is weak against someone else's weapon, and finding the optimal sequence is half the fun.

Added to this is an uncompromising but fair difficulty, precise jumping and shooting. After defeating all eight bosses comes a series of final fortresses belonging to Dr. Wily, Mega Man's eternal rival, where the game truly bares its teeth. Death never feels unjust; it's always your own fault, and that's exactly what makes overcoming the levels such a satisfying experience.

The game was created by Capcom and released in 1987. Behind its form stands a team led by Akira Kitamura and designer Keiji Inafune, who designed the final look of the character. In Japan the game bore the name Rockman; it received the name Mega Man only for the Western market, where it also became famous for the rather unfortunate box art of the American version, on which the main hero didn't resemble the game's robot at all and was clutching a pistol. This cover has today become a legendary target of jokes among fans.

The first Mega Man wasn't a commercial hit at first, but it laid firm foundations. Critics praised its original structure and playability, and the title gradually built up cult status. Capcom was given the confidence to continue, and it was the following installments that turned this brand into one of the pillars of the eight-bit era. Later installments simplified and made some elements more accessible, but the core conceived here has remained untouched to this day.

Culturally, Mega Man's significance is immeasurable. It defined an entire subgenre of action platformers, its chiptune music ranks among the best the NES sound chip offered, and the character itself became Capcom's mascot. The series expanded with dozens of installments and spin-offs like Mega Man X, Battle Network, and Zero, and the blue bomber even appears in crossovers across the gaming world, most recently in the fighting game Super Smash Bros.

**Why play it:** Experience the birth of a legend and try out the original system of stealing weapons from bosses that defined the entire action-platformer genre.

nes__mega-man-4.article:
When a series reaches its fourth installment, it risks running out of steam. Mega Man 4, however, showed that the blue robot still had plenty of energy in reserve and introduced one novelty that forever changed the way the player shoots on screen.

That novelty is the charged shot, the so-called Mega Buster. By holding the button you can build up a stronger blast, which fundamentally changes the pace of fights and your approach to ordinary enemies. Suddenly you don't have to frantically mash the button, but can meter out one crushing blow at the right moment, expanding the tactical palette. Otherwise the game honors the series' proven structure: eight Robot Masters, their levels to be chosen in any order, weapons gained after defeating bosses, and a final series of castles.

Mega Man 4 also offered a more elaborate story background with a new villain, Dr. Cossack, who initially confuses the player as to who the real mastermind of evil actually is. This plot with a false trail gave the series a somewhat more dramatic tone and showed that even a simple action platformer can work with surprise and twist. The levels are imaginatively themed, from mines through diving sections to Cossack's fortress in a snowy landscape.

It was released under the Capcom banner in 1991, at a time when the NES was already beginning to give way to the emerging sixteen-bit generation. The development team therefore had to squeeze the maximum out of the eight-bit hardware, and this showed in the detailed graphics and elaborate levels with rich backgrounds. The series was releasing at a very fast, practically yearly pace at that time, which testifies to how sought-after the brand was.

The charged shot became a permanent part of the blue robot's arsenal, and in later installments as well as the follow-up subseries Mega Man X, the game could no longer be imagined without it. It was one of those design elements that went from experiment to standard and defined the feel of gameplay for decades to come. That alone ranks the fourth game among the important milestones of the series.

There is consensus among fans that the fourth installment closes the first, classic phase of the series on the NES, even though two more installments were released on the console. Mega Man 4 holds a reputation as a solid, technically advanced installment that reliably serves up what you expect from the brand while adding a mechanic that proved utterly timeless.
